1 package active dry yeast
1 cup sugar
7 1/2 cups unbleached all-purpose flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
1 1/2 teaspoons ground mahlepi (see Notes)
1 teaspoon powdered mastic (mastiha; see Notes)
8 tablespoons (1 stick) butter, cut into small pieces, at room temperature
4 large eggs, beaten until frothy
Olive oil, for coating the dough and the baking sheets
1 egg yolk beaten with 1 tablespoon milk, for the wash
1/2 cup (about 2 ounces) sliced almonds
4 to 6 Red Eggs (recipe follows)
3 cups water
2 tablespoons red wine vinegar
2 teaspoons red food coloring
4 to 6 eggs (see Note)
Olive oil
Pour 3/4 cup of the milk into a bowl. Add the yeast, 1 tablespoon of the sugar, and 1 cup of the flour and stir to mix. Set aside in a warm place until lightly spongy all the way through, 30 minutes. Sift the remaining sugar, 5 cups of the flour, and the salt into a large mixing bowl. Add the mahlepi, mastic, and butter and briefly mix with your fingers. Make a well in the center and pour in the beaten eggs, yeast mixture, and remaining 3/4 cup milk. Knead with your hands until you can gather the mixture into a ball, 1 to 2 minutes. Dust a work surface with some of the remaining 1 1/2 cups flour. Transfer the dough to the floured surface and knead, dusting the surface with flour as needed, until the dough is smooth and elastic and no longer sticky, 10 minutes. Lightly coat the dough ball with oil and place it in a clean bowl. Cover the bowl with a cloth and set it aside in a warm place to rise until the dough has doubled in bulk, about 2 hours. Punch down the dough and transfer it to a lightly floured surface. Knead the dough again for 1 minute, then divide it in half. Cover the two portions with a cloth and let them rest until puffed up again, 20 minutes. Divide one of the portions of dough into thirds. With your hands, roll each third to form a rope about 20 inches long. When you have three ropes, braid them together. Pinch the ends together, tuck them under the braid and place the braid on a lightly oiled baking sheet. Repeat with the remaining portion. Set the braids aside, covered, in a warm place until doubled in bulk, about 1 hour. When you are ready to bake the bread, preheat the oven to 350F. Brush each braid with the egg wash. Press 2 or 3 red eggs into each braid and sprinkle the almonds over the top. Bake until very golden on the top and sides, 40 to 45 minutes. Remove from the oven and let rest on the baking sheets for 30 minutes. Slice and serve while still warm, or cool completely and wrap in plastic wrap. The bread will keep at room temperature for up to 1 week. Some cooks also add about 1 tablespoon coarsely grated orange zest to the dough. If youre one who loves warm bread, you can slice the loaf right after it comes out of the oven; the texture will be more spongy and cakelike than bread like. Workers sort and grade newly harvested mastic tears on Hios. As much as the lamb, eggs are an emblem of the Greek Easter. To Greeks, spring eggs denote sudden wealth, the fertility of the coming summer, abundance, and above all else, joy. Announcing Christs resurrection in a splendid splash of color, the eggs for the Easter bread are dyed red. In earlier days this was done in water tinted scarlet from beets, the first spring vegetable, or, where it was available, reddish wood. Now cooks generally use commercial packets of dye. The dyeing begins on Holy Thursday, before the solemnity of Good Friday wraps the week in black. Indeed, Holy Thursday is sometimes called Kokkinopefti, the day red falls, to symbolize Christs blood. Place the water in a saucepan just large enough to hold the eggs in one layer and bring to a boil over high heat. Add the vinegar and red food coloring. Reduce the heat to just below the boiling point, and gently, one at a time, add as many eggs as will fit in one layer. Cook for 15 minutes, adjusting the heat so the liquid simmers without boiling. Then remove the pan from the heat and set the eggs aside to cool in the liquid for at least 40 minutes. Lift the eggs out of the liquid and pat them dry on paper towels. Grease your hands with olive oil and rub the eggs to make them glossy. Use right away or store in the refrigerator for up to 3 days.

As smartphones continue to become an integral part of our daily lives, new research has shown that they are being used for an average of 20 years before being replaced.

The study by Ofcom, the UK's media regulatory authority, found that people keep their mobile phones for much longer than previously thought. In fact, the average person now keeps their phone for around eight years and six months, with some models lasting even longer.

This is largely due to the increasing popularity of smartphones, which offer a wide range of features and functions beyond just making calls and sending messages. From social media to streaming video, gaming, and more, smartphones have become essential tools for many people.

However, this also means that we are using our phones for much longer periods of time, leading to concerns about data privacy and security. With so much personal information stored on these devices, it is important to take steps to protect ourselves from potential threats such as hacking or identity theft.

Ofcom has called on manufacturers and retailers to be transparent about how long their products will last, and to provide users with clear information about the risks associated with keeping their phones for extended periods of time. They have also urged consumers to consider purchasing refurbished or second-hand phones instead of always buying new ones.

We examine how various components interact and assess their compatibility when combined in both synchronous and asynchronous configurations. The behavior of components is modeled using I/O-transition systems. Synchronous configuration involves executing shared output and input actions simultaneously, whereas asynchronous configuration employs unbounded FIFO buffers for message transfer. In both scenarios, we analyze compatibility concepts grounded on the principle that outputs from one component must be recognized as inputs by another. We differentiate between strong and weak forms of compatibility, with the latter permitting internal actions to be executed prior to message acceptance. We explore open systems and determine the conditions under which (strong/weak) synchronous compatibility is both sufficient and necessary for achieving (strong/weak) asynchronous compatibility. These conditions are shown to define half-duplex systems. Subsequently, we focus on verifying weak asynchronous compatibility for potentially non-half-duplex systems and present a decidable condition that guarantees weak asynchronous compatibility. We also investigate the completeness of this condition—specifically, whether its failure implies that the system is not weakly asynchronously compatible. Finally, we address deadlock-freeness and explore the relationship between deadlock-freeness in synchronous and asynchronous settings.

When mathematical or computational problems involve infinity, extending analysis and numerical calculations past it presents significant challenges. We propose that by applying suitable singular transformations—which can be detected computationally—it becomes feasible to surpass infinity and proceed to the other side, resulting in a well-behaved solution and normal computations. In our lumped ODE examples, the crossing of infinity occurs instantly; however, at the spatially distributed PDE level, the crossing may last for a finite duration, requiring the inclusion of conceptual and computational buffer zones where appropriate singular transformations are continuously and locally detected. These findings and associated methods could pave the way for a structured approach to circumventing infinity in broader classes of evolution equations. They also offer the potential to perform the necessary computations effectively and smoothly. Throughout our analysis, we present a regularization method through complexification and examine its effects on system behavior. Additionally, we consider a set of compactification transformations and their underlying principles.

Matt Williams insists he has no thoughts of quitting as national coach as a result of the power struggle currently gripping Scottish rugby.
The chairman, chief executive and three non-executive directors all departed in a row over the game's future direction. But Williams said: "I want to make it clear that I'm committed totally to Scottish rugby. "I've brought my family here and we've immersed ourselves in Scottish life. There's no way that I'm walking away." However, he attempted to steer clear of taking sides in the dispute. "I'd like to stress that the national team is separate to the political situation," he said.
"When you come to an undertaking like this and you are trying to make a difference then there are always people who will begrudge you, who are jealous and want to try to drag you down. "When you have that situation, you have to have the courage of your convictions to see it through. "There was some very unhelpful and uninformed comment that the national team had received a massive increase in budget at the expense of other parts of Scottish rugby and that is simply not the case. "Like all good coaches, you go and ask for an increase. But we were told in no uncertain terms that the financial situation did not allow that. "The idea that we are lighting cigars with £20 notes while the rest of Scottish rugby flounders is absolutely untrue. "We also attracted criticism because of the number of days players spent with the national team. "But let me give you the truth. Our Irish counterparts, whom we have to compete with in a few days' time, had 70 days together at the summer. "They are currently in camp now and they will have another 21 days in camp before the Six Nations. "That means they will have 91 days away from their club from July until the Six Nations. We, on the other hand, will have 16. "There must be a win-win philosophy and attitude within Scottish rugby and that is what we are after - both groups winning, not competing."

Given a 3D surface defined by an elevation function on a 2D grid as well as
non-spatial features observed at each pixel, the problem of surface
segmentation aims to classify pixels into contiguous classes based on both
non-spatial features and surface topology. The problem has important
applications in hydrology, planetary science, and biochemistry but is uniquely
challenging for several reasons. First, the spatial extent of class segments
follows surface contours in the topological space, regardless of their spatial
shapes and directions. Second, the topological structure exists in multiple
spatial scales based on different surface resolutions. Existing widely
successful deep learning models for image segmentation are often not applicable
due to their reliance on convolution and pooling operations to learn regular
structural patterns on a grid. In contrast, we propose to represent surface
topological structure by a contour tree skeleton, which is a polytree capturing
the evolution of surface contours at different elevation levels. We further
design a graph neural network based on the contour tree hierarchy to model
surface topological structure at different spatial scales. Experimental
evaluations based on real-world hydrological datasets show that our model
outperforms several baseline methods in classification accuracy.

Internet search engine users constitute a diverse group, combining both simplicity and sophistication, according to a study on search behavior. The Pew Research Center's report highlights that 87% of users typically find what they need when using a search engine. It also indicates that many struggle to distinguish between paid and organic search results. The report notes that 84% of internet users regularly use Google, Ask Jeeves, MSN, and Yahoo. Approximately 50% of respondents stated they would lose trust in search engines if they learned about hidden pay-per-result information. On average, users spend around 43 minutes monthly engaging in 34 searches and view 1.9 pages per session. About 36% of respondents conduct searches weekly, while 29% do so occasionally. For 44% of those surveyed, the information sought is vital and must be obtained. 

Users often exhibit loyalty toward search sites, preferring one or two platforms once they establish trust. According to Pew Research, 44% use only one engine, 48% use two or three, and 7% consult more than three. Tony Macklin from Ask Jeeves noted that preferences vary due to how sites collect data, leading to differing results for the same query. While half of respondents said they could obtain similar info through other methods, 17% claimed they wouldn't miss search engines if they disappeared. The remaining 33% couldn't live without them. Over two-thirds (68%) believed the results were fair and unbiased.

Six corn on the cob, fresh as possible  
¼ cup olive oil  
¼ cup sliced onion (or scallions)  
6 tablespoons butter (check compound butter above)  
Pull the husks down to the bottom of the corn without removing the husks. Remove the silk. Place the corn in a sink or pot filled with ice-cold water. Let the ears soak in the ice-cold water for at least two hours. Dry the ears thoroughly. Rub oil on the kernels and place a few slices of onion on the cobs, covering with the husks. Preheat the smoker to 225°F with good smoke, such as mesquite, fig, hickory, apple, etc. When ready, place the corn in the smoker, leaving a bit of space between each ear to allow smoke to circulate. Alternatively, use a gas grill by placing wood chips in foil with a small hole punched for smoke to escape. Once smoke begins, reduce the heat to 225°F. Cook the corn over indirect heat. A good time to prepare compound butter as described above. After about 30 minutes of smoking, take the butter you made and carefully scoop a teaspoon of it under the husk of each ear, coating as much of the exposed ear as possible. Repeat this process 30 minutes later. Continue smoking for another 30 minutes. Enjoy!

Vanilla Bean Rooibos Ice Cream
1 cup Whole Milk (avoid ultra-pasteurized)
2 cups Heavy Cream (avoid ultra-pasteurized)
2 tablespoons Organic Rooibos Tea Leaves
1 Madigascar Vanilla Bean, split and seeds scraped
3 tablespoons Honey
6 Large Egg Yolks
1 tablespoon Amaretto Liquer
3/4 cup Chopped Raw Almonds
Dulce de Leche
1 quart Whole Milk (avoid ultra pasteurized)
1 cup Sugar
3 tablespoons Honey
1 Vanilla bean, split and seeds scraped
1/2 teaspoon baking soda
Place the milk, sugar, vanilla bean, and honey into a medium saucepan, over medium heat. Bring the mixture just to a simmer, stirring occasionally to dissolve the sugar, and remove from the heat. Add the rooibos tea leaves, cover, and steep for 1 hour (NOTE: the long steep is critical for the best flavor). Add one cup of the cream to the tea/milk base, and warm the mixture (do NOT boil). Strain to remove the rooibos leave and vanilla bean (but don't worry if there are a few leaves remaining (they will be strained again). Discard the rooibos leaves; rinse and retain the vanilla bean. Set aside the remaining one cup of heavy cream in a medium bowl with a strainer on top. In a medium mixing bowl whisk the egg yolks until they lighten in color. Gradually add the warm cream base to the eggs. Temper the cream mixture into the eggs by gradually adding small amounts, until the remainder is incorporated. Return the egg and cream mixture to the saucepan and place over low heat. Continue to cook, stirring frequently, until the mixture thickens slightly and coats the back of a spoon and reaches 170 to 175 degrees F. Strain the mixture into the one cup of cream previously set aside. Return the previously used vanilla bean to the mixture and place into an ice bath for 30 minutes. Place the mixture into the refrigerator for 4 to 8 hours or until the temperature reaches 40 degrees F or below. Remove the vanilla bean, pour the cooled cream mixture into an ice cream maker. Add one teaspoon of amaretto and process according to the manufacturer's directions. This should take approximately 25 to 35 minutes. In the last 5 minutes, add the raw almonds to incorporate (this step can be skipped if you don't care for nuts). Scoop the ice cream into a freezer proof container in sections, layering spoonfuls of the (refrigerated) Dulce De Leche between the layers, swirling to create a random pattern. Freeze for 3 to 4 hours to allow the ice cream to harden. Combine the milk, sugar, honey, vanilla bean and seeds in a large, 4-quart saucepan and place over medium heat. Bring to a simmer, stirring occasionally, until the sugar has dissolved. Once the sugar has dissolved, add the baking soda and stir to combine. Reduce the heat to low and cook uncovered at a bare simmer. Stir occasionally, but do not re-incorporate the foam that appears on the top of the mixture. Continue to cook for 1 hour. Remove the vanilla bean after 1 hour and continue to cook until the mixture is a dark caramel color and has reduced to about 1 cup, approximately 1 1/2 to 2 hours. Strain the mixture through a fine mesh strainer. Store in the refrigerator in a sealed container until thoroughly cooled.

More than 5.2 million Germans were out of work in February, new figures show.
The figure of 5.216 million people, or 12.6% of the working-age population, is the highest jobless rate in Europe's biggest economy since the 1930s. The news comes as the head of Germany's panel of government economic advisers predicted growth would again stagnate. Speaking on German TV, Bert Ruerup said the panel's earlier forecast of 1.4% was too optimistic and warned growth would be just 1% in 2005.
The German government is trying to tackle the stubbornly-high levels of joblessness with a range of labour market reforms. At their centre is the "Hartz-IV" programme introduced in January to shake up welfare benefits and push people back into work - even if some of the jobs are heavily subsidised. The latest unemployment figures look set to increase the pressure on the government. Widely leaked to the German newspapers a day in advance, they produced screaming headlines criticising Chancellor Gerhard Schroeder's Social Democrat-Green Party administration. Mr Schroeder had originally come into office promising to halve unemployment.
Still, some measures suggest the picture is not quite so bleak. The soaring official unemployment figure follows a change in the methodology which pushed up the jobless rate by more than 500,000 in January. Adjusted for seasonal changes, the overall unemployment rate is 4.875 million people or 11.7%, up 0.3 percentage points from the previous month. Using the most internationally-accepted methodology of the International Labour Organisation (ILO), Germany had 3.97 million people out of work in January. And ILO-based figures also suggest that 14,000 new net jobs were created that month, taking the number of people employed to 38.9 million. The ILO defines an unemployed person as someone who in the previous four weeks had actively looked for work they could take up immediately.

We propose Deep Neural Network (DNN)-based image analysis technique to segment raw RGB images taken of thin polished concrete samples under a digital optical microscope. Deep learning is gaining significant popularity in computer vision. We employ a state-of-the-art fully convolutional DNN (FCN) to extract semantic image segmentation of the microscopic RGB image. The network is trained on our custom-annotated concrete microscopy set (CS-Concrete Microscopy). Using the FCN-based semantic segmentation approach provides several key advantages in concrete petrographic image analysis. First, the resulting segmentation masks make it easier to interpret the images by automatically selecting the desired elements of interest and removing irrelevant information. Second, DNN-based segmentation enables precise measurement of petrographic image features and avoids the tedious process of manual human annotations that are highly susceptible to human subjectivity. To show the utility of our deep learning image analysis framework, we developed a quantitative segmentation evaluation metric, called Segmetric Index of Fidelity (SiF) for our CS-Concrete Microscopy. The segmentation metric is designed to evaluate the segmentation quality of the model on an unbiased test dataset. We found a correlation between the SiF score and the accuracy of automatic segmentation of microscopic image features. The automatic segmentation approach using SiF has the potential to significantly reduce time and effort of manual microscopic image analysis.
The paper is authored by a team of researchers/scientists from the Civil and Environmental Engineering Department at the University of Wisconsin–Madison, the Wisconsin Center for Advancing Research in Transportation, the Department of Engineering Professional Development, the Department of Civil Engineering at Pohang University of Science and Technology, and from Korea Research Institute of Standards and Science (KRISS).
While the research paper appears to suggest that deep learning-based image recognition/ segmentation is better (objective) and more reliable, it's unclear to me why one cannot just measure concrete with digital callipers. It doesn't look like these researchers did a comparative study of the various image segmentation techniques on a standard dataset containing different variations of the images in their dataset. But then again, the study wasn't meant to be a comparison and may have other benefits.
One could also argue that while deep learning-based image segmentation is objectively better, it is also more expensive as it requires expensive deep learning-based AI

3 eggs  
2 cups water  
3 cups low-sodium chicken broth  
2 boneless chicken breasts  
11 garlic cloves  
1 teaspoon salt  
2 bay leaves  
1 teaspoon olive oil  
6 tablespoons grated parmesan cheese  
6 thin slices of country-style French bread  
1 tablespoon herbes de Provence  
1/2 teaspoon dried lavender  
1/2 teaspoon dried rubbed sage  
dried parsley  
ground black pepper  
olive oil, for toasting  

Pour the water and broth into a deep pot with the salt. Peel and crush 10 of the garlic cloves (using the base of your glass measuring cup), then add to the broth. Add the bay leaves and 1 teaspoon of olive oil. Cook for 15 minutes on medium-high heat. Cut the chicken into pieces and stir them into the soup along with all the herbs except the parsley. Peel and finely dice the remaining garlic clove and add to the pot. Continue cooking for about 10 more minutes until the chicken is fully cooked. Meanwhile, brush both sides of the bread slices with olive oil and cook them on medium heat until golden. (Alternatively, you can bake them.) Set the toast aside and fry each egg individually. Sprinkle with parsley and black pepper. Set these aside. Bring the soup to a boil for 5 minutes, strain it into a bowl, and return the broth to the pot. Rinse the herbs from the chicken pieces and add them back into the soup. Remove all other solid ingredients. To serve, place 2 slices of toast in the center of each wide, shallow bowl. Sprinkle 2 tablespoons of Parmesan cheese over each. Pour the soup over the bread and cheese, then top with an egg. Sprinkle with parsley and serve hot. (Eat immediately, or the bread may become soggy.) Serve with fresh apple slices and lightly steamed broccoli or asparagus tips.

Ingredients:

- 4 large potatoes, peeled and cubed
- 1 large onion, chopped
- 2 cloves garlic, minced
- 4 cups low-sodium chicken broth
- 1 cup skim milk
- 1/2 cup low-fat sour cream
- 1/2 teaspoon salt
- 1/4 teaspoon black pepper
- 1/4 teaspoon paprika
- 2 tablespoons chopped fresh chives
- 1/2 cup shredded low-fat cheddar cheese

Instructions:

1. In a large pot, combine the potatoes, onion, garlic, and chicken broth. Bring to a boil over high heat.

2. Reduce the heat to medium-low and let it simmer until the potatoes are tender, about 15-20 minutes.

3. Use an immersion blender to puree the soup until smooth. If you don't have an immersion blender, you can transfer the soup to a regular blender in batches and puree it that way. Just be careful as the soup will be hot.

4. Return the soup to the pot (if you used a regular blender) and stir in the skim milk, low-fat sour cream, salt, pepper, and paprika. Heat the soup over medium heat until it's heated through.

5. Ladle the soup into bowls and top each serving with a sprinkle of chives and shredded low-fat cheddar cheese.

6. Serve the soup hot with a side of crusty bread if desired.

This Creamy Potato Soup is low in fat but high in flavor. It's the perfect comfort food for a cold day. Enjoy!

An increase in the number of students from southern regions applying to Scottish universities has been noted. However, Lifelong Learning Minister Jim Wallace emphasized that this trend would not lead to Scottish students being excluded. Between January 2005 and the prior year, applications from England and Wales grew by 17%, reaching 27,700. Concerns existed about a surge in "fee refugees" attempting to circumvent annual tuition fees of up to £3,000 in England. In June 2005, Mr. Wallace proposed raising tuition fees for English students attending Scottish universities by £2,000 to deter a potential cross-border influx, though a specific figure has not been finalized. The legislation for implementing top-up fees in England is scheduled to take effect in autumn 2006, ensuring that students starting before that date will not incur extra costs.

The data was disclosed by the admissions service Ucas. Universities Scotland, representing university leaders, stated that the rise in applications does not indicate Scottish students are disadvantaged. Director David Caldwell mentioned that some students might apply to avoid potential increases in English university fees, but this is not a significant factor. He explained that students choose Scottish universities because they perceive them as high-quality, offer appealing programs, and view Scotland as an attractive location. They are aware that starting in 2006, they may face top-up fees if enrolling in an English university, which could be a reason for the increased applications. Nevertheless, it is not expected that thousands more students from England will study in Scotland. Mr. Wallace concurred, stating the figures must be assessed within context. He noted that when applications were converted into numbers, the context was considered.

Dough:
2 cups quick-cooking rolled oats  
1/4 teaspoon salt  
1 1/2 teaspoons baking powder  
1 cup brown sugar, lightly packed  
1 1/2 cups all-purpose flour  
1 cup margarine or 1 cup butter  

Fillings:
2 tablespoons cornstarch  
1 cup granulated sugar  
1 large egg, beaten  
3 cups chopped fresh rhubarb or 3 cups frozen rhubarb  
1 cup canned crushed pineapple, drained  
1 teaspoon cinnamon  

Dough Preparation: In a medium mixing bowl, combine quick-cooking rolled oats, salt, baking powder, brown sugar, and all-purpose flour. Mix well. Add margarine or butter and use a fork or pastry blender to mix until crumbly. Transfer half the mixture to a 9x12 inch oven-proof casserole dish and press it down with a spatula. Reserve the remaining mixture for the topping.

Fillings Preparation: Preheat oven to 350°F. In a medium bowl, mix cornstarch and granulated sugar. Combine beaten egg with the mixture and mix until smooth. Add chopped rhubarb, crushed pineapple, and stir well. Pour the mixture over the crumbly dough in the casserole dish. Sprinkle with cinnamon. Top with the remaining crumbly mixture. Bake for 45–50 minutes or until lightly browned. Let cool slightly before serving. Serve with ice cream or whipped cream.

In the future  
I foresee what will happen.  
The earth, which was once asleep,  
Will rise and search for its creator.  
The barren land will become a gentle garden.  
In the southern region,  
Where summer never fades,  
Lively Lyca lived.  
Seven summers ago,  
Lively Lyca spoke,

Sweet sleep came to me  
Under this tree;  
My father and mother wept.

Lost in the desert's vastness,  
Is your small child.  
How can Lyca sleep?  
If her mother weeps.  
If her heart is troubled,  
Let Lyca awaken;  
If my mother sleeps,  
Lyca will not weep.  
Frowning at night,  
Over this bright desert,  
Let the moon appear.  
While I close my eyes.  
Sleeping Lyca lies:  
The beasts of prey,  
Coming from deep caves,  
Watched the girl sleep.  
The king-like lion stood,  
And the pure virgin viewed.

Over the sacred ground:

The Ambedkar cartoon sparked significant controversy in the Indian Parliament on May 11, 2012. Both houses of Parliament were suspended that day due to the heated debates among the opposing factions. The matter was brought before the Lok Sabha by Thirumavalavan, a member of the Tamil Nadu Legislative Assembly. Initially, he was refused permission to address the assembly on the issue. Subsequently, he presented a copy of the contentious cartoon, which depicted former Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru holding a whip while Dr. B. R. Ambedkar drove a snail, symbolizing the Indian Constitution. The Scheduled Tribes and Scheduled Castes viewed the cartoon as offensive. The book containing the cartoon was published by NCERT under the guidance of the Ministry of Human Resources during the UPA government led by Sonia Gandhi. Later, the HRD Minister, Kapil Sibal, apologized for the incident, and NCERT was requested to remove the cartoon from its textbooks.

"Dave at Night" is a novel by Gail Carson Levine about a boy named Dave who is sent to live at the Hebrew Home for Boys in New York City in the 1920s. Dave is unhappy at the home and runs away, but is soon recaptured. He then decides to make the best of his situation and befriends some of the other boys at the home. Dave also becomes interested in the theater and starts to perform in the home's talent shows. One night, Dave sneaks out of the home to see a vaudeville show and is caught by the police. He is then sent to live with his grandparents, who are much stricter than the Hebrew Home. Dave eventually runs away from them as well and ends up living on the streets. He is eventually taken in by a kindly woman named Mrs. Rosen, who helps him get a job at a local theater. Dave eventually becomes a successful actor and is able to help Mrs. Rosen and the other boys at the Hebrew Home.

Marigold Lesley is an imaginative young girl whose father died before she was born. She grew up at her paternal relatives' estate, Cloud of Spruce. Marigold's family includes her loving but bossy mother, steely Young Grandmother, shrewd Old Grandmother, her Uncle Klondike who is a former sailor, and her Aunt Marigold, a doctor who saved Marigold's life as a baby. Because of that, the Lesleys named Marigold after her Aunt, and Uncle Klondike married her. These people made Marigold's life mostly pleasant and carefree, but she nonetheless had her share of adventures, fancies and troubles, many related to the peculiar environment she grew up in. The book relates Marigold's seemingly incurable jealousy of her father's first wife, Clementine; an encounter with a Russian princess; several attempts to be "good"' and a surprising cooking triumph. One long-lasting product of Marigold's imagination was Sylvia, her imaginary playmate whom she loved dearly and who took the place of many real-life friends for her. But as Marigold grew up and began having trouble with boys, she eventually had to say goodbye to Sylvia and her childhood.

By Edna St. Vincent Millay

Among the many hundred thousand people of Paris,
There is one who is quite unusually fair,
And when I saw her for the first time I felt uneasy,
As though I knew not what to do or where to turn.

It was not her eyes, though they were sweet and mild;
It was not her mouth, though the lips were fresh and red:
It was not her cheeks, though they were soft and warm;
It was not even he breast, though it was beautiful and round.

It was her hair: oh, glorious, glossy stuff!
It gleamed and it shone, a rich golden brown,
The glory of Youth, the joy of Summer's day,
And my heart stopped, and I forgot to run.

And then I knew 'twas not her hair alone,
But all of her body, and her spirit as well,
That made me know I had never seen anyone
Who looked, or felt, or thought, as she did.

And so I loved her, though I knew it all along,
From the moment that I first set eyes on her sweet,
Dear face, and her lovely, perfect body,
I loved her, and every day I love her yet.

But what is the use of talking about love?
For Heaven knows, in this dull world Love's dreams are vain,
And so I shut my eyes and dream about her none,
But live and work, and pray for a better time.

And though there were a million other girls
Just as lovely as she is anywhere,
I know that in all the world there is only one
Who is exactly like she is, and that is she.

And when I die, I will surely go to her,
For Death could not come between us, were it tried,
And so I have no fear of dying suddenly,
For I shall only be going to her side.

Though she will not know it, unless God should will
That women here on earth should have a soul as men,
Still, when I reach the other side, and leave this world of sin,
I'll find her waiting, and tell her all.

About how much I love her, and learn from her lips
The story of her life, and what makes her so sweet:
I'll ask

Gordon Brown is to freeze petrol duty increases, fund a £1bn package to avoid big council tax rises and boost childcare and maternity leave.
In an upbeat pre-Budget report, he slightly increased borrowing but insisted economic targets would be met. The chancellor also hailed the longest period of growth in UK "industrial history" but denied he was "gloating". But Oliver Letwin, for the Tories, attacked government red tape and debt, dubbing Mr Brown "Sir Wastealot".
The shadow chancellor said Mr Brown's "golden rule" had "turned to dross in his hands" and said he was borrowing to spend, not invest, with predicted debt over the coming years totalling £170bn. Mr Letwin told MPs: "The tide is going out on the chancellor's credibility. He is spending, borrowing and taxing so much because he is not getting value for taxpayer's money."
Vincent Cable, for the Liberal Democrats, accused Mr Brown of ducking tough choices.
He said: "Last week the prime minister gave us the politics of fear; this week the chancellor has offered the economics of complacency. "There are serious challenges ahead from the falling dollar and from the rapid downturn in the UK housing market and rising personal debt. But they have not been confronted." Mr Brown rejected the Lib Dem's call to open up the government's books to the National Audit Office, saying decisions on tax and spending should be made by ministers. Some economists say his forecasts on public finances are wishful thinking. BBC economic editor Evan Davis said the figures were plausible but also a gamble.
Mr Brown's insistence he was not "gloating" was a pointed rebuttal of a warning from new European Commissioner Peter Mandelson. In his speech, he set out a 10-year childcare strategy for if Labour wins the next election.
It includes a £285m cash injection to extend paid maternity leave from six months to nine, with parents able to transfer leave from the mother to the father. He also promised to increase free nursery education for three and four-year-olds to 15 hours from April 2007. And funds would be provided to keep schools open from 0800 to 1800GMT to look after children while their parents were at work. Taken together, the measures would create a "welfare state that is truly family-friendly for the first time in its history", said Mr Brown. He also announced a cash hand-out for older pensioners, with payments of £50 for the over-70s as part of the winter fuel allowance. In a move ministers say should keep council tax rises below 5% next year, the chancellor said he was providing an extra £1bn for local councils. The money is expected to come from government departments such as health and education.
Mr Brown said he was set to meet his two fiscal rules - to borrow only to invest and keep debt "low and sustainable" - both in this economic cycle and the next. Borrowing figures for 2003/4 are £35bn - £2.5bn less than the £37.5bn predicted in March's budget, as already announced by the Office for National Statistics. Borrowing is tipped to fall to £31bn by 2005/06 - but that is still £2bn more than Mr Brown predicted in his March budget. Inflation would be 1.75% next year and 2% in the years to follow, Mr Brown forecast. He also pledged an extra £105m for security and counter-terrorism. Business groups have welcomed efforts to improve competitiveness and invest more in skills and innovation. But there worries about the costs of more family-friendly working. Simon Sweetman, from the Federation of Small Businesses, said: "The proposals on maternity leave have clearly been made with a general election in mind and with little thought to the impact on small employers."

Here is the abstract for the academic paper titled "A 2D dilated residual U-Net for multi-organ segmentation in thoracic CT":

Abstract: We present a 2D dilated residual U-Net for multi-organ segmentation in thoracic CT scans. Our network is designed to address the challenges of segmenting multiple organs in thoracic CT, which often have complex shapes and overlapping structures. The key innovation in our network is the use of dilated convolutions, which enable the network to capture more context and details from the input images. We also introduce a residual connection module that facilitates the training process and improves the performance of the network. Our network is trained on a large dataset of thoracic CT scans and evaluated on the publicly available MICCAI 2017 Multi-Organ Segmentation Challenge dataset. We achieve competitive results on the challenge dataset and demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in segmenting multiple organs in thoracic CT.

The sachem (sakim, sagamore, sagamo, sahe) was the chief or head among the indigenous people of New England. The title was used during the 17th and 18th centuries. According to the Oxford English Dictionary the word is a corruption "by folk etymology" of the phrase "by and by chief", in imitation of the Algonquian expression for it, meaning "Great Sachem" or "Head-Man-By-And-By" (cf. Byram).
The English word "sachem" derives from the earlier pronunciation "sagamore".
The title Sachem was typically used for the leaders of a given sachemdom or wampum belt. Wampum belts were similar to the Roman "tribute of nations" or Iroquois "league of nations", representing a confederacy of tribes. A sachemdom could comprise numerous individual (or autonomous or semi-autonomous?) bands, which could be identified by a local term. There was great fluidity among bands, so that at any given time one could identify many bands but any particular band might represent a different collection of tribes several decades hence.
Sachemdoms were ruled by a "Great Sachem". The Great Sachem was usually selected in a way similar to other forms of autocracy, sometimes through a trial by combat. In some places there was a council of sachems who advised the Great Sachem. However, it is not clear that the Great Sachem actually held sway over all the sachems (e.g. if he could override their decisions, etc.), but in general seemed to rule through consensus.
The Sachemship of Narragansett, for example, was established in 1643 and the first Great Sachem was Canonicus, son of Miantunnomu.
After the Great Sachem's death or retirement, his son often became successor. In some cases, when there was no clear heir, the Narragansett elected a Great Sachem. The last Great Sachem of the Narragansett, Joseph Jenks, was elected and ruled until 1858, when the Great Sachem was deposed, and the sachemship was abolished.

In the long, narrow hallway of home,  
a faded and bleached picture of my four-year-old self hangs:  
holding hands with his round-faced grandfather,  
wearing a plaid wool cap  
that children once wore,  
and a button-up sweater  
with reindeer embroidered on it.  
This me looks at the camera, smiling gently,  
his forehead slightly pale from a recent haircut,  
his expression so innocent it seems almost foolish.  
Tiptoeing through the bars of sorrow,  
I wish to tell him about things  
in his grandfather’s backyard,  
in Rochester, New York,  
in 1951.  
I’d warn him that life is harsh,  
there are tough realities out there:  
broken hearts,  
sudden accidents,  
nighttime sirens,  
loved ones lost,  
shiny but fragile funeral arrangements,  
and dreams that fade away.  
I’d tell him that there is an empty space out there—  
deep and twisting,  
black enough to break the heart.  
I’d remind him to check both ways before crossing,  
and to keep warm during the cold months.  
I’d ask him to be careful.  
'I must be careful,' I’d say.  
'Please, be careful.'  
He doesn’t listen.  
He smiles sweetly.  
(Nothing I can do for him.)  
Life took him.  
That was always the truth  
in the backyards of Rochester,  
in the season of fireflies,  
in 1951.  
Thus, what remains is this:  
I have come, somehow, to love that child.  
I’d like him to know.  
(Written 1984, revised 2004)

Other People's Money begins just before the 1987 stock market crash, and describes the conflict between a ruthless, predatory leveraged buyout specialist, Larry Crowne, and his longtime rival, Henry Ross, who is the CEO of a well-established family-owned bank. Crowne specializes in hostile takeovers of companies, buying them, and breaking them up for profit. In this instance, Crowne is attempting to buy United States Electrical, a lighting fixture company based in Providence, Rhode Island. Ross is convinced that UE is a solid company and will not break up the company, and he tries to rally the UE employees to fight off the takeover.

As the story progresses, Crowne's leveraged buyouts grow larger and more daring, and he becomes increasingly entangled with the political establishment, most notably with GovernorDX, who is running for the United States Senate. Crowne initially supports DX's campaign, but ends up supporting his opponent Jack Riley when DX takes a stance that favors organized labor, which would make it more difficult for Crowne to take over companies.

The novel traces Crowne's meteoric rise as he arranges ever-larger takeovers of major corporations, while Henry Ross tries in vain to rally the company owners whose businesses are being taken over. Meanwhile, DX's political career becomes increasingly entangled with Crowne's business dealings. In the end, Crowne's ambitions get the better of him when he attempts to buy a major New York bank, and instead ends up being wiped out when the stock market crash of 1987 occurs.

The story is of three sisters, of whom the youngest is chosen by Tsar Saltan (Saltán) to be his wife, while he makes the other two his royal cook and royal weaver. The Ncut objective function, commonly applied in data clustering and image segmentation, measures the cost of graph partitioning by favoring clusterings that have more uniform distributions of node values compared to unbalanced ones. This preference leads to the avoidance of singleton partitions, even when nodes have minimal connections to other parts of the graph. Inspired by the Bühler-Hein family of balanced cut costs, we introduce the Compassionately Conservative Balanced (CCB) Cut costs, which are defined by a parameter allowing a balance between preventing excessive singleton partitions and ensuring overall balance across all partitions. We demonstrate that CCB-Cut minimization can be transformed into an orthogonally constrained ℓτ-minimization problem equivalent to computing Piecewise Flat Embeddings (PFE) for a specific parameter value, and propose an iterative algorithm using reweighted Rayleigh quotients (IRRQ) to solve the relaxed version. Experiments on images from the BSDS500 dataset reveal that CCB-Cut-based image segmentation achieves higher accuracy relative to ground truth and exhibits greater variation in region sizes compared to Ncut-based approaches.

Engineering firm Balfour Beatty and five railway managers are to go on trial for manslaughter over the Hatfield rail crash in 2000.
Four people died when a section of rail broke and a high speed train derailed. Balfour Beatty's railway maintenance arm was in charge of the upkeep of the line at Hatfield, Hertfordshire. Balfour Beatty managers Anthony Walker and Nicholas Jeffries, and Railtrack managers Alistair Cook, Sean Fugill and Keith Lea all face individual charges. All five men, along with four others, are also accused of breaches of health and safety laws. Balfour Beatty Rail Maintenance faces a corporate manslaughter charge. It is expected the trial could last as long as a year. The accident, on 17 October 2000, happened when the London to Leeds express came off the tracks at 115 mph, when it was derailed by a cracked section of rail. The accident on the East Coast Main Line sparked major disruption. The overall responsibility for the line was Railtrack's - the company that has now become Network Rail. Those who died in the accident were Steve Arthur, 46, from Pease Pottage, West Sussex; Peter Monkhouse, 50, of Headingley, Leeds; Leslie Gray, 43, of Tuxford, Nottingham; and Robert James Alcorn, 37, of Auckland, New Zealand.

Osteoarthritis (OA) is a significant health concern among the elderly population. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is widely used to monitor and assess the progression of OA. However, the high labor costs associated with MRI analysis make the process less efficient and costly. Additionally, human errors and the subjective nature of the task result in considerable variability between and within observers. Computer-assisted knee MRI segmentation is an emerging area of research as it helps reduce the workload for physicians and radiologists, thereby enhancing diagnostic accuracy. Over the past several decades, numerous studies have focused on developing automated or semi-automated methods for knee MRI segmentation. Nevertheless, to date, there is no comprehensive review article in this domain. This paper aims to categorize existing approaches based on their methodologies, examine the current state of research, and identify key directions for future exploration.

In this paper, we present a state-of-the-art architecture for real-time person segmentation. Our method is fully automatic, requires no user input, and can be run on CPUs. We do so by training a single deep network that operates on RGB images of a whole person. Our network is trained to predict a confidence map that is used to obtain pixelwise human masks. Our main contribution is a novel loss function for training the network, composed of pixel-wise and group-wise losses. The group-wise loss explicitly penalizes segmentation errors on the boundary, leading to precise predictions in challenging situations, such as occlusions and self-occlusions. To achieve real-time performance, our network, dubbed keypoint transfer (KT), is based on keypoint detection and transfer, where segmentation masks are predicted for keypoint locations, and transferred to all pixels of the image. This step requires very few operations, compared to convolutions, and therefore is suitable for efficient inference on a CPU. We also use it to generate new training data, which is made compatible with the network through the use of a group-wise loss. KT provides state-of-the-art segmentation accuracy for multi-person scenarios, while also running at 30 frames per second on an unmodified CPU.

China's biggest spirits maker, Kweichow Moutai, has signed a deal to boost its presence in Italy's booming wine market by distributing its products through Illva Saronno, one of the country's oldest and biggest liquor companies.

The partnership, sealed on Thursday, gives Illva Saronno, producer of the Disaronno liqueur, distribution rights to Moutai's portfolio of baijiu, a distilled grain spirit usually made from sorghum.

Illva said in a statement that the partnership aimed to "strengthen the presence of both companies on their respective home markets and to develop business opportunities in third countries".

Moutai, whose fiery liquor is a favourite tipple of China's ruling Communist Party elite, has been looking to expand its global footprint.

The company's lustre has dimmed somewhat in China in recent months as its flagship baijiu product has fallen out of favour with some younger consumers, who have turned to imported spirits such as Scotch whisky.

However, it remains immensely popular in China, with its sales jumping 25% in the first half of 2022, and it is hoping to win over new consumers in Europe and elsewhere.

Chinese drinks companies have been looking to expand abroad as domestic consumption slows and foreign sales of Chinese spirits, wine and beer are growing quickly.

China's beer giant Budweiser Brewing Co Ltd, formed by the merger of Budweiser and local giant Tsingtao, has said it aims to become one of the world's top 10 beer companies within a decade.

In July, Budweiser Brewing signed a deal with Coca-Cola Co's Costa coffee chain to roll out a line of coffee-flavoured drinks in China.

The unemployment rate in Australia has reached its highest point in four years, according to recent data released by the Australian Bureau of Statistics. The jobless rate increased from 5.5% in December 2018 to 5.7% in January 2019, marking the first rise since August last year.

While this increase may be cause for concern, experts have noted that it is still within the range considered healthy for the economy. In addition, they pointed out that the participation rate - which measures the proportion of working-age people who are either employed or looking for work - remained steady at 65.6%, indicating that there was no significant drop in workforce engagement.

Furthermore, Prime Minister Scott Morrison hailed the figures as evidence that his government's economic policies were paying off. He emphasized that over 500,000 jobs had been created under his administration and vowed to continue supporting businesses and workers alike.

However, opposition leader Bill Shorten criticized the government's handling of the situation, arguing that inadequate investment in education and training was contributing to skill shortages and wage stagnation. He called on the government to do more to address these issues and ensure sustainable growth for all Australians.

Overall, while the latest employment numbers paint a mixed picture, they serve as a reminder that Australia's labour market remains resilient despite global uncertainties and domestic challenges.

We present a fully relativistic calculation of the observed galaxy number
counts in the linear regime. We show that besides the density fluctuations and
redshift-space distortions, various relativistic effects contribute to
observations at large scales. These effects all have the same physical origin:
they result from the fact that our coordinate system, namely the galaxy
redshift and the incoming photons' direction, is distorted by inhomogeneities
in our universe. We then discuss the impact of the relativistic effects on the
angular power spectrum and on the two-point correlation function in
configuration space. We show that the latter is very well adapted to isolate
the relativistic effects since it naturally makes use of the symmetries of the
different contributions. In particular, we discuss how the Doppler effect and
the gravitational redshift distortions can be isolated by looking for a dipole
in the cross-correlation function between a bright and a faint population of

12 shrimp

2 eggs

To Make Dipping Sauce: In a bowl, combine apricot jelly, crushed pineapple, apple cider vinegar and red pepper flakes. To Make Coleslaw: In a food processor, add water, olive oil, scallions, cilantro, garlic, salt and lime juice. Pulse until combined. Then add sour cream and pulse again. In a bowl, add chopped green and purple cabbage. Drizzle olive oil mixture over the cabbage and mix well. To Make Coconut Shrimp: In a bowl, whisk beer, egg, milk, flour, baking powder, and salt. Dip peeled, headless shrimp in the batter. Then coat with coconut flakes. Fry the breaded shrimp in hot oil until the coconut flakes are golden bown. Place shrimp on a drying rack over a sheet tray to allow the excess oil to drip off. Let cool. Assembling the Roll: On a sheet of moistened rice paper, place a scoop of coleslaw in the middle, edge of the paper (think of it as about 1/3 in from the edge). Then roll and fold until the top of the coleslaw is covered by the rice paper. After the shrimp cools down and excess oil drips off onto the rack, place two shrimp on the roll and continue to wrap until the shrimp is sealed well. Slice in half and serve with the dipping sauce.

Mitzvah Day International is an annual day of faith-based social action that takes place in November each year, primarily in the United Kingdom. On Mitzvah Day each year, community groups and individuals undertake a range of volunteer projects for those in need in their local community. Organizations register with Mitzvah Day, which in turn helps match volunteers with local projects. The objective is to encourage people to give their time, rather than their money, to worthwhile local causes, whilst also creating deeper linkages within communities and supporting charities. In 2013, close to 30,000 people participated in Mitzvah Day around the world.
Though based within the UK's Jewish Community, Mitzvah Day traditionally marks the first day of UK National Inter Faith Week, and as a result has expanded to include participants from other faith communities as well.
'Mitzvah' is the Hebrew biblical term for 'deed' or 'commandment', which has come to mean 'good deed' or 'charitable act' in contemporary English. The 2020 date was Sunday November 15.

The human brain consists of multiple layers that facilitate both forward and backward processing. Forward processing occurs from lower layers to higher layers, while backward processing involves signals traveling from higher layers back to lower ones. Each layer comprises neurons, and a neural network represents the functionality of these neurons mathematically. Although neural networks replicate the brain's structure, individuals typically employ only the forward processing pathway, disregarding the backward process. Consequently, this study introduces Feedback U-Net, which incorporates Convolutional LSTM—a segmentation technique—along with a feedback mechanism. The output of the U-Net influences the input, enabling a second iteration. Using Convolutional LSTM, features from the second iteration are derived from those obtained in the first iteration. Our approach demonstrated superior performance on both Drosophila and mouse cell image datasets compared to traditional U-Net, which relies solely on forward processing.

Dinosaurs. Amusement Park. Tourists. Disaster.

Jurassic World has them all.

Naturally, I had to see it.

The beginning holds much promise, and it gets your hopes up for the disaster to come. When it does, there are some great action sequences, especially ones with the glass ball containing the soft, chewy child centre.

Unfortunately the final act unravels into outright farce.

Chris Pratt is great as the affable yet bad-ass Raptor Whisperer. He's got an easy going charisma that could easily carry an iconic character like Indiana Jones.

Bryce Dallas Howard plays Claire Dearing, the uptight park manager, who initially clashes with the laid back Owen. Of course you know where the tension goes.

The film tries to flesh out Claire's character by throwing in her two nephews (someone and another kid), who do double duty as McGuffins.

Vincent D'Onofrio shows up as Hoskins, a villainous representative of the military-industrial complex angling to weaponize velociraptors. He's all sneers and scenery chewing, so obviously evil he's got a goatee. D'Onofrio does it well but the evil plan he's been saddled with by the writers makes no sense at all.

The director, Colin Trevorrow, said in interviews that he wanted the dinosaurs to act like real animals, not cartoon monsters. Quelle surprise! I had no idea, as he has well-fed winged dinos (or near enough to dinos) go on a crazed orgy of violence against hapless tourists. Why? Because cool action sequence!

One poor soul is even treated to the most outlandishly elongated death sequence I've ever seen, all to no end. It didn't justify anything, paid nothing back, offered no comeuppance. It was just gleeful indulgence in sadistic torture of a minor character. It was an Itchy & Scratchy moment.

Which brings us to the final act: turn off your brain before it begins.

The first movie proved you could have a smart script and dinosaurs in the same movie. After that, the IQ of the series dropped with each outing. The first one had chaos theory and amber and DNA extraction and cleverness up the whazoo. It was AWESOME.

What does this one have? Hackneyed evil plans, a clunky plot, and characters so smart they run from T-Rex's in high heels.

The franchise has had a lobotomy.

The Indianapolis Zoo is a zoo located in White River State Park, in Indianapolis, Indiana, United States, housing more than 3,800 animals of more than 320 species and subspecies. The institution is accredited by the Association of Zoos and Aquariums (AZA) and the American Alliance of Museums as a zoo, an aquarium, and as a botanical garden. The zoo is a private non-profit organization, receiving no tax support and is supported entirely by membership fees, admissions, donations, sales, grants, and an annual fundraiser. History
In 1944, Lowell Nussbaum, columnist for the Indianapolis Times, and later the Indianapolis Star, began to advocate for a zoo through his column "Inside Indianapolis", which inspired the incorporation, in October 1944 of the Indianapolis Zoological Society.  Soon the members of this group had outlined the plans for their zoo. Group members were adamant that "the zoo will rely on admissions, in-park sales, contributions, and memberships to support the zoo". However, it would not be until 20 years later, in 1964, that the zoo opened to the public.

It forms an integral part of the film, acting as a character unto itself, and helping unveil the depths of emotions and pivotal plot developments. From classical pieces to folksy tunes, the score permeates every scene, enhancing the dynamics between the characters and their environment.

"Moonrise Kingdom" is a heartwarming tale of young love, rebellious spirit, and the enchanting pull of the great outdoors; it is as charming and quirky as it is insightful. Its clever additives of humor are well-placed, providing a balanced mix of laughter, sentimentality, and intensity.

It is a brilliant, emotionally rich film that reminds us of the rousing whirlwind that is young love and the indomitable spirit of childhood. Thus, "Moonrise Kingdom" is much more than an escapist adventure; it is a precious tribute to the youthful courage, uncomplicated love, and unvanquished imagination we often forget after crossing the bridge to adulthood. segmentation, as dense labels demand significant human intervention. Generally,
the annotation burden is mitigated by labeling datasets with weaker forms of
supervision, e.g. image-level labels or bounding boxes. Another option are
semi-supervised settings, that commonly leverage a few strong annotations and a
huge number of unlabeled/weakly-labeled data. In this paper, we revisit

annotation budget (in terms of total labeling time of the training set)
compared to previous approaches. With a very simple pipeline, we demonstrate

Boyer's comprehensive work explores how religious ideas emerge from the cognitive mechanisms of the mind, akin to pareidolia and the perception of religious symbols in nature, which arise from facial recognition processes in the human brain. He substantiates this naturalistic perspective by drawing on insights from various fields such as biological anthropology, cultural anthropology, cognitive science, linguistics, evolutionary biology, cognitive psychology, evolutionary psychology, neuroscience, and information processing. *Religion Explained* presents religious behaviors and doctrines within the context of contemporary cognitive neuroscience findings regarding the modularity of the mind. This framework emphasizes cognitive "modules"—internal devices or subroutines—that underpin inference systems and intuitive judgments. For example, Boyer posits that widespread cultural beliefs in "supernatural entities" (such as deities, ancestors, spirits, and witches) originate from the intuitive process of detecting agency, irrespective of whether those agents are physically present. "When we observe moving branches in a tree or an unusual sound behind us, we instinctively attribute these events to an external agent, even without knowing its exact nature." Boyer references E. E. Evans-Pritchard’s seminal Zande narrative concerning a roof collapsed by termites. To the anthropologist, the collapse was due to termites, but for the Zande, it was clear that witchcraft was responsible. Yet they recognized the termites as the immediate cause. What they sought to understand was the timing of the incident during a specific gathering. According to Boyer, religion functions as a "parasite" or "spandrel" arising from cognitive modules, much like how reading depends on linguistic modules.

His family included himself, his father, and his two maternal uncles. All were uneducated yet eager to learn, working in construction and boxing occasionally to make extra income. His uncles initiated his boxing training at the age of three and read classic literature to him at night. The central storyline follows Spenser's journey with a female companion, Jeannie Haden. Jeannie, roughly his age, was merely a friend, though her father was an alcoholic who frequently abused her. One day, Spenser observed her in her father's vehicle, repeatedly saying "Help." Alongside his canine companion, Pearl, Spenser followed the vehicle and eventually reached Jeannie's father's boat downstream. He located her and her father on a small island near a lean-to. After a brief confrontation with Luke Haden, the father, Spenser successfully rescued Jeannie later. They escaped downstream on Spenser's rowboat, ultimately leading to Luke Haden's demise. Spenser's father and uncles reassured him that he "did good" and did not need to report the incident or his involvement. Yet, he does report it, and the local authorities do not pursue charges against him. Spenser shares that Jeannie harbored a crush on him, but he reciprocated none of her affection. Nevertheless, he offered her assistance and maintained their friendship. In gratitude for her help, Spenser subsequently safeguards a student of Mexican origin, Aurelio Lopez. Lopez faced bullying from white peers and was often assaulted. Following Spenser's intervention, Lopez no longer endured such harassment. However, this relationship strained Spenser's rapport with his white classmates, many of whom he had known since kindergarten. Ultimately, Spenser concludes his story.

Jonathan Larkin, born on January 30, 1984, was a former American politician who served as a Democratic representative in the Arizona House of Representatives from 2013 to 2017. After graduating from high school, he joined the Marines through JROTC and participated in the invasion of Iraq. He later served tours in the Philippines and Iraq. In addition to his legislative work, Larkin worked at Fry's Food Stores. 

In the 2016 election, Larkin ran for re-election, while Debbie McCune-Davis stepped down from office. Larkin finished third behind Democratic candidates Ray Martinez and Tony Navarrete, who both won the general election. 

In 2014, Jonathan Larkin and Debbie McCune-Davis were unopposed in the Democratic primary. In the Republican primary, Michael Gidwani and John Lyon were unopposed. Larkin and McCune-Davis defeated Gidwani, Lyon, and Angel Garcia (I) in the general election.

In 2012, Larkin and the incumbent Debbie McCune-Davis defeated Mike Snitz in the Democratic primary on August 28, 2012. They won the general election on November 6, 2012.

Orleanna Price narrates the introductory chapter in five of the novel's seven sections. The narrative then alternates among the four daughters, with a slight preference for the voice of the most outspoken one, Leah. The four girls increasingly mature, as each adapts differently to African village life, to the misogyny of their father Nathan, and the political turmoil that overtakes The Congo in the 1960s. Since the Congolese villagers are seen through the eyes of the growing daughters, the view changes. At first, they appear as ridiculous savages. But as the girls mature, the villagers become fully fleshed-out human beings, immersed in a complex and sophisticated culture. Nathan's lack of responsiveness to this culture wears out his family's welcome, but he refuses to leave. Only after a series of misfortunes—culminating in the death of one of the daughters—do the women leave Nathan Price to his folly. The survivors take different paths into their futures, the novel ending at the time of Mobutu Sese Seko's death in the 1990s. Rachel, the eldest, marries Axelroot at seventeen, and after two more marriages is the owner of a luxury hotel close to what is now Brazzaville. Leah marries Anatole, has a large family of four boys, and remains in the impoverished Congo. Adah returns to the United States with their mother Orleanna, attending college and later, medical school. She undergoes a lengthy experimental treatment that restores full use of her legs and she begins to speak. Orleanna herself returns to spending life on the Georgian coast, enjoying Adah's occasional visits.

Quasi-power law ensembles are analyzed through the lens of nonextensive Tsallis distributions, which are defined by a nonextensive parameter $q$. Several potential origins of these distributions are explored in greater depth. It is further established that empirical data indicate that nonextensive parameters derived from Tsallis distribution functions $f(p_T)$, $q_1$, and from multiplicity distributions (related to Tsallis entropy), $q_2$, are distinct and related by the equation $q_1 + q_2 = 2$. Additionally, it is shown that Tsallis distributions can be derived directly from Shannon information entropy, under certain specific conditions. These distributions are associated with the nature of the underlying dynamical processes—either additive or multiplicative. Finally, it is demonstrated how a Tsallis distribution can account for the observed log-oscillatory behavior in some multiparticle data.

The Liberal Democrats have unveiled plans to build 100,000 new "affordable" homes on publicly owned land.
The party's scheme would allow people to buy a share in a home through a mutual home ownership trust, as a way of getting onto the housing ladder. The Lib Dems would also encourage the conversion of existing buildings in an effort to protect greenfield sites. Labour has already announced plans to help first-time buyers and the Tories would extend right-to-buy schemes.
All the major parties are focusing on the issue in the run-up to the election after a survey suggested first-time buyers could not afford a home in 92% of UK towns. The Lib Dems say their "mutual homes" would let people buy a share of a property, usually worth about 5% of the building costs. Party leader Charles Kennedy said the homes would be affordable because they would be built on surplus public sector land, donated by central or local government. People would also only have to pay for the cost of the building and not the land, he added.
They would spend about 30% of their monthly salary on rent and buying extra shares in the property. When they moved house, they would be able to cash in on any rise in property prices by selling their share. It would also allow councils to vary discounts to tenants given the right to buy their council homes so local needs were taken into account. Mr Kennedy said: "Mutual homes will offer people the opportunity to build up an equity stake in a home gradually, investing only as much as they can afford."
There are also plans to prevent high house prices forcing people out of their local communities. The kind of "golden share" used by the Lib Dems in South Shropshire could be rolled out more widely. Under the plan, councils secure deals with developers where they keep a 1% share in a property scheme so properties cannot be sold on the open market. Instead, they are sold at "build cost" to people who the local council decides have local needs. The party says its help for first-time buyers can be funded at no extra cost to the taxpayer. But the plans involve changing the VAT system, which the party says often makes it too expensive to renovate existing buildings.
The Conservatives claimed the plans would amount to an extra tax of up to £11,000 on every new house. "This is typical of Lib Dem hypocrisy," said Tory shadow local government secretary Caroline Spelman. "They claim that they want to help people on to the property ladder, but the small print of their policies reveal how they intend to price even more people out of the housing market." The flagship Tory proposal on housing policy is to give a million more housing association tenants the right to buy their homes. Labour has said it will allow 300,000 council and housing association tenants to buy a share in their homes. Housing Minister Keith Hill said much of the Lib Dem plans mimicked the government's strategy. "However, as usual, the Lib Dems' proposals are completely uncosted," he said. Mr Hill said he also asked whether the Lib Dems would match Labour's promise to spend £42bn on making refurbishing and repair council homes by 2010.

Reading the back cover of the DVD and seeing that Colin Firth and Ben Kingsley are given top billing, I expected an intelligent King Arthur story. Well, it really wasn't either, although I did find it entertaining. I must not have read the description carefully enough. No matter; overall, it was fun but just a little too silly. I'm beginning to wonder about the discernment of some of these actors, how they can play such intelligent roles for a film or two and then revert to something like this.

Anyway, the story is really a Roman empire one, not a King Arthur story. We only see the tie-in to the later in the last few minutes of the film, in the epilogue. This action story is all about the last Caesar, a small boy, and the last legion that fought as Rome had now been taken over by the Goths. The Roman Empire had come to an end.

Mixed in with that tale was the famous "excalibur" sword. We see the origins of that and how it eventually got into the hands of King Arthur. But, once again, that is only explained in the final minutes. However, the sword is used by the good Roman general who protects the last Caesar from the Goths, who want him imprisoned for life, or killed.

What made the story interesting, at least for me, was the chase-scene type atmosphere of a small band of heroes protecting a little boy, fleeing the bloodthirsty Goths until they could mount some sort of counter-attack in the north in Brittania. That, and the pretty computer-generated scenery and action stunts, kept it interesting. However, don't look for credibility in those action scenes and expect the typical political-correctness of today (i.e. where a woman beats up hundreds of men and the good guys of all colors prevail despite ridiculous odds).

Some parts of this will leave you shaking your head in disbelief. You will feel you're watching a kids' film at times. However, if you want an hour-and-a-half of decent escapist fare, and can put your brain on hold for that time, it fits the bill and will at least entertain you.

Ingredients:

2 poblano peppers, seeded and thinly sliced
3 cloves garlic, minced
1 tablespoon olive oil
1 teaspoon dried thyme
Salt and pepper, to taste

Instructions: 

Preheat the oven to 350°F (180°C). Rinse the turkey inside and out with cold water and pat dry with paper towels. Place the turkey breast side up in a roasting pan or a turkey roaster. 

In a small bowl, mix together the garlic, olive oil, thyme, salt, and pepper. Rub the mixture all over the turkey, both inside and out.

Stuff the turkey cavity with apple and poblano pepper slices. Season the apples and peppers lightly with salt and pepper to taste.

Cover the turkey with aluminum foil and place it in the preheated oven. Roast for approximately 2-2 1/2 hours, until the internal temperature of the thigh reaches 165°F (74°C). Remove from the oven and let rest for at least 1 hour before carving.

Recycling used mobile phones is beneficial both environmentally and socially. Studies show that in certain developing regions, these devices can bridge the digital gap by providing affordable access. A study by the Forum for the Future noted that the low cost of repurposed phones allows them to serve valuable roles in less developed areas. However, the organization emphasized that more efforts are required to collect old phones rather than letting them accumulate in landfills.

The report indicates that about 15 million mobile phones are discarded annually in the UK. Out of this number, only 25% are returned for recycling or reuse. As a result, the growing pile of unprocessed devices now amounts to 90 million handsets, equivalent to 9,000 tonnes of waste. James Goodman, the report’s author, highlighted that it's common for individuals to possess multiple outdated phones. 

He warned that these devices may end up in landfills, releasing harmful substances into the environment. Instead, he suggested returning phones to service providers who can transport them abroad for further use. Goodman stressed that while environmental concerns are valid, the social impact is equally significant. In poorer nations, mobile phones are crucial for communication, yet many cannot afford the latest models. The Forum’s report examined Romania, where refurbished phones are highly sought after. Despite its poor economic conditions, the country has a high demand for mobile services.

In this study, we propose a novel approach to medical image segmentation called PGL (Prior-Guided Local Self-supervision). Our method leverages prior knowledge about the structure of the target object in an image and uses it to guide self-supervision during training. Specifically, we use local patches from the input image as well as corresponding patches from a set of reference images with known labels to train a neural network. We also incorporate a regularization term that encourages the learned features to be consistent across different patches within each image. The results show that our method outperforms state-of-the-art methods on several benchmark datasets, demonstrating the effectiveness of incorporating prior knowledge into self-supervised learning for medical image segmentation tasks.

Zest of 1 lemon, in long pieces

4 teaspoons maple syrup

To make the broth, stir the pear nectar, agave nectar, lemon zest, ginger, maple syrup, and saffron together in a large saucepan or 3-quart saute pan over medium-high heat. Bring to a boil, then place the pear halves in the saucepan, flat side down. Place a piece of parchment paper over the pears and cover with a small plate to weight the pears down as they simmer. Lower the heat and simmer until the pears are tender and a knife pierces them all the way through without resistance. Remove the pears from the saucepan. Return the liquid to the heat, bring to a lively simmer, and cook until syrupy, about 10 minutes. Taste the liquid for a quick FASS check. It may need a pinch of salt and a squeeze of lemon juice to balance the flavors. Serve the pears drizzled with the poaching liquid and topped with a dollop of nut cream if you like. For vanilla broth, omit the lemon zest, ginger, maple syrup, and saffron, and instead stir 2 teaspoons of agave nectar into the pear nectar. Cut a vanilla pod in half lengthwise, scrape the seeds into the saucepan, then throw in the pod. Proceed with the recipe as above. For star anise broth, omit the lemon zest, ginger, maple syrup, and saffron, and instead stir in 4 pods of star anise, 4 whole cloves, 2 cinnamon sticks, 2 teaspoons of agave nectar, and 2 teaspoons of freshly squeezed lemon juice. Proceed with the recipe as above. To seed and stem a pear beautifully, once its cut in half, use a melon baller to scoop out the center, making sure to remove all of the seeds. Then use a sharp paring knife to make a small angled slice on each side of the core, running out from the center of the pear to the stem. This will remove a clean and even triangle-shaped piece where the stem and the core had been. You can garnish the pears with the solids from the broth. Lemon peel, vanilla pods, star anise pods, and cloves all make beautiful garnishes. Store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 3 to 5 days. Disappearance and capture

From Israel’s borders to distant lands.

Shone upon each dark and violent gathering;  
Kings called upon him for rape and attack,  
Seeking his fierce assistance in verse and song.  
III  
Upon wounds and scars, bruises and seams,  
He cast his radiant light across blades and arrows;  
His halos illuminated the most bloody scenes,  
And corpses bore his glorious glow.

Often, an early King or Queen,  
Or a storied hero, saw his brilliance;  
Wolfe, Ney, and Nelson glimpsed his radiance,  
Though far from their own lands.  
V  
But new light has come. The god’s golden hue,  
And its heraldic markings, have faded dimly;  
Even his bright form begins to decline,  
Leaving only a shadow of his former self.  
VI  
This modern reflection broke his enchantment,  
And the pleas of penmen brought about a blow;  
Some claimed, others that such crimes were grave,  
Hurting greatly his crimson robe.  
VII  
Indeed, seeds of deep compassion  
Were planted by those who were greater than he;  
Known long, yet long ignored until then—  
The gods of men in harmony.  
VIII  
Souls have become seers, and thoughts surpass  
The sorrow of many-faced existence;  
Foes become friends, and wrath is quelled,  
By the giving of gifts and fire!

They fight and dare, but with pale faces;  
Would they dare to raise the arm  
Of this faint, unknown form?

Wars still rise, though enthusiasm wanes;  
At times, as in old traditions,  
He appears, painted and adorned,  
Yet never truly the old one!  
XI  
Let men celebrate, let them grieve;  
The lurid deity of yesteryear  
Falls to a more rational choice;
