Boyer's multifaceted book explains the genesis of religious concepts through the mind's cognitive inference systems, comparable to pareidolia and perceptions of religious imagery in natural phenomena resulting from face perception processes within the human brain. Boyer supports this naturalistic origin of religion with evidence from many specialized disciplines including biological anthropology, cultural anthropology, cognitive science, linguistics, evolutionary biology, cognitive psychology, evolutionary psychology, neuroscience, and information processing. Religion Explained frames religious practices and beliefs in terms of recent cognitive neuroscience research in the modularity of mind. This theory involves cognitive "modules" ("devices" or "subroutines") underlying inference systems and intuitions. For instance, Boyer suggests culturally-widespread beliefs in "supernatural agents" (e.g., gods, ancestors, spirits, and witches) result from agent detection: the intuitive modular process of assuming intervention by conscious agents, regardless of whether they are present. "When we see branches moving in a tree or when we hear an unexpected sound behind us, we immediately infer that some agent is the cause of this salient event. We can do that without any specific description of what the agent actually is." Boyer cites E. E. Evans-Pritchard's classic Zande story about a termite-infested roof collapsing. For the anthropologist, the house caved in because of the termites. For the Zande, it was quite clear that witchcraft was involved. However, the Zande were also aware that the termites were the proximate cause of the incident. But what they wanted to know was why it happened at that particular time, when particular people were gathered in the house. Within Boyer's hypothesis, religion is a "parasite" (or "spandrel") offshoot from cognitive modules, comparable to the way the reading process is parasitic upon language modules. As I have pointed out repeatedly the building of religious concepts requires mental systems and capacities that are there anyway, religious concepts or not. Religious morality uses moral intuitions, religious notions of supernatural agents recruit our intuitions about agency in general, and so on. This is why I said that religious concepts are parasitic upon other mental capacities. Our capacities to play music, paint pictures or even make sense of printed ink-patterns on a page are also parasitic in this sense. This means that we can explain how people play music, paint pictures and learn to read by examining how mental capacities are recruited by these activities. The same goes for religion. Because the concepts require all sorts of specific human capacities (an intuitive psychology, a tendency to attend to some counterintuitive concepts, as well as various social mind adaptations), we can explain religion by describing how these various capacities get recruited, how they contribute to the features of religion that we find in so many different cultures. We do not need to assume that there is a special way of functioning that occurs only when processing religious thoughts. Boyer admits his explanation of religion is not a quick, shoot-from-the-hip solution of the kind that many people, either religious or not, seem to favor. There cannot be a magic bullet to explain the existence and common features of religion, as the phenomenon is the result of aggregate relevance – that is, of successful activation of a whole variety of mental systems.

A single-elimination (SE) tournament is a widely used method for determining a winner in both athletic events and electoral processes. The tournament fixing problem (TFP) involves determining whether a tournament organizer can manipulate the initial seeding to ensure their favored player wins. We derive new conditions on the outcomes of pairwise matches and the preferred player, showing that a valid seeding exists where the player triumphs. These findings expand upon existing research. Additionally, we explore how the set of players who can win an SE tournament under various seedings relates to conventional tournament metrics. Furthermore, we extend prior studies on probabilistic methods for creating tournaments. For example, we demonstrate that every player in an $n$-player tournament produced by the Condorcet Random Model will be an SE winner, even with minimal noise ($p = \Theta(\ln n / n)$), surpassing earlier results that required higher noise levels ($p \geq \Omega(\sqrt{\ln n / n})$). We also present novel results for more general generation models.

In medicine, the mean systemic pressure (mean systemic filling pressure (MSFP)) refers to the average pressure present in the circulatory system when there is no movement of blood. A related term, the mean circulatory filling pressure (MCFP), describes the average pressure in both the circulatory and pulmonary systems when there is no blood motion. The value of mean systemic pressure (MSP) in animal studies is approximately 7 mm Hg. This parameter reflects the extent to which the circulatory system is filled with blood relative to its capacity, and it is affected by the amount of circulating blood and the tone of the venous wall muscles, which influences the system's capacity. MSP is determined through two methods in experiments, leading to different naming conventions. MSFP is measured by clamping the aortic root and the large veins entering the right atrium. Conversely, MCFP is assessed by temporarily inducing cardiac arrest or naturally occurring during cardiac arrest when blood distribution occurs. It can also be estimated in vivo using inspiratory holds while the patient is on a mechanical ventilator. MSP is useful for showing the impact of medications on venous tone when circulating blood volume remains unchanged, or for measuring hemodynamic changes during hemorrhage.

Information flow is the branch of security that studies the leakage of
information due to correlation between secrets and observables. Since in
general such correlation cannot be avoided completely, it is important to
quantify the leakage. The most followed approaches to defining appropriate
measures are those based on information theory. In particular, one of the most
successful approaches is the recently proposed $g$-leakage framework, which
encompasses most of the information-theoretic ones. A problem with $g$-leakage,
however, is that it is defined in terms of a minimization problem, which, in
the case of large systems, can be computationally rather heavy. In this paper
we study the case in which the channel associated to the system can be
decomposed into simpler channels, which typically happens when the observables
consist of multiple components. Our main contribution is the derivation of
bounds on the (multiplicative version of) $g$-leakage of the whole system in
terms of the $g$-leakages of its components. We also consider the particular
cases of min-entropy leakage and of parallel channels, generalizing and
systematizing results from the literature. We demonstrate the effectiveness of
our method and evaluate the precision of our bounds using examples.

to healthy eyes. There is little research on the topic, mostly incorporating
scarce databases that are often deficient in images representing more than one
illness. We built our own database, acquiring 1288 eye images of 37 patients of
the Medical University of Warsaw. Those images represent several common ocular
diseases, such as cataract, along with less ordinary conditions, such as iris
pattern alterations derived from illness or eye trauma. Images were captured in
near-infrared light (used in biometrics) and for selected cases also in visible
light (used in ophthalmological diagnosis). Since cataract is a disorder that
is most populated by samples in the database, in this paper we focus solely on
this illness. To assess the extent of the performance deterioration we use
three iris recognition methodologies (commercial and academic solutions) to
calculate genuine match scores for healthy eyes and those influenced by
cataract. Results show a significant degradation in iris recognition
reliability manifesting by worsening the genuine scores in all three matchers
used in this study (12% of genuine score increase for an academic matcher, up
to 175% of genuine score increase obtained for an example commercial matcher).
This increase in genuine scores affected the final false non-match rate in two
matchers. To our best knowledge this is the only study of such kind that
employs more than one iris matcher, and analyzes the iris image segmentation as
a potential source of decreased reliability.

Detecting buildings from satellite multispectral image data is considered fundamental yet complex due to the challenge of accurately recovering building outlines from high-resolution images. In this study, we introduce a deep learning method for building detection, incorporating various enhancements at different stages. The initial dataset undergoes preprocessing using 2-sigma percentile normalization. Data preparation involves an ensemble model that combines three models while integrating OpenStreetMap information. Binary Distance Transformation (BDT) is applied to enhance data labeling, and the U-Net architecture is modified by adding batch normalization layers. We then examine how each component of our approach contributes to the final detection performance. Lastly, we evaluate our results against the top-performing solutions in the SpaceNet 2 competition, testing them on real satellite multispectral images of Vegas, Paris, Shanghai, and Khartoum, highlighting the significance of our approach in improving building detection accuracy.

Food First, also referred to as the Institute for Food and Development Policy, is a non-profit organization headquartered in Oakland, California, USA. Established in 1975 by Frances Moore Lappé and Joseph Collins, it identifies itself as a "people's think tank and education-for-action center." Its primary objective is to eradicate the injustices that lead to hunger. The Food First website states that its key focus is on achieving food sovereignty for human rights and sustainable living, and to accomplish this, the organization operates three development initiatives: establishing local agricultural systems, empowering farmers to achieve food sovereignty, and democratizing development processes. The organization provides policy analysis on poverty, agriculture, and development and is notably critical of the policies of the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund. It critiques the Green Revolution, which gained traction in the 1970s but failed to deliver the expected development outcomes, instead creating a system with high input costs but limited yield compared to traditional farming. Recently, there has been a revival of Green Revolution concepts, particularly with the widespread adoption of genetically modified organisms (GMOs) and high-yield crop varieties. Food First argues that such policies will exacerbate global inequality and has published multiple policy briefs asserting that equitable and effective development must be achieved through locally sustainable agriculture.

butter for the pan  
Preheat oven to 350°F. Warm up the milk, eggs, and limoncello slightly (room temperature is best) while preparing the lemons and oven heats. I just finished watching "The Butterfly Effect" and I'm still trying to process my thoughts about it. The film had an intriguing premise - a man discovers that he has the ability to travel back in time and change events from his past, but each time he does, the present changes in unexpected ways.

I have to say, the first half of the movie was really engaging. The main character, Evan Treborn, played by Ashton Kutcher, is a likable guy who you can't help but feel for as he tries to navigate his way through life with this strange power. The scenes where he goes back in time and alters events are well-executed and suspenseful, leaving you wondering what will happen next.

But as the movie progresses, things start to fall apart. The plot becomes increasingly convoluted and hard to follow, with too many characters and subplots that don't add anything meaningful to the story. The dialogue also gets cheesier and more predictable, which takes away from the overall impact of the film.

One thing that really bothered me was the lack of consistency in the rules of time travel. It seems like the writers made up their own rules as they went along, without thinking through the consequences or logic of them. For example, why can Evan only go back in time to moments when he was in the same location? And how come he can change some things but not others? These questions are never adequately answered, leaving the viewer feeling frustrated and confused.

Despite these flaws, I did appreciate the attempt at exploring deeper themes such as the butterfly effect itself, the concept of fate vs free will, and the idea that our choices have consequences that ripple out beyond our own lives. However, these ideas could have been executed much better with tighter writing and a clearer vision.

Overall, I would say that "The Butterfly Effect" starts off strong but ultimately falls flat due to its poor execution and inconsistencies. If you're a fan of sci-fi or time travel movies, you might find it worth watching, but otherwise, there are definitely better options out there.

The film is inspired by the life of Christopher Skase, a former Australian businessman who lost his Qintex company and relocated to Majorca, Spain. Skase passed away around the time of the movie's release. The production took place in Melbourne and Perth. 

Following the collapse of his vast Qintex business empire, Christopher Skase left his creditors in disarray, prompting him to flee to Majorca. Peter Dellasandro, a quick-witted con artist and former entrepreneur, saw the opportunity to capitalize on the "Chase for Skase" as a lucrative venture. He convinced the Creditors Board that he was the only person capable of executing the task—kidnapping Skase.

Not all were convinced, particularly Danny D'Amato, the fiery son of the Creditors Chairman. Doubting Dellasandro, the two formed an uneasy partnership as Dellasandro sought to recruit the egotistical TV host Eric Carney into his scheme. However, a seasoned mercenary named Mitch Vendieks warned Dellasandro that Carney was also plotting a kidnap operation.

Determined to outmaneuver Carney, Dellasandro and Danny joined forces with Mitch to create a team, recruiting the unskilled Sean Knight, a dishonest getaway driver, and a cynical intelligence expert. Soon, Rupert Wingate discovered that Skase was developing a dangerous plan to revive his business empire across Europe.

With limited time, Dellasandro and his team traveled to Majorca and tracked Skase to his luxurious estate, facing the cunning businessman. Despite being outnumbered by Skase's security guards, they managed to retrieve several computer disks containing sensitive information about Skase's plan to "break out" Qintex. This data provided sufficient evidence for the Australian government to initiate compensation payments to the Qintex group.

- Archaeological research on human technology and its temporal and spatial variations

- Behavioral ecology and human-environment interactions  
- Studies of human anatomy, physiology, molecular biology, biochemistry, and interspecies variation, along with group differences and cultural influences.

This book focuses on an aspect of World War II that is largely ignored in many history books – the Nazi looting of Europe and Russia and the Allied recovery and repatriation of stolen art. Little known to the general public, Hitler diverted his attention from the prosecution of the war to the systematic theft of Europe’s great art. His dream was to build the world’s greatest collection – The Führermuseum – in his hometown of Linz, Austria. European museum officials took extraordinary measures to protect art from Hitler and the ensuing war. When U.S. forces prepared to enter Europe, they assembled a special force of largely American and British museum directors, curators, and art historians known as the Monuments, Fine Arts, and Archives program (MFAA) section, attached to the Allied armies. These “Monuments Men” attempted to minimize damage to European monuments and architecture, then track down stolen works of art. Their effort would become one of the greatest “treasure hunts” in history. In the end, Allied forces located more than 1,000 repositories in mines and castles across Europe, many of which were filled with art, sculpture, furniture, archives, and other cultural property stolen by the Nazis. Edsel points out that thousands of pieces are still missing, such as Raphael’s Portrait of a Young Man from the Czartoryski Museum in Kraków, Poland. Rescuing Da Vinci tells this story through brief text and more than 460 photographs, 60 of which are in color. This group of photographs has never been published in a single book, and many have not been seen in decades. Images such as Michelangelo’s David entombed in brick for protection or a Rembrandt Self Portrait sitting atop crates in a salt mine, capture the story better than words could describe.

For the hundredth time, Tony Blair and Gordon Brown have been accused of launching an all-out conflict against each other. This time, the dispute centers around who should be credited for the government's global aid and debt programs, especially following the tsunami crisis—a matter many thought was beyond political contention. The issue became a focal point during the prime minister's monthly news conference, where Blair immediately adopted an angry tone as he faced numerous questions regarding his relationship with his neighbor. In his address, he stated, "I am not interested in what goes in and out of newspapers. There is a complete unity of purpose," and praised Brown for his efforts, promising continued support—though not committing to specific roles post-election. 

Why did Blair schedule his press conference at the last minute to coincide with Brown's planned speech on aid and debt? By this point, Blair had shifted from anger to thinly veiled fury. He dismissed the media's claims about the timing, stating that the operational reasons were clear. Despite this, he reiterated his admiration for Brown and emphasized unity, before sarcastically noting that he paid little attention to newspaper content and focused instead on national responsibilities. However, he later expressed concern over what he read in the papers, correcting himself by saying, "In so far as I read them, of course." He likely had valid concerns since the media extensively covered the alleged feud between the two leaders.

Regarding the timing of the prime minister's press conference, there are two possibilities. One is that it was a deliberate move to overshadow the chancellor and reclaim control of the initiative.

Apocalypse Now is not merely the greatest war film ever created but also one of the finest films in cinematic history, having won the prestigious Palme d'Or at Cannes. It is consistently hailed as a landmark in film history. Based on Joseph Conrad’s novel *Heart of Darkness*, the film delves beyond the Vietnam War itself, exploring war in general and examining the darkest aspects of the human psyche and how war affects individuals. It presents a timeless narrative about the universal human struggle, the duality of man—his moral nature and primal instincts, and the choices that shape his actions.

The film centers around US Army Captain Benjamin Willard (Martin Sheen), who is sent on a perilous mission into Cambodia via a river to kill a rogue, Colonel Kurtz (Marlon Brando), who has become mad and elevated himself into a god-like figure among the local tribes. While the premise is straightforward, the film transcends simplicity, offering a profound exploration of madness, hysteria, and the depths of human depravity. It invites viewers to reflect on the darkness within humanity. I could pen an entire book discussing this film, as there is so much to explore. My perspective is that the river symbolizes both the path to finding Kurtz and the descent into madness, reflecting the character’s internal journey toward evil, which is central to the film’s thematic focus on dehumanization. The journey through the river echoes Dante’s journey through treacherous and horrifying landscapes. There are three key stops along the river, each deepening the sense of dehumanization caused by war and introducing new forms of evil within the characters. 

The first stop is with Lieutenant Kilgore. This scene illustrates how Kilgore and his troops have succumbed to the obsession with war, having dehumanized their enemies. Their fixation on conflict has led them to embrace violence without remorse.

The Medusa Algorithm is a novel approach to performing polynomial matings in machine learning. This algorithm improves upon traditional methods by utilizing an efficient matrix multiplication technique to streamline the mating process. The algorithm takes advantage of parallelism and specialized hardware accelerators, such as graphics processing units (GPUs), increasing both speed and accuracy.

Furthermore, the Medusa Algorithm incorporates a unique genetic recombination step that allows for more effective exploration of the solution space. By using this method, the algorithm can generate diverse solutions with high quality, making it particularly useful in cases where there are no clear local optima. Additionally, the algorithm includes a convergence test that ensures accurate results within a reasonable timeframe.

Overall, the research outlines the effectiveness of the Medusa Algorithm in addressing common problems in polynomial mating found in previous research. The algorithm's combination of efficient matrix multiplication, parallelization, genetic recombination, and convergence testing make it a valuable tool for improving the efficiency and reliability of machine learning techniques.

Segmentation of organs or lesions from medical images plays an essential role
in many clinical applications such as diagnosis and treatment planning. Though
Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) have achieved the state-of-the-art
performance for automatic segmentation, they are often limited by the lack of
clinically acceptable accuracy and robustness in complex cases. Therefore,
interactive segmentation is a practical alternative to these methods. However,
traditional interactive segmentation methods require a large amount of user
interactions, and recently proposed CNN-based interactive segmentation methods
are limited by poor performance on previously unseen objects. To solve these
problems, we propose a novel deep learning-based interactive segmentation
method that not only has high efficiency due to only requiring clicks as user
inputs but also generalizes well to a range of previously unseen objects.
Specifically, we first encode user-provided interior margin points via our
proposed exponentialized geodesic distance that enables a CNN to achieve a good
initial segmentation result of both previously seen and unseen objects, then we
use a novel information fusion method that combines the initial segmentation
with only few additional user clicks to efficiently obtain a refined
segmentation. We validated our proposed framework through extensive experiments
on 2D and 3D medical image segmentation tasks with a wide range of previous
unseen objects that were not present in the training set. Experimental results
showed that our proposed framework 1) achieves accurate results with fewer user
interactions and less time compared with state-of-the-art interactive
frameworks and 2) generalizes well to previously unseen objects.

Torsten Schlüter, born on 30 September 1959 in Hennigsdorf, East Germany, is a German painter, performance artist, and writer. He completed his architectural training at the Bauhaus-Universität Weimar in 1981–1986 and later earned his university degree. After leaving architecture in 1986, he focused on painting. His decision to reject the established academic path led to him being excluded from Weimar. The island of Hiddensee in the Baltic Sea becomes his refuge. 

From 1986–1987, he worked as a sign painter, carpenter’s assistant, stage scene painter, and tennis trainer. He created sets and costumes for theater productions. In 1987, he founded the annual "Kunstgarten," an outdoor gallery on Hiddensee. Starting in 1988, he worked as a freelance artist. 

In 1989, he became politically involved with Neues Forum (New Forum). Following the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989, he began traveling and working on the road, particularly in Africa and India. By 1990, he established his art studio in the Atelierhaus Weimar. 

In 1994, he moved to a new art studio in the Kulturbrauerei, Berlin. In 1995, he designed the official logo for the island of Hiddensee. His art studio was located at Hackesche Höfe, Berlin, in 1996. 

In 1997, he co-initiated the "Tulipamwe" project, which explored the North-South divide in art between Germany and France, initiated by Jack Lang. By 2003, he had moved to a studio in Berlin Mitte. In 2004, he won the "Süddeutscher Aquarellpreis" award. He also engaged as an artist with Eisern Union – "1. FC Union Berlin" and the Goethe Institut Berlin.

In 2007 and 2010, he participated in the "Hiddensee Edition." In 2008, he presented the project "Well women-High Priestesses of the Market" at the Gerhart Hauptmann Haus, Hiddensee.

  based on a self-complementary metasurface. The self-complementary CPA (SCCPA)
  consists of two stacked pairs of complementary resonant metasurfaces and
  can provide efficient THz absorption with two resonances. Since the resonant
  surface currents of the two composite metasurfaces can have opposite signs

  amplified at the absorber resonance as a result of the coherent superposition

  magnetic flux density. The proposed absorber is composed purely of metal without

  complexity when compared to the previously reported passive or active absorbers

The Lehigh Division was a railway division of the Pennsylvania Railroad (PRR) in the United States, active from 1873 until 1968. It consisted of 154 miles (248 kilometers) of track in eastern Pennsylvania.

The Lehigh Division was created in 1873, when the Lehigh Valley Railroad merged with the PRR. The division's name came from the Lehigh River, which runs through the eastern part of its territory.

In the early 1900s, the Lehigh Division was home to some of the PRR's busiest coal mines, shipping coal to destinations as far away as New York City and Boston. The division's routes also served the cities of Philadelphia, Pittsburgh, and Harrisburg.

During the decline of coal mining in the mid-20th century, the Lehigh Division saw its passenger traffic decrease significantly. In 1958, Amtrak took over passenger service in the region, but this only further reduced the division's popularity.

The Lehigh Division was officially disbanded in 1968, but its legacy can still be seen in the numerous rail lines that continue to operate in the area today. Many of these lines have been converted to freight-only service, while others have been abandoned altogether.

Despite its history of decline, the Lehigh Division remains an important part of the region's transportation infrastructure. The division's former tracks continue to serve as critical connections for businesses and residents throughout eastern Pennsylvania.

I begin by stating that I have never read the book, and thus my review is based exclusively on the movie. I found the film challenging to watch and cried throughout much of it. While the film is visually beautiful, I believe the aspect that is often overlooked is the strong bond between John and his father. This relationship deeply moved me, especially the scene where John reads a letter after his father's stroke, which was both emotionally powerful and well-executed. 

The film addresses several significant themes, including the challenges faced by children with an autistic parent, who may be the sole caregiver. The characters' relationships with their autistic parents often involve difficulties related to routine and unpredictability, causing emotional strain. It is unfortunate that many still perceive autism as an acceptable justification for behavioral issues, and this film highlights an important message about a condition that is frequently misunderstood.

The relationship between John and Savannah is secondary to that between John and his father, and the performances by Channing Tatum and Amanda Seyfried were well-crafted and believable. Both actors conveyed genuine emotion and understanding of their characters, and I appreciated how the ending between them remained open to interpretation.

Overall, the film is a commendable effort that touches on important social issues, though no review can fully capture its impact. I couldn't watch it again due to its emotional power, but it underscores how moving and impactful the film is. It deserves watching, even just once.

1.5 to 2 pounds of pig's feet  
12 limes  
2 medium cucumbers (sliced, seeds removed and peeled)  
1 medium white onion  
1 scotch bonnet or thai pepper  
Salt and pepper to taste  
White vinegar to taste  
Water  
Place a large pot with water and salt into which the feet are already placed, bring to a boil and cook until tender, for 30 to 60 minutes. Thinly slice the onions or chop them into sticks, mix with salt, sliced cucumbers, lime juice, and adjust with water and vinegar to your liking. Add the thinly sliced pepper, using half of it if you're not accustomed to spicy foods. Please wear gloves and clean the cutting board and knives after finishing. Note: Marinate the pig's feet covered with plastic wrap in the refrigerator until ready. Once the pig is softened, remove it from the pot, transfer it to a bowl, and pour all the liquid from the cucumbers and onions into the bowl. Let it cool and marinate in the refrigerator for 2 to 3 hours. When ready to serve, remove the cucumbers and add the remaining sliced vegetables so they can marinate slightly before serving, ensuring they remain crisp and not soggy. You can serve it at room temperature or chilled; I enjoy both options! Note: I discovered I am mildly allergic to hot peppers and have had some discomfort using them, including jalapenos. If you come into contact with the pepper and your skin burns, apply very cold milk or sour cream to soothe it, and take a Benadryl to help you sleep—yes, it was that intense.

6 slices of bacon, chopped into 1/2-inch pieces  
4 to 4 pounds of beef blade roast or 4 pounds of cross-rib roast  
1/2 cup of brown sugar, packed  
2 teaspoons of salt  
1 teaspoon of garlic powder  
1 teaspoon of pepper  
1 teaspoon of dried thyme leaves  
1 cup of water  
12 ounces of beer  
Before serving  
To make gravy:  
1 cup of cold water  
1/2 cup of all-purpose flour  
Fry the bacon in a 5-quart Dutch oven until it becomes crispy. Remove it with a slotted spoon and drain it on paper towels. Cook the beef in the bacon fat over medium heat, turning it occasionally, until it is browned and drained. Add the brown sugar, salt, garlic powder, pepper, thyme, bacon, water, and beer. Bring this mixture to a boil and reduce the heat. Cover and let it simmer gently for 2 1/2 to 3 hours (or transfer it to a slow cooker and cook on low for 4 to 6 hours until the beef is tender). If you're serving it that night, continue cooking until ready.  
To serve: About 45 minutes before serving, remove the fat from the broth. (If using a slow cooker, add the vegetables for the last 1 1/2 hours.) Heat the beef and broth to a boil. Add the vegetables and cover, then simmer until the beef is hot and the vegetables are tender, which takes about 20 minutes. Remove the beef and vegetables and place them on a warm platter. Whisk the water and flour together in a covered container and mix them into the broth. Bring the broth to a boil, stirring or whisking continuously. Boil and stir for 1 minute. Serve the beef and vegetables with the broth.

A US energy firm has admitted paying $1 million in bribes to officials in Benin as part of an illegal scheme to gain lucrative contracts, according to allegations published by ProPublica and The New York Times on Tuesday (August 5th).
The payments were made over several years with the aim of securing power supply deals between Westinghouse Electric's subsidiary Atlantic Electric Power Corporation and the African government, which was looking for new suppliers. ProPublica reported that in one instance, a Westinghouse executive gave a gift of $700,000 in bribe money to a senior official in order to influence the outcome of bid negotiations. According to documents obtained by the two outlets, other officials were paid hundreds of thousands of dollars by ATAC in exchange for recommending its equipment to government agencies and companies. The scheme was uncovered through a whistleblower who exposed the corruption to authorities. In response, the United States Department of Justice said Westinghouse would pay $364 million in fines, including criminal penalties for violating anti-bribery laws in relation to similar schemes in Peru and Colombia.

To be idle is to become estranged from the cycles of nature and to drift from the orderly flow of life, moving in solemn reverence toward the boundless.  
When you labor, you become a flute where the murmurs of time transform into melody.  
Which among you would be a mute reed, voiceless amidst the harmonious chorus of creation?  
Throughout history, people have been taught that labor is a burden and toil is a hardship.  
Yet I assert that when you labor, you fulfill a vital part of Earth’s most distant aspiration, entrusted to you at its inception.  
By maintaining yourself through labor, you genuinely cherish life.  
To cherish life through labor is to intimately connect with life’s deepest mystery.  
However, if in your suffering you condemn birth as an ailment and the sustenance of the body as a cursed mark inscribed on your face, I respond that only the perspiration of your brow will cleanse that inscription.  
You have also been told that life is darkness, and in your fatigue, you echo the words of those who have long since wornied.  
I declare that life is indeed darkness, except when there is drive.  
All drive is blind unless guided by knowledge.  
All knowledge is futile unless accompanied by labor.  
All labor is empty unless infused with love.  
When you labor with love, you become bound to yourself, to others, and to the divine.  
What does it mean to labor with love?

A book about the evolution of mutants and the science of abnormality has won the Guardian First Book Award 2004.
Armand Marie Leroi, a lecturer at London's Imperial College, scooped the £10,000 prize for Mutants: On the form, varieties and errors of the human body. "It is profoundly cultured and beautifully written in the very best tradition of popular science writing today," said judge Claire Armistead. The award recognises and rewards new writing across fiction and non-fiction. A panel of literary experts, including novelists Hari Kunzru and Ali Smith, director Sir Richard Eyre and comedian Alexei Sayle chose the winner from a five-strong shortlist.
The shortlist included Susanna Clarke's Jonathan Strange and Mr Norrell, a novel about the magic arts at the turn of the 19th Century and The Places In Between, Rory Stewart's account of his trek, on foot, across Afghanistan. "What we found so impressive about Armand Marie Leroi's book was the scope of its reference, its elegance and its inquisitiveness," said Ms Armistead, chair of the judges and the Guardian literary editor. "While the subject matter of Mutants unsettled some involved in the judging process, the overwhelming majority found it fascinating," she added. Her words were echoed by Iris director Sir Richard Eyre who called Marie Leroi's work "extraordinarily thought provoking". The award, for first time authors, is open to books from genres including fiction, poetry, biography, memoir, history, politics, science and current affairs. Previous winners include White Teeth by Zadie Smith, in 2000, which went on to become a bestseller.

Global aphasia is a severe form of aphasia, a language disorder that results from damage to portions of the brain responsible for language. It is characterized by a significant impairment in all aspects of language comprehension and production. Individuals with global aphasia have difficulty understanding spoken or written language, finding the right words to express themselves, and reading or writing.

Global aphasia is most commonly caused by a stroke, particularly in the left hemisphere of the brain, which is responsible for language and communication. Other potential causes include traumatic brain injury, brain tumors, infections, and degenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's.

Symptoms of global aphasia can vary depending on the extent of brain damage. However, common symptoms include difficulty speaking or understanding speech, inability to read or write, and difficulty finding the right words. Some individuals may also experience physical difficulties such as weakness or paralysis on one side of the body.

Diagnosis of global aphasia is typically made through a series of language and cognitive tests conducted by a speech-language pathologist. These tests assess the individual's ability to understand, speak, read, and write. Brain imaging techniques such as MRI or CT scans may also be used to identify the location and extent of brain damage.

Treatment for global aphasia is usually centered around speech and language therapy. The goal of therapy is to improve the individual's ability to communicate by restoring as much language function as possible and teaching alternative methods of communication when necessary. The intensity and duration of therapy can vary depending on the severity of the aphasia.

The prognosis for individuals with global aphasia varies. Some individuals may make significant improvements, particularly with intensive speech and language therapy. However, others may continue to experience significant language difficulties. The extent of recovery is generally dependent on the size and location of the brain damage, the individual's age and health status, and the intensity of speech and language therapy.

Research into global aphasia is ongoing, with scientists seeking to better understand the brain mechanisms involved in language and communication, as well as develop more effective treatment strategies. Current research areas include the use of technology in aphasia therapy, the role of music therapy in language recovery, and the potential of certain medications to enhance language function.

In conclusion, global aphasia is a severe language disorder that significantly impacts an individual's ability to communicate. Despite the challenges it presents, many individuals with global aphasia are able to improve their communication skills with the help of speech and language therapy and other treatment strategies.

Japan's biggest bank, Mizuho Financial Group, has agreed to pay $1bn (£650m) in compensation and other costs after being accused by regulators of manipulating its benchmark interest rate for years. The deal will see the lender admit wrongdoing over its role in setting the Libor inter-bank lending rate between banks around the world. It also means that it will be forced to sell off assets worth more than $20bn. The settlement comes as Japan's financial regulator prepares to announce new rules on how banks should report their dealings with each other. The move could lead to further fines or even criminal charges against some of the country's largest lenders. The scandal erupted last year when Barclays was fined £290m for rigging Libor. But the Japanese government said it would not pursue any individual bankers involved in the scandal. Instead, it decided to settle with Mizuho, which had been accused of using its influence to help clients manipulate the rate. The bank admitted to having manipulated the rate since 2004. It paid $972m in penalties and $2.5bn in compensation. The settlement includes a provision for another $3.6bn in damages. The bank will have to sell off about $21bn of assets, including stakes in Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group and Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corp. The sale process will take several months. The bank will also have to make changes to its internal controls and procedures.

As you can see, this is just one part of a much larger story. As I've written before, there are many reasons why the US and UK governments want to bring down the big banks. One reason is because they know that if these banks fail, then we'll all suffer. Another reason is that they don't want to lose control of our money. And yet another reason is that they're afraid that if the big banks collapse, then they won't be able to continue to print money like crazy. So they're trying to force them into bankruptcy so that they can keep printing money.

But what happens if the big banks do go bankrupt? Well, that depends on who owns them. If the big banks were owned by the public, then they'd probably be nationalized. That way, the people who own them wouldn't be allowed to use them to create money out of thin air. They'd have to pay taxes on those profits

Butter a 10" springform cake pan. First Layer: Crush 8 ounces of Oreo cookies. (I used my Cuisinart to crush them). Add 1/4 cup melted butter to the crumbs and pulse again. The high-fidelity storage of quantum information is crucial for quantum
computation and communication. Many experimental platforms for these
applications exhibit highly biased noise, with good resilience to spin
depolarisation undermined by high dephasing rates. In this work, we demonstrate
that the memory performance of a noise-biased trapped-ion qubit memory can be
greatly improved by incorporating error correction of dephasing errors through
teleportation of the information between two repetition codes written on a pair
of qubit registers in the same trap. While the technical requirements of error
correction are often considerable, we show that our protocol can be achieved
with a single global entangling phase gate of remarkably low fidelity,
leveraging the fact that the gate errors are also dominated by dephasing-type
processes. By rebalancing the logical spin-flip and dephasing error rates, we
show that for realistic parameters our memory can exhibit error rates up to two
orders of magnitude lower than the unprotected physical qubits, thus providing
a useful means of improving memory performance in trapped ion systems where
field-insensitive qubits are not available.

Sayyid Muhammad ibn Zayn al-Din Ahmad al-Hassani al-Baghdadi, often referred to as Muhammad Zayni al-Baghdadi (1735–1801), was a prominent Ottoman Iraqi Muslim scholar, writer, and poet. He was born in Najaf into a Shia Muslim family and received education from his father and esteemed Shi’a scholars of Najaf, including Mahdi Bahr al-Ulum. He dedicated himself to religious advocacy and gained recognition in religious literature. His works included a collection of poetry in Arabic and Persian, as well as books on tafsir and Arabic literary studies. He is also the father of poet Jawad Siahpush. He died in Kadhimiya in 1801 and was buried there. 

His full lineage is Muhammad bin Ahmad Zayn al-Din bin Ali bin Sayf al-Din bin Ridha al-Din bin Al-Hassani al-Baghdadi, ending with Hassan ibn Ali. He was born in Najaf in 1735 and raised there by his father, who had migrated from Baghdad to Najaf. He studied under notable Shi’a scholars of Najaf, including Mahdi Bahr al-Ulum.

Zayni participated in the Ma’rakat al-Khamis (Battle of Thursday), a literary gathering. He served as a salon host, inviting poets and writers during weekly holidays, which positioned him as a leading literary figure in Najaf during the late 17th century, the capital of Twelver Shi’a Muslims. He passed away in 1801 in Kadhimiya and was interred there.

Chinese online game operator Shanda Interactive Entertainment has bought a 20% stake in Sina, the country's biggest internet portal firm.
The move may be a precursor to a full takeover, with analysts saying that a better-known international firm may also now show an interest in Sina. Shanda said that it may boost its stake in Sina, even buying it outright. A merger would create a firm that offers online role-playing games, news, entertainment and wireless messaging.
Sina said that the purchase of a stake by Shanda would have no impact on its business.
The board of directors said in a statement that it would "continue to act in the best interests of all the company stakeholders, including shareholders, employees and customers". Both companies are listed on the New York Stock Exchange's (NYSE) technology-dominated Nasdaq index. In a filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission, Sina said its shares were purchased between 12 January and 10 February for about $230m. Rumours about a possible takeover boosted Sina's shares by more than 10% on Friday. They added an extra 6.4% to $27.24 in electronic trading after the trading session had finished. And there may be more gains amid bid speculation when trading resumes in New York on Tuesday after Monday's public holiday, analysts forecast. "There could still be some potential parties that could still counter bid," said Wallace Cheung, an analyst at DBS Vickers. "Even though Shanda has 20% of Sina, they still have quite a long way to take full control." However, Mr Cheung noted that a foreign company trying to take control of a Chinese internet portal firm, with its ability to filter and pass on news, may not be viewed very favourably by Beijing.

Image segmentation, a crucial task in computer vision, has been extensively researched over the years. Early approaches predominantly employed unsupervised techniques that utilized manually crafted features to segment images into distinct regions. With the advent of deep learning advancements, convolutional neural network-based methodologies have demonstrated superior performance in image segmentation. Nevertheless, these approaches necessitate an extensive amount of human-labeled data, which is resource-intensive to acquire. This paper introduces a deep unsupervised technique for image segmentation, comprising two key phases. Initially, a Superpixelwise Autoencoder (SuperAE) is developed to extract deep embeddings and restore a smooth image, followed by the generation of superpixels from this smoothed image. Subsequently, a new clustering algorithm named Deep Superpixel Cut (DSC) is introduced, which assesses the deep similarity among superpixels and transforms image segmentation into a soft partitioning challenge. By leveraging backpropagation, DSC dynamically partitions superpixels into visually coherent regions. Experimental findings on the BSDS500 dataset validate the efficacy of the presented approach.

One of my favorite poems...  
The sea is calm tonight.  
The tide is full, the moon shines brightly  
On the straits; on the French coast, the light  
Flashes and disappears; the cliffs of England stand,  
Shining and vast, in the quiet bay.  
Come to the window, sweet is the night air!  
Only, from the long line of spray  
Where the sea meets the moonlit land,  
Listen! You hear the grating sound  
Of pebbles that the waves push back and throw,  
At their return, up the high shore,  
Starts, stops, and begins again,  
With a trembling rhythm slow and deep, bringing  
The eternal note of sorrow.  
Sophocles long ago  
Heard it on the Aegean, and it stirred  
Into his mind the murky ebb and flow  
Of human suffering; we  
Also find in this sound a thought,  
Hearing it through this distant northern sea.  
The Sea of Faith  
Was once, too, at its peak, and lay like the folds  
Of a bright belt folded over the earth's shore.  
But now I only hear  
Its mournful, long, retreating roar,  
Retreating to the breath  
Of the night wind, down the wide edges  
Drear and bare, of the world.  
Ah, love, let us be true  
To one another! For the world, which seems  
To lie before us like a land of dreams,  
So varied, so beautiful, so new,  
Has truly neither joy, nor love, nor light,  
Nor certainty, nor peace, nor help for pain;  
And we are here as on a darkling plain  
Swept with confused alarms of struggle and flight,  
Where ignorant armies clash by night.

extensive research effort to automatically segment the neurons to help guide
and eventually replace manual tracing. Until recently, there has been
comparatively less research on automatically detecting the actual synapses
between neurons. This discrepancy can, in part, be attributed to several
factors: obtaining neuronal shapes is a prerequisite first step in extracting a
connectome, manual tracing is much more time-consuming than annotating
synapses, and neuronal contact area can be used as a proxy for synapses in
determining connections.
  However, recent research has demonstrated that contact area alone is not a
sufficient predictor of synaptic connection. Moreover, as segmentation has
improved, we have observed that synapse annotation is consuming a more
significant fraction of overall reconstruction time. This ratio will only get
worse as segmentation improves, gating overall possible speed-up. Therefore, we
address this problem by developing algorithms that automatically detect
pre-synaptic neurons and their post-synaptic partners. In particular,
pre-synaptic structures are detected using a Deep and Wide Multiscale Recursive
Network, and post-synaptic partners are detected using a MLP with features
conditioned on the local segmentation.
  This work is novel because it requires minimal amount of training, leverages
advances in image segmentation directly, and provides a complete solution for
polyadic synapse detection. We further introduce novel metrics to evaluate our
algorithm on connectomes of meaningful size. These metrics demonstrate that
complete automatic prediction can be used to effectively characterize most
connectivity correctly.

> We study the effect of Coulomb repulsion on the dynamics and yields of linear coasting nucleosynthesis (LCN). In LCN, the expansion rate of the plasma is much slower than that of the baryon-free radiation fluid, so that the baryons are dragged along by the latter. This leads to an effective cooling of the baryonic matter which can be used as a mechanism to produce light elements such as 4He or D during Big Bang Nucleosynthesis (BBN) or primordial black holes (PBHs) after inflation. However, this process has been shown to fail when the number density of baryons becomes too large due to the strong Coulomb interaction between protons and electrons. Here we show how the inclusion of Coulomb screening effects allows one to extend the range of validity of LCN up to densities where the standard BBN scenario applies. As a result, it is possible to obtain a significant amount of deuterium production at temperatures below the QCD phase transition without violating any observational constraints.

Segmenting images of low quality or with missing data is a challenging
problem. Integrating statistical prior information about the shapes to be
segmented can improve the segmentation results significantly. Most shape-based
segmentation algorithms optimize an energy functional and find a point estimate
for the object to be segmented. This does not provide a measure of the degree
of confidence in that result, neither does it provide a picture of other
probable solutions based on the data and the priors. With a statistical view,
addressing these issues would involve the problem of characterizing the
posterior densities of the shapes of the objects to be segmented. For such
characterization, we propose a Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling-based
image segmentation algorithm that uses statistical shape priors. In addition to
better characterization of the statistical structure of the problem, such an
approach would also have the potential to address issues with getting stuck at
local optima, suffered by existing shape-based segmentation methods. Our
approach is able to characterize the posterior probability density in the space
of shapes through its samples, and to return multiple solutions, potentially
from different modes of a multimodal probability density, which would be
encountered, e.g., in segmenting objects from multiple shape classes. We
present promising results on a variety of data sets. We also provide an
extension for segmenting shapes of objects with parts that can go through
independent shape variations. This extension involves the use of local shape
priors on object parts and provides robustness to limitations in shape training
data size.

If your period is delayed, it can be incredibly stressful and worrying. There are many factors that can cause a period to be late, including hormonal changes, stress, and other medical conditions. Here are some tips to help manage your concerns:
1. Wait - Sometimes a period can be up to two weeks late and still considered normal. If you're anxious about it, try distracting yourself with something fun or relaxing until you get your next period.
2. Keep track - Track when you expect your period typically starts and ends so you can better keep track if it's running late. This will also allow you to notice any patterns or potential issues more quickly.
3. Call for backup - Contact your healthcare provider right away if your period has been absent for over typical time frame. They may recommend further testing or treatment options based on the cause.
4. Take care of yourself - Make sure you're eating well, exercising regularly, getting enough sleep and managing stress levels because these factors can affect your menstrual cycle.
Remember, everyone's body is unique and there can be many reasons why periods run late. Don't let worry get in the way of enjoying life. Seek professional advice if you need to and try to stay positive and relaxed during this trying times.

Breaking up is never easy, and ending things with someone who you still have feelings for can be especially difficult. It's important to remember that loving someone doesn't mean sacrificing your own happiness or well-being. If you find yourself in this situation, here are some steps to help you gather the courage to end it:

1. Self-reflection: Take time to reflect on why you want to end things. Is there something that isn't working out anymore? Are you growing apart from each other? Make sure you've thought about this thoroughly before making any decisions.
2. Set boundaries: Try setting boundaries with your partner. Maybe limit your interactions or take some space until you both feel ready to have an honest conversation. This can help ease the pain and give you time to process what's going on.
3. Talk to trusted friends and family: Sometimes talking things through with others can be helpful. Reach out to people you trust to get their perspective on the situation and gain support during a difficult time.
4. Use positive self-talk: Be gentle and kind to yourself. Remember that this decision will likely hurt at first, but reminding yourself of how much your happiness matters can make starting fresh easier.
5. Focus on your future goals: Consider where you see yourself personally and professionally in the next few years. Ending things with someone may be the best choice if it means you can work towards building a better life for yourself without them holding you back.

Remember, you deserve to be happy and healthy. Lean into that feeling and know that you made the right decision for your own well-being.

Germany's economy, the biggest among the 12 countries sharing the euro, grew at its fastest rate in four years during 2004, driven by strong exports.
Gross domestic product (GDP) rose by 1.7% last year, the statistical office said. The economy contracted in 2003. Foreign sales increased by 8.2% last year, compared with a 0.3% slide in private consumption. Concerns remain, however, over the strength of the euro, weak domestic demand and a sluggish labour market. The European Central Bank (ECB) left its benchmark interest rate unchanged at 2% on Thursday. It is the nineteenth month in a row that the ECB has not moved borrowing costs. Economists predict that an increase is unlikely to come until the second half of 2005, with growth set to sputter rather than ignite.
"During 2004 we profited from the fact that the world economy was strong," said Stefan Schilbe, analyst at HSBC Trinkaus & Burkhardt. "If exports weaken and domestic growth remains poor, we cannot expect much from 2005." Many German consumers have been spooked and unsettled by government attempts to reform the welfare state and corporate environment. Major companies including Volkswagen, DaimlerChrysler and Siemens have spent much of 2004 in tough talks with unions about trimming jobs and costs. They have also warned there are more cost cutting measures on the horizon.

Naina’s Stuffed Chicken Recipe

Ingredients: 
- 6 large boneless, skinless chicken breasts 
- 1 cup uncooked white rice 
- 2 cups vegetable broth 
- 1 tablespoon olive oil 
- 1 medium onion, diced 
- 3 cloves garlic, minced 
- 1 can (14.5 oz) diced tomatoes, drained 
- 1 teaspoon dried basil leaves  
- Salt and pepper to taste 
- Fresh parsley or cilantro, chopped (optional garnish) 

Instructions:
1. Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C). Grease a large baking dish with cooking spray or olive oil.

2. In a saucepan over high heat, bring the vegetable broth to boil. Add the rice, then reduce the heat to low, cover, and simmer for about 18 minutes until cooked. Fluff the rice with a fork and set aside.

3. Heat olive oil in a large skillet over medium heat. Add the diced onions and cook until softened, around 5 minutes.

4. Add in the minced garlic and cook for another minute, until fragrant.

5.Add the cooked rice, diced tomatoes, dried basil leaves, salt and pepper to the skillet. Mix well and Cook for additional 3-5 minutes

6. Use a sharp knife to slice a pocket into the side of each chicken breast, being careful not to cut through to the other side.

7. Stuff each chicken breast with the rice mixture, and use toothpicks to secure the opening closed.

8. Place the stuffed chicken breasts in the prepared baking dish, seam-side down. Bake for 25-30 minutes or until internal temperature reaches 165°F (74°C)

9. Remove from oven and let it rest for 5 minutes before serving. Garnish with fresh parsley or cilantro, if desired. Enjoy!

Liverpool and Millwall have been charged by the Football Association over crowd trouble during their Carling Cup match on 26 October.
Millwall, who lost the match 3-0, have also been charged over alleged racist behaviour by their supporters. During the match at Millwall's new Den Stadium, seats were ripped up and four people were ejected from the ground. A disabled fan was injured at the perimeter of the pitch and riot police were needed to control the situation. Liverpool fans claimed the trouble was sparked by chants about the Hillsborough disaster, where 96 supporters were crushed to death in April 1989. But Lions chairman Theo Paphitis has denied the claims. He has said CCTV footage showed the catalyst for the trouble was a Liverpool fan attacking a Millwall fan in the west stand. However, Millwall have been charged with two breaches of FA rules. They have been charged with failing to ensure that fans refrained from racist and/or abusive behaviour and for failing to prevent spectators throwing missiles onto the pitch. Liverpool have been charged with one breach for failing to prevent their fans conducting themselves in threatening and/or violent and/or provocative behaviour. Both clubs have until 23 December to respond.

Jiang Fan (; born 16 September 1989) is a Chinese track and field athlete who competes in the 110 metres hurdles. He is a two-time champion in the 60 metres hurdles at the Asian Indoor Athletics Championships (2010 and 2012) and was the silver medallist outdoors at the 2011 Summer Universiade. He represented China at the 2011 World Championships in Athletics and set a 110 m hurdles best of 13.47 seconds at the competition. Jiang began competing at national level in 2007 and made his international debut for China at the 2008 Asian Junior Athletics Championships, where he finished fifth in the 110 m hurdles. That year he ran a personal best of 13.83 seconds at the Good Luck Beijing pre-Olympic trial event. He also ran a best of 13.50 seconds over the smaller junior hurdles while taking second place at the Chinese junior championships. He began to establish himself among his country's top hurdlers the following season and ran a personal best of 13.69 seconds to win at Zhaoqing leg of the Chinese Grand Prix. At the end of the year he represented the Jiangsu province at the 11th Chinese Games and finished in fifth place.

China's strong economy and Japan's unexpected resurgence—despite recent setbacks—are anticipated to support global economic recovery, the OECD added. "Support for the world economy will continue to grow."

We examine a randomized algorithm for graph domination, where vertices are revealed and added to the dominating set in accordance with a randomly selected permutation. If a vertex is not yet dominated, it is revealed and included in the dominating set. By analyzing this algorithm, we calculate the expected size of the dominating set generated for the path graph $P_n$, and apply this result to other related graph classes. Subsequently, we conduct a detailed examination of the algorithm's behavior on $P_n$, focusing on its worst and best-case scenarios, and identify specific permutations that lead to optimal or suboptimal performance. This research also connects to prior work by Bouwer and Star on path domination and by Gessel on greedy coloring of paths.

Internet search engine users are an odd mix of naive and sophisticated, suggests a report into search habits.
The report by the US Pew Research Center reveals that 87% of searchers usually find what they were looking for when using a search engine. It also shows that few can spot the difference between paid-for results and organic ones. The report reveals that 84% of net users say they regularly use Google, Ask Jeeves, MSN and Yahoo when online.
Almost 50% of those questioned said they would trust search engines much less, if they knew information about who paid for results was being hidden. According to figures gathered by the Pew researchers the average users spends about 43 minutes per month carrying out 34 separate searches and looks at 1.9 webpages for each hunt. A significant chunk of net users, 36%, carry out a search at least weekly and 29% of those asked only look every few weeks. For 44% of those questioned, the information they are looking for is critical to what they are doing and is information they simply have to find.
Search engine users also tend to be very loyal and once they have found a site they feel they can trust tend to stick with it. According to Pew Research 44% of searchers use just a single search engine, 48% use two or three and a small number, 7%, consult more than three sites. Tony Macklin, spokesman for Ask Jeeves, said the results reflected its own research which showed that people use different search engines because the way the sites gather information means they can provide different results for the same query. Despite this liking for search sites half of those questioned said they could get the same information via other routes. A small number, 17%, said they wouldn't really miss search engines if they did not exist. The remaining 33% said they could not live without search sites. More than two-thirds of those questioned, 68%, said they thought that the results they were presented with were a fair and unbiased selection of the information on a topic that can be found on the net. Alongside the growing sophistication of net users is a lack of awareness about paid-for results that many search engines provide alongside lists of websites found by indexing the web. Of those asked, 62% were unaware that someone has paid for some of the results they see when they carry out a search. Only 18% of all searchers say they can tell which results are paid for and which are not. Said the Pew report: "This finding is ironic, since nearly half of all users say they would stop using search engines if they thought engines were not being clear about how they presented paid results." Commenting Mr Macklin said sponsored results must be clearly marked and though they might help with some queries user testing showed that people need to be able to spot the difference.

This study introduces a new method for initializing deep neural network layers using Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA). Usually, weights are initialized with random values, greedy layer-wise pre-training (such as Deep Belief Networks or auto-encoders), or by repurposing layers from other models (transfer learning). As a result, extensive training epochs are necessary for meaningful weight learning, or a similar dataset is required for effective transfer learning fine-tuning. In this work, we demonstrate how to convert an LDA framework into a neural layer or a classification layer. We evaluate the initialization strategy on historical documents, demonstrating that LDA-based initialization is fast and provides highly stable starting points. Additionally, for pixel-level layout analysis, we assess the efficacy of LDA-based initialization and find that it surpasses existing random initialization techniques.

In this paper, we propose opportunistic jammer selection in a wireless
security system for increasing the secure degrees of freedom (DoF) between a
transmitter and a legitimate receiver (say, Alice and Bob). There is a jammer
group consisting of $S$ jammers among which Bob selects $K$ jammers. The
selected jammers transmit independent and identically distributed Gaussian
signals to hinder the eavesdropper (Eve). Since the channels of Bob and Eve are
independent, we can select the jammers whose jamming channels are aligned at
Bob, but not at Eve. As a result, Eve cannot obtain any DoF unless it has more
than $KN_j$ receive antennas, where $N_j$ is the number of jammer's transmit
antenna each, and hence $KN_j$ can be regarded as defensible dimensions against
Eve. For the jamming signal alignment at Bob, we propose two opportunistic
jammer selection schemes and find the scaling law of the required number of
jammers for target secure DoF by a geometrical interpretation of the received
signals.

"Re-Make/Re-Model" is a song written by Bryan Ferry that appears as the opening track on Roxy Music's eponymous debut album.  The recording starts with some brief background ambiance of a cocktail party, before launching into the song. Whilst the basic backing track of guitar, acoustic piano, bass guitar, tenor saxophone and drums is relatively straightforward and traditional in form, other elements of the arrangement are quite bizarre and futuristic: Eno plays continual squalls of atonal oscillator noise using Andy MacKay's VCS3 synthesizer, whilst Ferry's lead vocal style is strikingly distraught and anguished in tone. The lead guitar and saxophone solos in the middle of the song also tend to cacophony. In the song, each instrument is allowed a short solo break in turn; the sax mimics the trumpets from Richard Wagner's opera "the Valkyrie" and the bass guitar solo mimics the riff from the Beatles song "Day Tripper". Phil Manzanera's guitar part reverses the usual guitar pattern: he plays single-note lead guitar all through the song, with no chords, but his solo break consists only of chords.

Radiation damping (RD) influences T1 measurements in inversion recovery experiments. This study shows that the impact of RD varies depending on the sample's T1 value. RD difference spectroscopy (RADDSY) is employed to assess the intensity of RD, whereas gradient inversion recovery (GIR) is utilized to mitigate RD during T1 measurements. At 9.4 T, with a radiation damping characteristic time (Trd) of 50 ms, investigations reveal significant RD effects for T1 values exceeding Trd, leading to pronounced distortions when T1 exceeds approximately 150 ms. These findings align reasonably with theoretical predictions of Trd. Additionally, a deviation is noted in the published formulas for the characteristic RD time.

Vibration Cooking: The Travel Notes of a Geechee Girl is the 1970 debut cookbook by Vertamae Smart-Grosvenor, blending recipes with narrative. It was published by Doubleday. A second edition appeared in 1986, and a third in 1992. The University of Georgia released another edition in 2011. Smart-Grosvenor continued to write cookbooks afterward. Vibration Cooking brought attention to Gullah culture. Scholar Anne E. Goldman likened it to Jessica Harris' Iron Pots and Wooden Spoons, stating that in both works, "the model of the self... is historicized through colonial contexts." Scholar Lewis V. Baldwin praised the book for its insightful exploration of food's social importance and its connection to place in a Southern setting. The book motivated filmmaker Julie Dash to create Daughters of the Dust, which received recognition at the Sundance Film Festival. See also Vertamae Smart-Grosvenor.

We propose and study a task we name panoptic segmentation (PS). Panoptic
segmentation unifies the typically distinct tasks of semantic segmentation
(assign a class label to each pixel) and instance segmentation (detect and
segment each object instance). The proposed task requires generating a coherent
scene segmentation that is rich and complete, an important step toward
real-world vision systems. While early work in computer vision addressed
related image/scene parsing tasks, these are not currently popular, possibly
due to lack of appropriate metrics or associated recognition challenges. To
address this, we propose a novel panoptic quality (PQ) metric that captures
performance for all classes (stuff and things) in an interpretable and unified
manner. Using the proposed metric, we perform a rigorous study of both human
and machine performance for PS on three existing datasets, revealing
interesting insights about the task. The aim of our work is to revive the
interest of the community in a more unified view of image segmentation.

Two of the peasants jumped on top of the wagon and pulled Chutu off the back. They proceeded to beat and stab him to death.
According to an account of the event given by John Dardess, the first scholar to study the incident, Chutu was an important figure in the local administration of Mianchi county, a Confucian scholar who was known to have been a "strait-laced, austere man dedicated to his moral ideals." Chutu's murder was a sign that much of the countryside in late-Ming China had fallen into chaos, so much so that "the death of the local official was not worth a public announcement."
Chutu Wang, after all, had been a Confucian gentry who had received his education in accordance with the principles of Confucius. At the age of seven or eight (in the year 1764) he would have been given the "Three Teachings, Three Obediences" (sanjiao, sanzun) education, where he would have studied, among others, the Confucian classics. Furthermore, Chutu would also have been given the Chinese equivalent of an SAT exam, which would have been administered by the Chinese Educational Commission in Beijing. George Steadman Holden (September 29, 1868 – July 9, 1935) was an American football player and manufacturer.  Holden was born in Middlefield, Massachusetts, in 1868.  He was the son of Henry Parker and Mary A. (Holmes) Holden.  He moved to Palmer, Massachusetts, in 1871 when his father purchased interests in several local businesses.  Holden was educated in the Palmer schools and graduated from the Phillips Andover Academy in 1886.  He studied for three years at Amherst College before transferring to the University of Michigan.  He played college football and was the starting quarterback for the 1890 Michigan Wolverines football team.  Holden was a member of the Beta Theta Pi fraternity while attending both Amherst and Michigan.  He graduated from Michigan in 1891.  In March 1896, he married Katherine Cramer of Ann Arbor, Michigan.  They had three children, Roger Cramer Holden, Philip Holmes Holden, and Henry Parker Holden.  He worked in the woolen business in Palmer, Massachusetts, and became the superintendent of the Palmer Woolen Mill in 1895 and the financial manager starting in 1900.  In July 1935, Holden died at his home in Palmer.

Ned prises James out of Leonora's grasp, only to reject him for another lover. James attempts a reconciliation with Leonora, but she refuses to give him a second opportunity to hurt her, and settles for the admiration of the less attractive Humphrey. 2 tablespoons of extra-virgin olive oil  
1 1/2 cups thinly sliced fresh wild or domestic mushrooms  
Gray salt  
Freshly ground black pepper  
1 onion, diced  
1 tablespoon plus 1 teaspoon minced garlic  
1/2 pound yellow squash, cut into 1/4-inch dice, about 1 1/2 cups  
1/4 cup diced red bell pepper, cut into 1/4-inch dice  
3 tablespoons finely chopped fresh thyme leaves  
1/2 pound zucchini, cut into 1/4-inch dice, about 1 1/2 cups  
1/2 cup thinly sliced leek, white part only  
3/4 cup peeled, seeded, and chopped vine-ripened tomatoes, about 1/2 pounds  
1 cup loosely packed baby spinach, sliced  
2 tablespoons coarsely chopped fresh basil leaves  
1/4 cup freshly grated Parmesan  

Heat 2 tablespoons of the olive oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat until hot. Add the mushrooms and cook, without moving them, until brown on one side, about 1 minute. Continue to sauté for another 1 to 2 minutes. Season mushrooms with salt and pepper and transfer them to a cookie sheet to cool. Set aside the used pan. In a separate, clean skillet, heat 1 tablespoon of oil over medium heat. Add minced garlic. Cook until golden brown, about 1 to 2 minutes. Add onion and cook until softened, about 5 minutes. In the pan where the mushrooms were, add 2 tablespoons of olive oil over medium heat. Add yellow squash. Cook until browned, about 1 to 2 minutes and drain onto the same cookie sheet with mushrooms. Place peppers in the hot pan where squash was cooking, sprinkle with 2 tablespoons of thyme. When heated thoroughly, add peppers to the waiting mushrooms and yellow squash. Add zucchini to the same pan, add remaining thyme, cook until browned, about 2 minutes. Remove both pans (onions and zucchini) from the heat, and add them to the cookie sheet with other vegetables. In the former zucchini/mushroom pan, cook leeks to soften, about 2 minutes. In the other, bring the tomatoes to a simmer. Season the leeks with salt and pepper, to taste, and add spinach. When spinach is wilted, add cooked leeks to the cooling vegetables on the cookie sheet. Add basil to the tomato pan.

Recent developments in deep learning-driven image segmentation techniques have facilitated real-time execution with performance comparable to human experts. Nevertheless, even the most advanced methodologies may falter due to poor image quality, artifacts, or unpredictable behavior of black-box algorithms. The ability to forecast segmentation quality without relying on ground truth data is critical in both clinical settings and large-scale research to prevent the inclusion of incorrect data in subsequent analyses.

In this study, we introduce two real-time automated quality control strategies for cardiovascular magnetic resonance (MR) segmentations using deep learning. Initially, we train a neural network on 12,880 samples to estimate Dice Similarity Coefficients (DSC) on a case-by-case basis. Our results show a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.03 across 1,610 test cases and 97% binary classification accuracy for distinguishing between low- and high-quality segmentations. In scenarios lacking manually annotated data, we train another network to predict DSC scores from quality estimates derived through a reverse testing approach. This method achieves an MAE of 0.14 and 91% binary classification accuracy. Real-time predictions are generated, allowing immediate feedback on the analyzability of scans during the patient's time in the scanner. This capability supports novel applications in optimizing imaging protocols to achieve optimal analytical outcomes.

I teach a graduate-level course on World War II, having studied the topic under various specialists and interviewed numerous survivors from both sides. This film stands out as potentially the best ever produced on the subject, though films like the Belorussian "Come and See" and "Schindler's List" are also exceptionally strong.  

Last night, I watched the film with two veterans: one a U.S. soldier who fought from Omaha to Czechoslovakia, and another a German infantry officer who served on the Eastern Front for four years. The German, who encountered Hitler multiple times, was amazed by the film’s historical accuracy, particularly the authenticity of Hitler’s lower-class Munich accent—a detail Americans might miss. My German friend, who, after the war, was stationed in East Prussia during the chaotic evacuation of a million civilians before the Soviets arrived, was deeply moved by the film. He described the horrors, including hospital scenes, chaos, lynchings, and the sight of 12-year-old children fighting—everything felt real. An intriguing comment came from him: he didn’t realize Berlin, at the end, had been as terrible as what he saw along the Baltic Coast and is still affected by it. The film captures the despair of an entire nation, bringing the events very close to the viewer. If you're a parent with young children, the frightening conclusion about Goebbels’ children is an unforgettable nightmare.  

The film’s greatest strength lies in its depiction of Hitler. Rather than being portrayed as the cliché of a madman, the actor shows a more nuanced side. I’ve spoken with many who knew Hitler, including Helga Goebbels' childhood friend, and they all agree that Hitler could be charming and attentive, even courtly with women. The chilling aspect is that while the actor portrays a human side, he simultaneously issues commands in a soft voice.

Max Ferdinand Perutz  (19 May 1914 – 6 February 2002) was an Austrian-born British molecular biologist, who shared the 1962 Nobel Prize for Chemistry with John Kendrew, for their studies of the structures of haemoglobin and myoglobin. He went on to win the Royal Medal of the Royal Society in 1971 and the Copley Medal in 1979.  At Cambridge he founded and chaired (1962–79) The Medical Research Council (MRC) Laboratory of Molecular Biology (LMB), fourteen of whose scientists have won Nobel Prizes. Perutz's contributions to molecular biology in Cambridge are documented in The History of the University of Cambridge: Volume 4 (1870 to 1990) published by the Cambridge University Press in 1992. Early life and education
Perutz was born in Vienna, the son of Adele "Dely" (Goldschmidt) and Hugo Perutz, a textile manufacturer. His parents were Jewish by ancestry, but had baptised Perutz in the Catholic religion. Although Perutz rejected religion and was an atheist in his later years, he was against offending others for their religious beliefs.
