Shortly after Dreamworks screwed up with the uninspired "Shark Tale", Pixar contains its remarkably success story with "The Incredibles". And while I have to say that I liked "Finding Nemo" a bit better, "The Incredibles" is still an amazing movie.

First of all, this is because it's funny. It's not so funny that you're constantly laughing out loud, but there are more than enough good jokes in the movie to keep you entertained, and it's full of good observations about superhero movies (note all the ridiculous superhero and villain names) and references to other movies. It's also a brilliant James Bond spoof/homage, containing all the gadgets, secret island bases and crazy schemes that made early Bond movies so much fun.

Secondly, this movie has heart and charm in droves. It's full of memorably and likable characters you can really identify with and care about. Characters like Edna are instant classics. The voice acting is universally excellent, but Holly Hunter steals the show as Elastigirl. This is a movie that doesn't need toilet humor, characters modeled like celebrities, or a "hip" soundtrack...it easily succeeds on charm and style alone.

Also, I found it to be a surprisingly good action movie. The plentiful action sequences are full of energy, extremely fast-paced, and exciting, and put many a live-action movie to shame.

Finally, I also liked the tone and message of the movie. "The Incredibles" basically makes a plea against mediocrity, breaking with the politically correct idea that "everybody is special" (and thus nobody really is), and encouraging people to use the talents they have been given. I think this couldn't be more true. Not all people are equally talented (just compare Pixar to Dreamworks), but this is no reason to keep the talented people from not reaching their full potential just because it makes the less talented ones feel bad.

"The Incredibles", while maybe not as hilarious as I had hoped (though it's still very funny), is nonetheless an extremely entertaining movie, that manages to charm you wit its combination of great characters, lots of style, tongue-in-cheek attitude and good message. Highly recommended.

5 - 6 quarts water  
2 pounds dried large lima beans (rinsed)  
2 - 3 medium onions (peeled and quartered)  
6 - 7 medium potatoes (diced)  
2 additional medium potatoes (grated)  
2 pounds bacon (cubed and browned)  
2 carrots (diced)  
2 stalks celery (diced)  
4 cups tomatoes (diced, canned will do)  
2 bay leaves  
3/4 tablespoon thyme  
3/4 tablespoon paprika  
2 tablespoons lemon juice  
salt  
pepper  
flavorful hot sauce (optional)  

1. Rinse lima beans and place them in water along with quartered onions, carrots, and celery in a pot or Dutch oven.  
2. Bring the mixture to a boil over medium heat.  
3. Reduce the heat and simmer for an hour.  
4. Add the two grated potatoes and simmer for an additional half hour.  
5. Add the remaining potatoes along with the golden brown bacon (omit the bacon drippings unless you prefer the fat and extra calories).  
6. (Optional) Add one cup of grated cauliflower or one cup of flour for a thicker broth.  
7. Continue to simmer for another half hour, then add four cups of diced tomatoes (canned will work), two bay leaves, 3/4 T thyme, 3/4 T paprika, 2 T lemon juice, salt, and pepper to taste, and optional flavorful hot sauce.  
8. Simmer for three to four more hours until ready, stirring occasionally and adding water as needed to prevent burning. Alternatively, remove from heat and transfer to a 7-qt or 8-qt crockpot for five to six hours on low settings. If the consistency is too thin, add warm water before serving. The broth can be refrigerated overnight and transferred to the crockpot the next day, adding a little extra water if needed, for six to seven hours. However, wait until after the time is up to add lemon juice. Some find the soup bland, so avoid over-seasoning during cooking and let each person adjust their seasoning. It pairs well with cornbread, a multi-grain muffin, or a roll. An ale enhances the flavor.

Brewers' profits lose their fizz

 Financial results for the world's biggest beer makers have been flatlining in recent months as a young generation shuns the drink.

AB InBev, the owner of Budweiser and Stella Artois, reported a 0.5% fall in organic revenue in the first three months of the year.

The company blamed bad weather in Europe for a 1.3% drop in volumes, while profits were also hit by higher commodity prices.

Heineken, the world's second biggest brewer, reported a 0.9% fall in beer volumes in the first three months of the year.

also announced a 0.5% drop in revenues, blaming "Korea and Nigeria".

Carlsberg, the third biggest global brewer, posted a 0.4% drop in beer sales in the first three months of 2018.

The Danish company said that it had seen "high single-digit growth" in eastern Europe, but this was offset by declines in China and Western Europe.

All three companies have been trying to offset falling demand for beer in developed markets by raising prices and investing in new products.

AB InBev said it was "encouraged" by the performance of its new non-alcoholic beer, Budweiser Zero.

But it is clear that the global beer market is struggling to find growth.

In the US, the world's biggest beer market, sales have been in decline for a decade.

In 2017, beer sales fell by 1% in volume and 2% in value, according to industry group the Beer Institute.

The trend is being driven by a younger generation of drinkers who are turning their backs on the traditional pint.

"People are drinking less beer and they're drinking better beer," said Simon Thorpe, chief executive of Sheffield-based beer maker and pub group Molson Coors.

"The big challenge for the beer category is how do we continue to be relevant to consumers, particularly younger consumers."

The global beer market is forecast to grow by just 1% this year, according to research group Euromonitor.

The Medusa algorithm accepts two postcritically finite quadratic polynomials as inputs and produces the quadratic rational map resulting from their mating, if it exists. The output consists of a series of approximations for the parameters of the rational map along with an image of its Julia set. Convergence of these approximations is determined by Thurston's topological classification of rational maps.

This algorithm was developed by John Hamal Hubbard and implemented in 1998 by Christian Henriksen and his REU students David Farris and Kuon Ju Liu. In this paper, we present the algorithm and its implementation, explore some results generated by the software (including numerous visual illustrations), and address associated inquiries. We also include images and discussions regarding certain shared matings, Lattes examples, and tuning sequences of matings.

Kodomo is the pseudonym of electronic musician Chris Child, an Emmy-nominated full-time composer based in Portland, Maine. As Kodomo, he is renowned for his contributions to the Harmonix video games Amplitude and Frequency, as well as the iPod game Phase, which includes his track "Spira Mirabilis." The term "Kodomo" refers to the Japanese word for "child," both honoring his surname and reflecting his upbringing in Japan. His debut album, Still Life, is a concept-driven work where all the music was inspired by a collection of photographs taken during his travels across the United States and abroad. Each track is named after the photographic images rather than using words. For instance, "Concept 13" began with a photo depicting Fibonacci proportions, which are commonly found in nature. These proportions influenced the musical composition, including its melodic structure, sound design, and progression. The governing number here is approximately 1.618, with themes introduced at these intervals, creating a balanced and organic feel throughout the piece.

The book begins in April 1979 at a small academic conference at the University of Rummidge. It is the first conference that Persse McGarrigle, (a reference to Percival the grail knight), an innocent young Irishman who recently completed his master's thesis on T. S. Eliot, has attended. He teaches at the fictional University College, Limerick, after having been mistakenly interviewed because the administration sent the interview invitation to him instead of someone else with the same last name. Several important characters are introduced: Rummidge professor Philip Swallow, American professor Morris Zapp, retired Cambridge professor Sybil Maiden, and the beautiful Angelica Pabst, with whom McGarrigle falls immediately in love. Much of the rest of the book is his quest to find and win her. Angelica tells Persse that she was adopted by an executive at KLM after she was found, abandoned, in the washroom of an airplane in flight. Persse professes his love for her, but she leaves the conference without telling him where she has gone. Morris Zapp and Philip Swallow, who are seeing each other for the first time in ten years after the events of Changing Places, have a long evening talk. Since the previous novel, Swallow has become a professor and head of the English Department. Zapp has discovered deconstructionism and reinvented himself academically. Swallow tells Zapp about an incident a few years before, when after almost dying in a plane crash he spent the night at a British Council official's home and slept with the official's wife, Joy. Soon after, Swallow read in the newspaper that Joy, the official, and their son had died in a plane crash. Part II of the book begins by going around the world, time zone to time zone, showing what different characters are doing all at the same time: Morris Zapp travelling; Australian Rodney Wainright trying to write a conference paper; Zapp's ex-wife Désirée trying to write a novel; Howard Ringbaum trying to convince his wife Thelma to sleep with him on an airplane so he can join the Mile High Club; Siegfried von Turpitz talking to Arthur Kingfisher about the new UNESCO chair of literary criticism; Rudyard Parkinson plotting to get that chair; Turkish Akbil Borak reading William Hazlitt to prepare for a visit by Swallow; Akira Sakazaki translating English novelist Ronald Frobisher into Japanese; Ronald Frobisher having breakfast; Italian Fulvia Morgana (a reference to Morgan le Fay) meeting Morris Zapp on a plane; and more.` Cheryl Summerbee is also introduced. She is a check-in clerk for British Airways at Heathrow and plays a small but very important role in helping, or hindering, other characters as they travel around the world. She loves reading romance novels, especially the kind published by "Bills and Moon" (a fictionalized Mills & Boon). People continue to move around from conference to conference around the world in Part III. Persse continues to pursue Angelica. At a meeting in Amsterdam, Persse hears the German literary scholar Siegfried von Turpitz speaking about ideas that he submitted in an unpublished book, and all but accuses von Turpitz of plagiarism. Zapp rises to defend Persse from von Turpitz. Later, Persse sees someone who looks like Angelica, and thinks she has appeared in pornographic movies and worked as a stripper. In Turkey, Phillip Swallow meets Joy, the woman he thought was dead. She explains that only her husband had been on the plane that crashed. They begin an affair, and Swallow plans to leave his wife. Events and characters move along in Part IV, often with direct reference to the genre of romance, such as Sybil Maiden (who at one point acts as a sibyl) saying that grail knights "were such boobies... All they had to do was ask a question at the right moment, and they generally muffed it." Zapp is kidnapped by an underground left-wing movement, but is later released after pressure from Morgana. Persse, who has won an award and got a credit card, has enough money to continue to chase Angelica but never manages to catch up with her. She does leave him a clue referencing The Faerie Queene and he discovers that she has an identical twin, and it is the twin, Lily, who made the pornographic movies. When Persse meets Cheryl Summerbee again, she is now reading not romance novels but romances such as Orlando Furioso and critics such as Northrop Frye after Angelica has passed through her line. Persse is happy to learn this, but Cheryl is shaken to see that Persse is infatuated with Angelica, because she loves him herself. Persse continues to chase Angelica around the world, to conferences in Hawaii, Tokyo, and Hong Kong, and Jerusalem, but he never catches up with her. At that Jerusalem conference, Philip Swallow is with Joy, but after he sees his son there he becomes psychosomatically ill, which people think might be Legionnaires' Disease in a moment of panic. This stops the conference, and leads to the end of Philip and Joy's affair. Part V takes place at the Modern Language Association conference in New York at the end of 1979. All of the characters in the book are there. Arthur Kingfisher oversees a panel discussion about criticism where Swallow, Zapp, Morgana, and others present their opinions on what literary criticism is. Zapp's kidnapping experience has cured him of his interest in deconstructionism. Persse (contrary to what Sybil Maiden had said about knights not asking the right question at the right time) asks, "What follows if everyone agrees with you?" Kingfisher is inspired by this question, and recovers from his mental and physical impotence. Persse finally finds Angelica and hears her read a paper about romances that directly reflects the structure of Small World itself: "No sooner is one crisis in the fortunes of the hero averted than a new one presents itself; no sooner has one mystery been solved than another is raised; no sooner has one adventure been concluded than another begins... The greatest and most characteristic romances are often unfinished - they end only with the author's exhaustion, as a woman's capacity for orgasm is limited only by her physical stamina. Romance is a multiple orgasm." After this talk, Persse runs through the hotel and sees a woman he takes to be Angelica, kisses her and declares that he loves her. She takes him up to her hotel room where they make love, in Persse's first sexual experience. However, after this encounter, she reveals that she is not Angelica, but the twin sister, Lily. Persse feels ashamed, but Lily convinces him that he was "in love with a dream". Later in the evening, Arthur Kingfisher announces that he will offer himself as a candidate for the UNESCO chair. Right afterwards, Sybil Maiden steps forward and announces that she is Angelica and Lily's mother and Kingfisher is their father, which throws the entire meeting into a joyous uproar. Angelica introduces Persse to her fiancee, Peter McGarrigle, the person whose job Persse was interviewed for back in Ireland. However, Peter is not angry, because as a result, he went to America and there met Angelica. Swallow has returned to his wife, saying "Basically I failed in the role of a romantic hero." All of the narrative threads of the novel wrap up but for one: Persse realizes that Cheryl Summerbee, not Angelica, is the woman for him, and he flies to Heathrow to see her. He arrives at the airport on New Year's Eve, but learns that Cheryl no longer works there, having been fired the day before Persse arrives. The new attendant tells Persse that Cheryl wanted to travel anyway at some point, and took this as her chance. No one knows where she has gone. The novel ends with Persse wondering "where in the small, narrow world he should begin to look for her."

Shrimal (Srimal) Jain is an ancient Jain and Hindu community originating from Rajasthan, specifically from Bhinmal town in southern Rajasthan. This caste is attributed to descent from the goddess Lakshmi, and their descendants are renowned for their business skills, owning Havelis and mansions bestowed by kings for their service as royal officials. The Shrimal (Srimal) Jain are considered the highest gotra within the Oswal merchant and minister caste, predominantly located in northern India. It is believed that the Srimal caste separated from the Oswal, as most Srimals are Jain, similar to the Oswal caste, which traces its lineage to the Raja of Osnagar, a Rajput prince who converted to Jainism after observing Sri Ratan Suri, a Jain ascetic, revive his son. Some Srimals practice Hinduism, following the Vaishnava tradition while worshiping their Kuladevi, the goddess Lakshmi. They primarily reside in Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, and Gujarat.

Microsoft is offering Windows XP users a free swap to a later version of the operating system, in an attempt to boost the number of computers that are secure against malware.

The company has promised to provide a free one-year licence for Windows 7, Windows 8 or Windows 10 to any XP user who visits a special website.

The offer is being run in partnership with the nonprofit group, Preserve Connectivity.

"Customers who browse the web with an unpatched browser on an unsupported operating system are more vulnerable to security risks," said Christine Hall, head of Microsoft's Windows marketing for Asia Pacific.

"This offer is for those consumers who are unaware or less informed about the risks of continuing to use an unsupported operating system."

Windows XP was released in 2001 and discontinuted in 2014. Nevertheless, analyst firm NetMarketShare reported that as of March this year, it was still running on 8.93% of desktops.

It is particularly popular in Asia, where it accounts for more than a quarter of desktops.

Windows 7, which was released in 2009, will also be discontinued next year.

However, it is still used on half of all desktops, according to NetMarketShare.

Microsoft is making the offer available in Hong Kong, Thailand, Indonesia, Malaysia, Vietnam, Philippines and India.

Background subtraction involves identifying moving objects in video sequences, such as vehicles on highways. This method entails subtracting the current frame from a time-averaged background image, isolating moving targets. However, it lacks precision in classifying individual pixels, struggles with slow-moving objects, and cannot differentiate between shadows and actual movement. The paper proposes using a pixel-based classification model that learns a mixture-of-Gaussians framework for each pixel through an unsupervised learning process—such as an efficient, incremental EM algorithm. This approach dynamically adjusts mixture components based on pixel likelihoods, effectively handling slow-moving objects. Additionally, it outperforms traditional methods like thresholding in detecting and removing shadows. Applying this method within the Roadwatch traffic monitoring system is anticipated to enhance vehicle recognition and tracking accuracy.

Philip Neil Hope, born on September 24, 1972, in Toronto, Ontario, Canada, was a Canadian actor renowned for his role as Derek "Wheels" Wheeler in the teen drama series Degrassi Junior High and Degrassi High, which aired from 1987 to 1991. After reappearing in two episodes of Degrassi: The Next Generation, Hope passed away in 2007, with his death not officially disclosed until five years later. 

Hope was born on September 24, 1972, in Toronto, Ontario, Canada, the fourth son and fifth child of his family. His parents struggled with alcoholism and had a tumultuous relationship, leading to their separation. He and his siblings frequently moved between their mother and father's homes. Despite this instability, Hope maintained a positive relationship with his father, who he viewed as supportive and loving. He often watched television with his father and siblings during dinners, which sparked his interest in the behind-the-scenes aspects of television production. He enrolled in a television training course funded by his father and had professional promotional photos taken of himself. His acting career began when he appeared in the Kids of Degrassi Street episode "Martin Meets The Pirates." Hope stated that television provided an escape from his personal struggles, and being involved in the industry allowed him to turn that escape into a tangible reality.

In this paper, we explore relationships between the initial extensions of simple modules and specific filtrations of standard modules within the framework of graded Hecke algebras. These filtrations include radical filtrations and Jantzen filtrations. Our methodology relies on insights from the Langlands classification and a more profound comprehension of certain module structures. These modules originate from the image of a Knapp-Stein-type intertwining operator and are quotients of generalized standard modules. During the process, we derive several findings regarding the blocks of finite-dimensional modules for graded Hecke algebras. As a practical example, we calculate the Ext-groups for irreducible modules within a block of the graded Hecke algebra of type $C_3$, provided that a version of the Jantzen conjecture holds true.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach to image segmentation based on affinity learning. Our approach is based on the principle of maximin affinity, which aims to maximize the similarity between neighboring pixels while simultaneously minimizing the similarity between dissimilar pixels. To learn the affinity between pixels, we use a convolutional neural network (CNN) which is trained using a novel loss function that is based on the maximin principle. We evaluate our approach on the Weizmann Horse Segmentation dataset and compare it to state-of-the-art methods. Our results show that our approach outperforms existing methods and offers a new way to approach the problem of image segmentation.

The families EPT (resp. EPG) Edge Intersection Graphs of Paths in a tree
(resp. in a grid) are well studied graph classes. Recently we introduced the
graph classes Edge-Intersecting and Non-Splitting Paths in a Tree ENPT, and in
a Grid (ENPG). It was shown that ENPG contains an infinite hierarchy of
subclasses that are obtained by restricting the number of bends in the paths.
Motivated by this result, in this work we focus on one bend {ENPG} graphs. We
show that one bend ENPG graphs are properly included in two bend ENPG graphs.
We also show that trees and cycles are one bend ENPG graphs, and characterize
the split graphs and co-bipartite graphs that are one bend ENPG. We prove that
the recognition problem of one bend ENPG split graphs is NP-complete even in a
very restricted subfamily of split graphs. Last we provide a linear time
recognition algorithm for one bend ENPG co-bipartite graphs.

2-1/2 cups Whole Milk
1/2 cups Heavy Cream
1/2 cups Light Agave Syrup
2 ounces, weight Unsweetened Baking Chocolate
1/2 cups Cocoa Powder
1/4 teaspoons Salt
4 whole Eggs
2 Tablespoons Cornstarch Stirred Into 1/4 Cup Cold Water
16 envelopes Sweet-N-Low
2 teaspoons Real Vanilla
Pour milk, cream and agave into a medium sized pot. Add chopped chocolate. Stir in cocoa and salt. Heat over medium heat, stirring frequently, until cocoa is dispersed and chocolate is melted. Continue to heat until mixture is quite hot. Meanwhile, crack eggs into a small mixing bowl. Stir cornstarch into water until smooth. Stir cornstarch water into eggs. Set aside. Open Sweet-N-Low packets and place into a small bowl. Measure vanilla into another small bowl. When milk mixture in pot is quite hot, like hot chocolate, spoon about 1 cup into the egg mixture and mix well. This tempers your eggs so they don't scramble when you add them to the pot. Once your eggs are well mixed, pour this egg mixture back into the pot with the rest of the hot milk, etc. Continue to cook until this mixture is very thick. It will coat a spoon thickly. At this point you can remove the pot from the heat and blend mixture with a stick blender, or pour into a blender and blend until completely smooth. Now add the vanilla and the sweetener to the mix. Blend well. Pour the pudding into serving-sized bowls or into one or two larger bowls. Place in the fridge until cold. Eat. Yum yum.

In this realm of flickering light,
Where shadows merge in deepest night,
I raise my voice, I take a stand,
To question judgments dealt by man.

To me, the death penalty is murder, see,
An act of violence, without mercy, free,
For who can claim the right to decide,
Another's fate, to cut their life's tide?

Does it not bleed the soul in every stroke,
To sentence a life to the hangman's yoke?
In the name of justice, so called divine,
Yet, tainted with vengeance from a darker shrine.

Does the hangman’s hand not shake with doubt,
As lever pulled, life snuffed out?
In that final gasp, the truth rings clear,
The executioner is now in fear.

What if, perchance, they've taken wrong,
Sentenced an innocent, played along,
With biased hearts and tainted minds,
A justice blind, deaf, and unkind?

In these halls of justice, bricks and stone,
Lies the fragility of the human zone,
A system errant, flawed by design,
Where the innocent condemned too often pine.

To me, the death penalty is murder, plain,
A stain upon a society's humane,
For how can we claim a moral high,
When our hands are stained with blood, a cruel lie?

Yet, let us not forget, for in these veins,
Lie heartaches deep, victims' cries of pain,
To balance scales, to right the wrongs,
Seeking justice, where it belongs.

But let us seek a path more just, more wise,
To hold those true accountable, recognize,
That vengeance, in a cloak of ordered law,
Seeds more sorrow, in its icy maw.

So, let us refrain from that final breath,
For death's embrace leads to no true death,
Instead, let compassion guide our way,
And find a justice truer every day.

14 pounds ground beef  
3 garlic cloves, minced  
1 cup onion, finely chopped  
8 ounces mushrooms, chopped  
6 ounces tomato paste  
32 ounces diced tomatoes with juice  
12 cups dry red wine  
1 teaspoon dried oregano  
1 bay leaf  
12 teaspoons salt  
14 teaspoons pepper  
1 tablespoon light brown sugar  
8 ounces lasagna noodles  
12 ounces cottage cheese  
1 egg  
8 ounces Swiss cheese  
14 cups Parmesan cheese, grated  

In a large deep skillet or Dutch oven, brown the beef, onions, and mushrooms in 1 tablespoon of olive oil. Season with some of the salt and pepper. Once nearly browned, add the garlic and cook until fragrant. Add the red wine, diced tomatoes, tomato paste, and seasonings. Stir well and bring to a boil, then reduce to simmer. Cover and let it cook for 20 minutes.  

Preheat the oven to 350°F. Cook the lasagna noodles as per the package instructions. Drain them and cover with cold water; set them aside. Mix the egg with the cottage cheese and set aside. Grate or slice the cheese and set aside. Prepare a 9 x 13 baking dish with non-stick spray. Pour some of the sauce into the bottom of the dish. Layer three noodles, then a third of the cheese, followed by a third of the meat sauce. If you're using ten noodles, place the extra one in the center layer. Top with grated Parmesan. Bake for 35 to 45 minutes until bubbly and slightly browned on top. If the top is browning too quickly, cover it loosely with foil and continue baking until done. Let it cool for 15 minutes before serving. It will make 12 servings. Serve with salad and garlic bread.

And sung their wit, their virtue and their grace,
So have we loved sweet Justice to the last,
That now lies here in an unseemly place.

Yet shall be seen no more by mortal eyes
Such beauty as here walked and here went down.
Like birds that hear the winter crying plain
Her courtiers leave to seek the clement south;
Many have praised her, we alone remain
To break a fist against the lying mouth
Of any man who says this was not so:
Though she be dead now, as indeed we know.

And be at peace, and be at peace forever,
Under the world, untroubled by the sound
Of mortal tears, that cease from pouring never?
Well for the heart, by stern compassion harried,
If death be deeper than the churchmen say, --
Gone from this world indeed what's graveward carried,
And laid to rest indeed what's laid away.
Anguish enough while yet the indignant breather
Have blood to spurt upon the oppressor's hand;
Who would eternal be, and hang in ether
A stuffless ghost above his struggling land,
Retching in vain to render up the groan
That is not there, being aching dust's alone?

Scaling properties of time series are usually studied in terms of the scaling
laws of empirical moments, which are the time average estimates of moments of
the dynamic variable. Nonlinearities in the scaling function of empirical
moments are generally regarded as a sign of multifractality in the data. We
show that, except for the Brownian motion, this method fails to disclose the
correct monofractal nature of self-similar L\'evy processes. We prove that for
this class of processes it produces apparent multifractality characterised by a
piecewise-linear scaling function with two different regimes, which match at
the stability index of the considered process. This result is motivated by
previous numerical evidence. It is obtained by introducing an appropriate
stochastic normalisation which is able to cure empirical moments, without
hiding their dependence on time, when moments they aim at estimating do not
exist.

"Ingredients: 1/2 cup butter, softened 4 cups shredded Cheddar cheese 3 tablespoons chopped green onions 1 teaspoon Worcestershire sauce 1 loaf French bread Directions Preheat oven to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C). In a medium bowl, mix together the butter, cheese, green onion and Worcestershire sauce until well blended. Cut the top off the loaf of bread, leaving about an inch at the bottom. Hollow out the inside of the bread, leaving a shell with about 1-inch thick walls. Fill the hollowed out center with the cheese mixture. Place the lid back onto the filled bread. Wrap in aluminum foil and bake at 350 degrees F (175 degrees C) for 30 minutes."

1 large onion, chopped
100 g smoked bacon lardons
2 tablespoons olive oil
500 g lean stewing beef, cubed
2 tablespoons plain flour
3 parsnips, cubed
500 ml brown ale
300 ml beef stock
2 tablespoons cranberry jelly or 2 tablespoons red currant jelly
4 fresh thyme sprigs
greens, to serve (optional)
butter, for greasing
300 g self-raising flour, plus extra for dusting
2 teaspoons English mustard powder
140 g shredded suet
Heat a large pan and cook the onion and lardons together for 5 mins until golden. Scoop out with a slotted spoon and set aside. Add the oil to the pan, dust the beef with the flour, then evenly brown over a high heat. Add the parsnips, ale, stock, jelly, thyme and lardon mixture to the pan. Bring to the boil, then cover and simmer for 1 1/2 hrs until the meat is tender. Generously butter a 1.5-litre pudding basin. To make the pastry, mix together the flour, mustard powder, suet and 1/2 tsp table salt. Add enough cold water, about 150ml, to make a soft dough. Remove one-quarter of the dough and set to one side. On a heavily floured surface, roll out the remaining dough to make a large round, big enough to line the basin. Carefully lay the pastry in the basin (aim to have 1cm of pastry overhanging the rim), then press the edges of the join together to seal. Roll out the remaining one-quarter into a circle big enough to cover the top. Pour off the cooking liquid from the filling into a small pan and set aside. Discard the thyme stalks. Spoon the filling into the lined basin and pour over 100ml of the cooking liquid. Fold over the overhanging pastry and brush with water. Place the lid on top, pressing firmly around the edges to seal. Butter a sheet of baking parchment, fold in a large pleat and lay, butter-side down, on top of the pudding. Cover with a pleated layer of foil and finally tie with string, making a loop for the handle so you can lift the pudding easily. Sit a small trivet or a large cookie cutter in the bottom of a deep saucepan that's big enough to take the basin easily. Half-fill the pan with water and bring to the boil. Lower in the pudding, cover and simmer for 2 hrs, topping up with boiling water when necessary. Reheat the cooking liquid, bubbling it down a little so it reduces into a tasty gravy. Carefully lift out the pudding. Run a knife around the rim, then turn out and serve with gravy and greens, if you like.

Culture appropriation is a sensitive issue and rightly so, as it involves taking elements from a less dominant culture by a more dominant one, often without understanding, acknowledgment or respect. This can include traditional clothing, language, music, dances, and even religious symbols. 

However, I am wondering where we draw the line between appreciating and borrowing from a culture and appropriating it. If one genuinely has an interest in a culture different from their own, appreciates it and borrows certain aspects of it, should it be seen as appropriation or appreciation? 

For instance, if I, as an individual with a deep admiration of Japanese culture adopt elements of it in my daily life, such as clothing or language, would that be considered appropriation? Is there a 'right way' for me to express my admiration for this culture? What guidelines should one follow to ensure they are not disrespecting or trivializing the values of a culture they admire?

Also, another question that keeps me awake at night revolves around global fusion. As our world becomes more interconnected and cultures meld together naturally, doesn't this open up a space for shared cultural elements? 

It would be great to hear your thoughts. Please remember to keep all responses respectful and understanding of differing viewpoints. Let's make this dialog a safe space for everyone who chooses to participate.

We build on recent works on Stein's method for functions of multivariate
normal random variables to derive bounds for the rate of convergence of some
asymptotically chi-square distributed statistics. We obtain some general bounds
and establish some simple sufficient conditions for convergence rates of order
$n^{-1}$ for smooth test functions. These general bounds are applied to
Friedman's statistic for comparing $r$ treatments across $n$ trials and the
family of power divergence statistics for goodness-of-fit across $n$ trials and
$r$ classifications, with index parameter $\lambda\in\mathbb{R}$ (Pearson's
statistic corresponds to $\lambda=1$). We obtain a $O(n^{-1})$ bound for the
rate of convergence of Friedman's statistic for any number of treatments
$r\geq2$. We also obtain a $O(n^{-1})$ bound on the rate of convergence of the
power divergence statistics for any $r\geq2$ when $\lambda$ is a positive
integer or any real number greater than 5. We conjecture that the $O(n^{-1})$
rate holds for any $\lambda\in\mathbb{R}$.

Few-shot semantic segmentation (FSS) has great potential for medical imaging
applications. Most of the existing FSS techniques require abundant annotated
semantic classes for training. However, these methods may not be applicable for
medical images due to the lack of annotations. To address this problem we make
several contributions: (1) A novel self-supervised FSS framework for medical
images in order to eliminate the requirement for annotations during training.
Additionally, superpixel-based pseudo-labels are generated to provide
supervision; (2) An adaptive local prototype pooling module plugged into
prototypical networks, to solve the common challenging foreground-background
imbalance problem in medical image segmentation; (3) We demonstrate the general
applicability of the proposed approach for medical images using three different
tasks: abdominal organ segmentation for CT and MRI, as well as cardiac
segmentation for MRI. Our results show that, for medical image segmentation,
the proposed method outperforms conventional FSS methods which require manual
annotations for training.

In this paper, we present a theoretical analysis of active contours on graphs, which are a generalization of traditional active contour models that operate on graph-structured data. We propose a new formulation of active contours on graphs, based on a probabilistic framework that allows for efficient inference and learning. Our approach enables the integration of domain knowledge into the segmentation process, leading to improved accuracy and robustness compared to traditional methods.

We derive a set of algorithms for active contour evolution on graphs, including a novel iterative algorithm that converges to an optimal solution under certain conditions. Furthermore, we establish a theoretical bound on the convergence rate of our algorithm, providing insights into its performance.

Our analysis also covers the case where the graph structure is uncertain or noisy, in which case we propose a robust variant of our algorithm that can handle such scenarios. Finally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through experiments on several real-world datasets, showcasing its ability to accurately segment complex objects in various domains.

Overall, our work provides a solid foundation for understanding and improving active contour models on graph-structured data, opening up new possibilities for applications in computer vision, machine learning, and related fields.

Tumor detection in biomedical imaging is a time-consuming process for medical
professionals and is not without errors. Thus in recent decades, researchers
have developed algorithmic techniques for image processing using a wide variety
of mathematical methods, such as statistical modeling, variational techniques,
and machine learning. In this paper, we propose a semi-automatic method for
liver segmentation of 2D CT scans into three labels denoting healthy, vessel,
or tumor tissue based on graph cuts. First, we create a feature vector for each
pixel in a novel way that consists of the 59 intensity values in the time
series data and propose a simplified perimeter cost term in the energy
functional. We normalize the data and perimeter terms in the functional to
expedite the graph cut without having to optimize the scaling parameter
$\lambda$. In place of a training process, predetermined tissue means are
computed based on sample regions identified by expert radiologists. The
proposed method also has the advantage of being relatively simple to implement
computationally. It was evaluated against the ground truth on a clinical CT
dataset of 10 tumors and yielded segmentations with a mean Dice similarity
coefficient (DSC) of .77 and mean volume overlap error (VOE) of 36.7%. The
average processing time was 1.25 minutes per slice.

The paper reports on an experimental investigation highlighting that automatic iris recognition techniques exhibit reduced performance in cataract-affected eyes compared to healthy ones. Limited research exists on this subject, with most studies relying on sparse datasets that often lack sufficient diversity in image representation. We developed our own dataset, collecting 1288 eye images from 37 patients at the Medical University of Warsaw. These images encompass various common ocular diseases, including cataract, alongside less frequent conditions like altered iris patterns caused by illness or injury. The images were captured under near-infrared light (commonly used in biometric systems) and, in some cases, under visible light (often employed in ophthalmic diagnostics). Given that cataract constitutes the majority of the data in our database, this study focuses exclusively on this condition. To evaluate the decline in recognition accuracy, we applied three iris recognition algorithms—both commercial and academic—to compute genuine match scores for healthy eyes and those affected by cataract. The results indicate a notable decrease in recognition reliability, evidenced by a 12% rise in genuine match scores for an academic algorithm and up to 175% for an example commercial method. This improvement in genuine scores impacted the final false non-match rates in two of the algorithms. To our knowledge, this is the first study of its kind that employs multiple iris matchers and examines iris image segmentation as a possible contributor to reduced reliability.

1 (5 to 6-pound) pork shoulder or Boston butt pork roast  
2 teaspoons salt  
10 pounds hardwood charcoal, divided  
Hickory wood chunks  
Sprinkle the pork with salt; cover it and refrigerate for 30 minutes. Set up a charcoal fire using half of the charcoal in the grill; allow it to burn for 15 to 20 minutes until it is covered with gray ash. Distribute the coals evenly across both sides of the grill. Place two hickory chunks on each pile and position a food rack on the grill. Place the pork, with its meaty side down, on the rack in the center of the grill. Cover the grill with the lid, ensuring all vents remain fully open. Create another charcoal fire with 12 briquettes in an auxiliary grill or fire bucket; let it burn for 30 minutes until it is covered with gray ash. Add six briquettes to each pile in the smoker and place two more hickory chunks on each pile. Follow this process every 30 minutes. Cook the pork, covered, for 5 hours and 30 minutes or until a meat thermometer inserted into the thickest part reads at least 165°F, turning the pork once during the final two hours. (Cooking to 165°F makes the meat easier to remove from the bone.) Remove the pork, let it cool slightly, then chop and serve with Cider Vinegar Barbecue Sauce or Peppery Vinegar Sauce.

One Hundred Years of Solitude (1967) recounts the tale of seven generations of the Buendía family in the town of Macondo. During a night on a riverbank, José Arcadio Buendía dreams of "Macondo," a city of mirrors that reflects the world around it. Upon waking, he decides to establish Macondo at the river's edge; after traversing the jungle for several days, the founding of Macondo is described as utopian. The founding patriarch believes Macondo is surrounded by water and constructs the world based on his own interpretations. Shortly after its establishment, Macondo becomes a town filled with strange and remarkable events involving the Buendía family, whose members are either unable or unwilling to escape their recurring (primarily self-inflicted) hardships. Eventually, a hurricane annihilates Macondo, the city of mirrors; this destruction symbolizes the cyclic nature of Macondo itself. At the conclusion of the narrative, a Buendía man deciphers an encoded message that generations of Buendía family members had failed to decode. This secret communication reveals the fortunes and misfortunes experienced by each generation of the Buendía family.

1/4 teaspoon rapid rise yeast
1 1/2 cups water at room temperature
1 3/4 teaspoons salt
4 cups all-purpose flour, or as needed
1/2 teaspoon cornmeal, or as needed
Place yeast into the bottom of a large mixing bowl and stir with water; mix in salt. Beat flour into yeast mixture with a wooden spoon until dough is thick and sticky and pulls flour from the side of the bowl, 5 to 10 minutes. Cover bowl with plastic wrap and let stand in a turned-off oven until doubled in size, 12 to 14 hours. Dough will be bubbly and very sticky. Place a silicone baking mat onto a baking sheet and dust generously with cornmeal. Use a floured spatula to scrape dough out onto a well-floured work surface and dust dough with flour. With well-floured hands, pat dough into a rectangle and cut into 4 equal-size pieces. Dust a piece of dough with flour and use your floured fingers to gently roll and stretch it out into a log about 10 inches long and 1 1/2 inches around. Gently transfer to prepared baking sheet. If desired, wipe off excess cornmeal with a damp paper towel. Repeat with another piece of dough. (Reserve remaining dough to bake later or prepare 2 baking sheets to bake all 4 at once). Dust loaves lightly with flour. Dust a large piece of plastic wrap with flour and drape plastic lightly over the baking sheet with floured side down. Let loaves rise, covered, until doubled, 1 to 1 1/2 hour. Move oven racks to the bottom and middle positions. Preheat oven to 500 degrees F (260 degrees C) or as high as your oven will go. Place an oven-safe baking dish full of water into bottom rack of the oven. Use a sharp kitchen shears to cut 4 or 5 angled slashes into the top of each loaf. Poke down the little sharp tips of dough left by the scissors. Spray loaves with water, using a spray bottle. Bake in the preheated oven until baguettes are browned, about 15 minutes, spraying loaves with water after 5 minutes and 10 minutes. Turn the pan around on the second spraying. Transfer baguettes to a cooling rack and let cool to room temperature before slicing with a serrated knife.

We introduce a new light-field dataset of materials, and take advantage of
the recent success of deep learning to perform material recognition on the 4D
light-field. Our dataset contains 12 material categories, each with 100 images
taken with a Lytro Illum, from which we extract about 30,000 patches in total.
To the best of our knowledge, this is the first mid-size dataset for
light-field images. Our main goal is to investigate whether the additional
information in a light-field (such as multiple sub-aperture views and
view-dependent reflectance effects) can aid material recognition. Since
recognition networks have not been trained on 4D images before, we propose and
compare several novel CNN architectures to train on light-field images. In our
experiments, the best performing CNN architecture achieves a 7% boost compared
with 2D image classification (70% to 77%). These results constitute important
baselines that can spur further research in the use of CNNs for light-field
applications. Upon publication, our dataset also enables other novel
applications of light-fields, including object detection, image segmentation
and view interpolation.

Bill Conti's job of musical director of the Oscars show is not for the faint-hearted since conducting the orchestra is the ultimate plate-spinning assignment.
This year marks Conti's 17th turn at the helm of the Academy Awards orchestra. "The excitement is a live performance as a musician," he says. "All of your colleagues, everyone in the film industry is in the theatre. All the important people. "I guess it's just a television show but we always think it's a bit more.' The orchestra strikes up more than 110 times during the average Oscars show. As well as playing the presenters and winners on and off stage, it also performs during the commercial breaks to entertain the live audience in the house.
"It's a very busy evening, it takes a certain amount of preparation of music, orchestrating, sketching rehearsing, before the show. But you don't know what the unexpected will be and as the musical director, it's exciting," explains Conti. And much of the preparation goes into mastering scores that will never be performed. "We don't know who the winners will be. So when they say, 'the winner is', we have five different pieces of music in front of us, they say the name, we play the appropriate one immediately," adds Conti.
The orchestra is often called upon to play when the winners ramble on too long during their acceptance speeches, despite being told to be brief by the show's producers.
The decision to drown out or 'kill' the offending star with music is relayed from the director's box to the orchestra via Conti's earpiece. "I don't feel good about it at all. It's not my call though," he says. "When the director says 'music' the orchestra plays and he takes a long shot of the hall. We don't usually see the person speaking while his microphone is cut off. "The person that's been cut off, who's 10 feet from me, is glaring at me like it's death time." On occasions, some stars have taken it upon themselves to send a warning shot across the bows of the musical director before they start to speak. "Julia Roberts, when she came on, she asked me to not get ready to play because she had so much to do," he says. Conti received an Oscar in 1983 for the original score of The Right Stuff. He also received two nominations in the original song category in 1976 for Gonna Fly Now from Rocky and in 1981 for the title song from For Your Eyes Only.
"It's a moment in the sun," he says. "When people get up there, some people, this is hard to believe, people that spend their lives in front of the camera or audiences entertaining, might get a little flustered. "But there's this moment in time when the biggest award that they could possibly get in their life has been handed to them and they're either not in control or they want to thank everyone that they ever met."
The image of the Oscars telecast is one of slick presentation and smooth transitions between performances and the award categories. Behind the scenes, the key players, such as Conti, have a bewildering array of technical props to deal with. "There's a big script and video monitors you have to watch and there are also audio controls. I can control hearing in my ears, the left ear or the right ear - different things at different times.
"I have to communicate with the director. I have a little microphone that's attached to my headset. To open up that microphone, I have a footswitch," he explains. Conti's most nerve-wracking moment came during his first Oscars show as musical director, in 1977, when a member of the orchestra alerted him that they could smell smoke. Conti immediately told the show's director: "I start cursing and screaming, I tell him we're not going to die for this show - you must do something or I'm going to climb out of this pit with 60 musicians and we're going to be home in 10 minutes. "'Oh no Bill don't do anything," came the response. "Imagine these elegantly dressed ladies and gentlemen of the orchestra, 60 or so of them in the pit and while we're playing, firemen with their helmets and their hatchets crawling among us trying to find the reason for the smoke." The smell turned out to be new paint smouldering on the music stands. "No one died, it's not a big story, but it was scary at the time," laughs Conti. When the ceremony is over, the music director attends the annual Governor's Ball with his family. "I have a drink and relive the show," he says. "I'm not for too much carousing. I go home and unwind. It takes me about a day."

When Sara's mother is fatally injured in a car accident, she moves to a predominantly Black neighborhood in Chicago. There, she becomes friends with Black Chenille and develops feelings for her brother Derek. Derek teaches her modern hip-hop dance routines to help her integrate into the community, and together they develop a romantic connection. However, a white girl who finds Derek attractive will never be popular, and the couple must navigate numerous challenges to achieve their goals and remain authentic.

This film is essentially a "Black Dirty Dancing," though slightly more urban in tone. It effectively portrays the journey of overcoming personal aspirations, delivering a compelling narrative. The love story is sincere without being overly romanticized, and the obstacles faced are typical of an "urban" movie—such as navigating mixed-race relationships, the temptation to stay within one's group, etc. While these themes are clichéd, they are executed well.

One issue I encountered was the portrayal of Black culture in the film. Not all Black individuals in a poor area speak like gangsters or use phrases like "ain't nothin' but a dirty dancing." Why did Sara only gain acceptance when she began imitating Black culture and adopting that language? While it might be realistic, I believed Sara should have remained true to herself rather than conforming to hip-hop norms. This is a minor concern for most viewers.

The cast is suitable for MTV teen audiences. Julia Stiles is appealing, and Thomas is charming. Other characters fit typical Black stereotypes—gangsta friends, over-the-top baby mama figures, useless baby fathers, and jealous exes. Though these stereotypes are expected, they do not significantly detract from the overall experience. Fredro Starr delivers a solid performance as Malakai, even if the character was somewhat cliché.

In a sign of a thaw in relations between Egypt and Israel, the two countries have signed a trade protocol with the US, allowing Egyptian goods made in partnership with Israeli firms free access to American markets.
The protocol, signed in Cairo, will establish what are called "qualified industrial zones" in Egypt. Products from these zones will enjoy duty free access to the US, provided that 35% of their components are the product of Israeli-Egyptian cooperation. The US describes this as the most important economic agreement between Egypt and Israel in two decades.
The protocol establishing the zones has been stalled for years. There has been deep sensitivity in Egypt about any form of co-operation with Israel as long as its peace process with the Palestinians remains blocked. But in recent weeks an unusual warmth has crept into relations between the two countries. Both exchanged prisoners earlier this month, with Egypt handing back an Israeli who has served eight years in prison after being convicted for spying.
Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak has described Israeli Prime Minister Ariel Sharon as the best chance for the Palestinians to achieve peace. The government in Cairo now believes Mr Sharon is moving towards the centre and away from the positions of right wing groups. It also believes the US, pressed by Europe, is now more willing to engage seriously in the search for a settlement. But there are also pressing economic reasons for Egypt's decision to enter into the trade agreement. It will give a huge boost to Egyptian textile exports, which are about to suffer a drop after new regulations come into force in the US at the beginning of the year.

Horace Cedric Lee (14 March 1909 – 14 July 1981) was an English cricketer. A right-handed batsman who also bowled right-arm fast-medium, Lee was born in North Shields, Northumberland. He made his debut in county cricket for Northumberland in the 1929 Minor Counties Championship against Durham. Before the outbreak of World War II in 1939, Lee appeared in 67 matches for the county in the Minor Counties Championship. In 1935, Lee made his first-class debut for a combined Minor Counties team against Oxford University at the University Parks. Batting first, the Minor Counties scored 251 all out. In their second innings, they scored 294 all out, with Lee scoring 45 runs before being dismissed by Whitehouse. Oxford University reached 23 without loss in their second innings, and the match ended in a draw. The following season, Lee played another first-class match for the Minor Counties against Ireland at Observatory Road, Dublin. Batting first, Ireland were dismissed for 102, and the Minor Counties responded with 69 all out, with Lee dismissed for 5 runs by James Graham. Ireland then scored 179 in their second innings, setting the Minor Counties a target of 213 for victory. The Minor Counties failed to meet this target, finishing at 133, with Lee dismissed for a single run by the same bowler. After World War II, Lee played a further Minor Counties Championship match for Northumberland against Staffordshire.

A Spanish football hooligan who stabbed a police officer to the death on the Spanish town of Fuengirola in April has admitted to detectives that he killed and had his victim decapitated.

Rios Romero Gomez, who was known as "Gomez the Jackal", was on Wednesday accused of killing 24-year-old Elisabeth Lopez at Fuengirola, and then "having her head shaved and put into a suitcase in a nearby garden", according to a statement released by prosecutors.

The 31-year-old spent three months in a psychiatric hospital and has since been released and is seeking legal action.

In the four-minute video Gomez admitted to throwing a stone to the officer's face that killed Lopez on April 23 in an incident that resulted in her death. He also said he "honestly believed".

In the video, when asked if he had killed Lopez Lopez answered: "Yes."

Lopez had fallen asleep on a sofa, then woke up, screaming and falling headfirst onto the carpet. Gomez allegedly rushed over and stabbed her several times.

After he was arrested he said she had been a "pig" who stole from others. He claimed he had been trying to clean a sink when the knife got stuck in a piece of metal on the floor.

After the stabbing, he went to the garden where he was joined by three other Fuengirola men. There they threw Lopez' head into the garden and sawed a plastic bag back together – only for Gomez to see them doing the same to a plastic bag containing a dead monkey, and to conclude that he should have used it to wash his hands before going out.

He then asked the four men if he could borrow a lighter from one of those who had been using it. The five made their way out of Fuengirola after a few minutes, before police found their red Ferrari parked up outside a hotel.

> Abstract: We study magnetic reconnection in two dimensions using resistive MHD simulations with an imposed guide field and periodic boundary conditions. In this configuration, we find that large scale effective potentials can be generated during the early stages of reconnection which reduce ion heating significantly compared to the case without such potentials. These potentials are created due to the presence of a strong guide field and are found to have a characteristic length scale comparable to the system size. This effect is not observed when the guide field is weak or absent. Our results suggest that the generation of these potentials may play an important role in reducing ion heating during magnetic reconnection in astrophysical systems where there is a significant guide field present.

A late header by young player Danny Graham secured a hard-fought draw for Middlesbrough against Charlton at the Riverside. Matt Holland opened the scoring in the 14th minute with a shot that deflected off Franck Queudrue. However, Middlesbrough pressed relentlessly after halftime, and Chris Riggott scored the equalizer. Shaun Bartlett's goal gave Charlton back the lead, but this advantage lasted only six minutes as Graham headed home from Queudrue's pass. The game erupted immediately, with Charlton defender Hermann Hreidarsson posing a threat just six minutes into the match. He received a free-kick from the right but struck wide of the goal. The Icelandic international appeared dangerous, prompting the Boro bench to issue urgent instructions to watch him.

Charlton's early aggression proved effective when Bartlett received a long pass from Talal El Karkouri and sent it to Holland, who fired a right-footed shot past the post. Szilard Nemeth, substituted for Joseph-Desire Job, was thwarted twice by Dean Kiely as Middlesbrough tried to equalize. The striker made a good one-two with Jimmy Floyd Hasselbaink but was covered by Kiely, who directed a header into the goalkeeper's net. Boro had ample time on the ball, but the Addicks managed to neutralize the pressure, with Kiely saving Hreidarsson's shot and directing a header over the bar. This allowed Boro to take the lead into halftime.

After the break, Middlesbrough pushed forward aggressively, and Kiely prevented Hreidarsson from scoring by palmming the ball away. However, Riggott's equalizer in the 74th minute sealed the victory. The Boro defender looked offside as he finished off Gareth Southgate's misdirection, but the goal stood despite Charlton's protests. Boro did not surrender, with Bartlett leaving the game.

* Olive oil for drizzling
* 1 can chickpeas, drained
* 60ml cold water, plus a 30ml for a looser consistency
* 1 small lemon, juiced then ½ zested
* 3 tbsp tahini
* 1¼ tsp salt, plus a pinch
* ¼ tsp black pepper
* 2 tbsp pastrami, very finely chopped

The advancement of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) has greatly enhanced the field of medical image segmentation, which is essential for various clinical applications. Nevertheless, these methods often struggle with capturing explicit long-range dependencies. Current solutions typically involve constructing deep encoders along with intensive downsampling processes, resulting in overly complex networks and the loss of important local details. As a result, there is an urgent need for a more effective approach to enhance the modeling of global context while preserving crucial low-level information. This paper introduces a new parallel architecture called TransFuse, which integrates Transformers and CNNs in a parallel configuration. This design enables the efficient capture of both global dependencies and fine-grained spatial details in a shallower network structure. Additionally, a novel fusion method, the BiFusion module, is proposed to effectively combine features from both branches. Experimental results show that TransFuse outperforms state-of-the-art models on both 2D and 3D medical imaging datasets, including polyps, skin lesions, hips, and prostates, with notable reductions in parameters and improved inference speeds.

Constance Eaton Hamilton (1862–1945) was a British-Canadian government official and activist. She engaged in activism for refugees and women in Winnipeg before moving to Toronto, where she continued to support causes like women's suffrage, serving as president of the Equal Franchise League of Toronto. She was elected to the Toronto City Council in the 1920 elections, becoming the first female member of the council and the first woman in Ontario to hold elected office at the federal, provincial, or municipal level. After serving two terms, she stepped down to focus on campaigning for immigrant settlement and refugee issues, as well as equal rights. In 1979, the Toronto city council awarded her the Constance E. Hamilton Award for the Status of Women. 

Born in Yorkshire, England in 1862, she was the daughter of Dr. George Fowler Bodington (1829–1902) and Caroline Mary Eaton (1825–1873). From a young age, she studied with private tutors and was fluent in German. She attended the Conservatory of Music in Leipzig, Germany, where she became a skilled pianist. Additionally, she worked as a part-time farmer during her early years. In 1887, she immigrated to Canada with her family and settled in Vancouver. The next year, she met and married Lauchlan Hamilton, an older businessman.

His first term lasted from 1960 to 1963, and his second from 1968 to 1971. He became nationally known during his second tenure for opposing the demands of striking sanitation workers in early 1968. Loeb, a segregationist, opposed civil rights for African Americans and supported white supremacy, continuing the legacy of former mayor and political leader E. H. Crump. 

Loeb's parents were Jewish and Irish Catholic respectively, and his paternal grandparents were Jewish German immigrants who moved to Memphis in the 1860s. His grandfather, Henry Loeb, established Loeb's Laundry. Loeb III attended Phillips Academy and Brown University before joining the Navy, where he served on a patrol boat during World War II. Post-war, he gained popularity among the white middle class by promoting his military service and opposing communism.

Information flow pertains to the field of security, focusing on the unauthorized transfer of information arising from correlations between secrets and observables. As these correlations are generally unavoidable, quantifying the leakage becomes essential. The primary methods for defining suitable measures rely on information theory. Notably, the $g$-leakage framework, introduced recently, incorporates many information-theoretic concepts. However, a challenge with $g$-leakage lies in its formulation as a minimization problem, which may become computationally intensive in large-scale systems. This paper investigates scenarios where the system's communication channel can be broken down into simpler components, a common situation when observables consist of multiple parts. Our key result involves deriving bounds on the multiplicative version of $g$-leakage of the entire system, expressed in terms of the $g$-leakages of its individual components. Additionally, we examine specific cases such as min-entropy leakage and parallel channels, extending and refining existing findings from the literature. We validate the efficacy of our approach through practical examples and assess the accuracy of our bounds.

The Edge Intersection Graphs of Paths in a tree (resp. in a grid), denoted as EPT (resp. EPG), have been extensively studied. Recently, we introduced the graph classes Edge-Intersecting and Non-Splitting Paths in a Tree (ENPT) and in a Grid (ENPG). It has been demonstrated that ENPG includes an infinite sequence of subclasses formed by limiting the number of bends in the paths. Inspired by this finding, this study focuses on one-bend ENPG graphs. We establish that one-bend ENPG graphs are contained within two-bend ENPG graphs. Additionally, we show that trees and cycles are one-bend ENPG graphs, and we classify the split graphs and co-bipartite graphs that are one-bend ENPG. We also prove that the recognition problem of one-bend ENPG split graphs is NP-complete even within a specific subset of split graphs. Finally, we present a linear-time recognition algorithm for one-bend ENPG co-bipartite graphs.

Marthinus Theunis "Tjol" Lategan, born on 29 September 1925 and passed away on 8 March 2015, was a South African rugby center. Lategan played for the University of Stellenbosch and the Western Province in provincial rugby, and represented South Africa eleven times between 1949 and 1953, making his debut against the 1949 touring New Zealand side. He was subsequently chosen for the 1951–52 South Africa rugby tour to Great Britain, Ireland, and France. This tour is regarded as one of the greatest South African teams, securing a victory record of 30 out of 31 matches, including all five international games.

Lategan was born in Stellenbosch in 1925 and attended Stellenbosch Boys' High School before matriculating to Stellenbosch University, where he pursued studies in accounting. He gained recognition as "Tjol," a family nickname, and later became a partner in a prominent accounting firm in East London before retiring in 1991. He was married twice; his first spouse passed away in 1970 due to a brief illness, and he remarried Trudie, living with her in a retirement home in Somerset West. He was the final survivor of the 1949 Springboks, who defeated the New Zealand 'All Blacks' in all four of their matches during their tour of South Africa prior to his death on 8 March 2015.

In 2004, China's economy grew at a rapid pace of 9.5%, surpassing expectations and exceeding the 9.1% growth recorded in 2003. This development might lead to tighter restrictions on investments and loans as Beijing seeks to cool down the economy. The country's expansion has been driven by the import of raw materials and energy, which could trigger global repercussions if the economy overheats. However, officials noted that industrial growth slowed, with services playing a key role in driving progress. Industrial production, the primary focus of government measures to limit credit and investment, reached 11.5% in 2004, down from 17% in the prior year. 

Consumer prices increased by 2.4%, outpacing the same period in 2004, raising concerns about potential inflationary pressures. Investment in fixed assets remained high, rising 21.3% compared to the previous year—though still far from the 43% peak observed in early 2004. In October 2004, China raised interest rates by 0.27 percentage points to 5.8%, marking the first increase in nearly nine years.

While economic restructuring appears to be underway, experts note that the overall growth outlook remains robust. Economist Tim Congdon of ING Barings stated, "There is no indication of a slowdown in 2005." China's economy is accelerating due to both domestic consumption and growing international exports. Exports hit a six-year high in 2004, increasing by 35%, partly because of the relatively low value of the yuan. The government maintains the yuan at a fixed exchange rate near $8.28, which has angered U.S. lawmakers who attribute job losses and competitive disadvantages to China. Although officials urge a gradual adjustment from the fixed rate, they remain far from ready to transition to a market-determined exchange rate. National Bureau of Statistics Chief Li Deshui emphasized, "We require a solid plan and the time to develop it."

In a k-linear triangulated category (with k a field), it is shown that the existence of Auslander-Reiten triangles ensures that objects are determined, up to shifts, by the dimensions of homomorphisms between them. In most cases, these objects are distinct by this information, a result also established under slightly different conditions in a theorem by Jensen, Su, and Zimmermann. The method involves examining bilinear forms on Grothendieck groups that resemble the Green ring of a finite group.

We focus specifically on the category of perfect complexes for a self-injective algebra, where the Auslander-Reiten quiver possesses a well-known structure. We determine the positions within the quiver of various types of perfect complexes, including those of lengths 1, 2, and 3, rigid complexes, and truncated projective resolutions. We fully characterize the quiver components containing projective modules. Additionally, we derive relationships between the homologies of complexes at different points in the quiver, demonstrating that every self-injective algebra with radical length at least 3 has indecomposable perfect complexes with arbitrarily large homology in any specified degree. We also observe that homology stabilizes outside the rim of the quiver. When the algebra is symmetric, one of the previously considered forms becomes Hermitian, enabling computation of its values based solely on data from objects on the rim of the quiver.

The graph Laplacian is a widely used technique in data science, machine learning, and image processing. It retains the intricate structure of the underlying network and often has a dense configuration in specific contexts. As a result, computing matrix-vector products involving the graph Laplacian can be computationally intensive. A common requirement is calculating multiple eigenvalues and eigenvectors, which becomes impractical when the graph's node count is large. To address this, we introduce a fast summation method leveraging the nonequispaced fast Fourier transform (NFFT) for efficient dense matrix-vector multiplications without explicitly constructing the full matrix. The versatility of the NFFT enables integration of this acceleration into Lanczos-based eigenvalue algorithms or iterative linear systems solvers, allowing the use of non-standard Gaussian kernels. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through various test cases, including image segmentation and semi-supervised learning using graph-based partial differential equations. Specifically, we evaluate our method against the Nyström method and present an improved, hybrid variant that incorporates the NFFT within its framework.

Quantitative image analysis often depends on accurate classification of
pixels through a segmentation process. However, imaging artifacts such as the
partial volume effect and sensor noise complicate the classification process.
These effects increase the pixel intensity variance of each constituent class,
causing intensities from one class to overlap with another. This increased
variance makes threshold based segmentation methods insufficient due to
ambiguous overlap regions in the pixel intensity distributions. The class
ambiguity becomes even more complex for systems with more than two
constituents, such as unsaturated moist granular media. In this paper, we
propose an image processing workflow that improves segmentation accuracy for
multiphase systems. First, the ambiguous transition regions between classes are
identified and removed, which allows for global thresholding of single-class
regions. Then the transition regions are classified using a distance function,
and finally both segmentations are combined into one classified image. This
workflow includes three methodologies for identifying transition pixels and we
demonstrate on a variety of synthetic images that these approaches are able to
accurately separate the ambiguous transition pixels from the single-class
regions. For situations with typical amounts of image noise, misclassification
errors and area differences calculated between each class of the synthetic
images and the resultant segmented images range from 0.69-1.48% and 0.01-0.74%,
respectively, showing the segmentation accuracy of this approach. We
demonstrate that we are able to accurately segment x-ray microtomography images
of moist granular media using these computationally efficient methodologies.

1 pound ziti or your preferred whole grain penne  
8 ounces fresh mozzarella  
1 cup fresh basil chopped  
1 tablespoon extra-virgin olive oil, cold-pressed organic  
4 organic garlic cloves, chopped  
14 ounces diced organic tomatoes  
8 ounces organic tomato paste  
1 cup water  
2 tablespoons dried oregano organic  
2 tablespoons dried basil organic  
salt  
pepper  

Heat the oil in a saucepan on medium heat for 3–4 minutes, add the garlic and let it brown, stirring occasionally for 4–5 minutes. Be cautious not to burn the garlic. Add the diced tomatoes, tomato paste, water, oregano, basil, salt, and pepper. Bring to a boil for 4–5 minutes, then reduce the heat to low and let it simmer for 1–2 hours or as long as you'd like, stirring occasionally.  

In a large pot, bring water to a boil and add about 1/2 teaspoon of sea salt right before adding the pasta. This enhances the flavor of the pasta. Add 1 pound of brown rice pasta (you may use other whole grain pastas for added health benefits). Add a tablespoon of olive oil to the water to prevent the pasta from sticking. Cook for 7–10 minutes until al dente, drain, and add it to the sauce.  

While the pasta is cooking, chop 8 ounces of fresh mozzarella into cubes. When you add the pasta to the sauce, keep the heat low and gently incorporate the mozzarella into the pasta, folding it in until it's melted, taking about 3–4 minutes. Be mindful not to over-melt it, as this can make it stringy. Serve immediately with a garnish of fresh basil and Parmesan cheese! Enjoy!

Overall, Simone Wilkie has established herself as a talented and versatile performer, who has made a significant contribution to the Australian entertainment industry.
