Recently, state-of-the-art results have been achieved in semantic
segmentation using fully convolutional networks (FCNs). Most of these networks
employ encoder-decoder style architecture similar to U-Net and are trained with
images and the corresponding segmentation maps as a pixel-wise classification
task. Such frameworks only exploit class information by using the ground truth
segmentation maps. In this paper, we propose a multi-task learning framework
with the main aim of exploiting structural and spatial information along with
the class information. We modify the decoder part of the FCN to exploit class
information and the structural information as well. We intend to do this while
also keeping the parameters of the network as low as possible. We obtain the
structural information using either of the two ways: i) using the contour map
and ii) using the distance map, both of which can be obtained from ground truth
segmentation maps with no additional annotation costs. We also explore
different ways in which distance maps can be computed and study the effects of
different distance maps on the segmentation performance. We also experiment
extensively on two different medical image segmentation applications: i.e i)
using color fundus images for optic disc and cup segmentation and ii) using
endoscopic images for polyp segmentation. Through our experiments, we report
results comparable to, and in some cases performing better than the current
state-of-the-art architectures and with an order of 2x reduction in the number
of parameters.

Charles Edward Lindblom (born March 21, 1917, died January 30, 2018) was an American academic who pursued studies in economics at the University of Chicago and held the title of Sterling Professor Emeritus of Political Science and Economics at Yale University. He served as president of the American Political Science Association and the Association for Comparative Economic Studies, as well as director of Yale's Institution for Social and Policy Studies. His scholarly contributions focused on the field of public administration.

Lindblom was among the pioneers and influential proponents of the incrementalist theory in policymaking and decision-making. This perspective, often referred to as gradualism, emphasizes a step-by-step, pragmatic approach to decision-making. It suggests that policy changes are typically evolutionary rather than abrupt, with decisions made through a process of trial and error. His development of this viewpoint was influenced by his extensive research on welfare policies and trade unions across the globe. His ideas were articulated in two seminal articles, "The Science of 'Muddling Through'" (1959) and "Still Muddling, Not Yet Through" (1979), both published in Public Administration Review.

John Robinson Jeffers (October 10, 1887 – February 20, 1962) was an American poet celebrated for his works centered on the central California coast. Many of his poems were crafted in narrative and epic styles, yet he was also recognized for his shorter verses and is regarded as a symbol of the environmental cause. Despite or due to his belief in "inhumanism," which posited that transcendence necessitated the marginalization of human concerns in favor of the vast whole, Jeffers opposed U.S. involvement in World War II, leading to his censorship by the media. 

Jeffers was born on October 10, 1887, in Allegheny, Pennsylvania (now part of Pittsburgh), the son of Reverend Dr. William Hamilton Jeffers, a Presbyterian minister and expert in ancient languages and Biblical history, and Annie Robinson Tuttle. His brother, Hamilton Jeffers, was a renowned astronomer associated with the Lick Observatory. During his youth, Jeffers visited Europe and studied in Germany, France, and Switzerland. A top student, he excelled in classical studies, including Greek and Latin, and became fluent in German, French, and English by the age of twelve. He graduated from Occidental College at 18, earning his bachelor’s degree. While studying, he was a passionate outdoorsman and actively participated in the school's literary groups.

In medical image diagnosis, semantic segmentation plays a crucial role in enhancing efficiency during pathological image analysis, particularly within digital pathology. Spatial augmentation is commonly employed for such tasks. Tumor images, especially those classified as malignant, are relatively scarce, making the annotation of nuclear region labels a time-intensive process. To optimize dataset utilization and enhance segmentation accuracy, it is anticipated that augmentations applied to general images can affect performance. This paper introduces a synthetic augmentation method utilizing label-to-image translation, which maps semantic labels to the structural features of real images. Specifically, this work focuses on staining slides of nuclei in tumors. In practice, we evaluate multiple segmentation techniques applied to an initial dataset containing both real images and labeled data, leveraging synthetic augmentation to generate generalized images. Our results indicate that the proposed synthetic augmentation approach improves segmentation accuracy.

Today, visitors can still see remnants of these historical periods, including ruins of temples, fortresses, and other structures.

The island's economy is based mainly on agriculture and tourism. Its fertile soil produces a variety of crops such as grapes, figs, olives, and citrus fruits. Irish Soda Bread Recipe

Ingredients 
4 cups all-purpose flour (plus extra for dusting)
1 teaspoon baking soda
1 teaspoon cream of tartar
1/2 cup golden raisins
1 teaspoon salt
2 cups boiling water
1/2 cup milk

Instructions
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. In a large bowl, combine flour, baking soda, cream of tartar, and salt. Mix well.
3. In a separate bowl, pour boiling water over raisins. Let soak for 5 minutes.
4. Add milk and raisin mixture to the dry ingredients, and stir gently with a fork until just moistened. The dough will be sticky.
5. Turn dough out onto a lightly floured surface, and shape into a round loaf.
6. Place on a baking sheet, and cut a deep cross in the top of the loaf.
7. Bake for 30 to 35 minutes, or until bread sounds hollow when tapped on the bottom.
8. Allow to cool on a wire rack.

In this paper we study the relative Chow and $K$-stability of toric manifolds
in the toric sense. First, we give a criterion for relative $K$-stability and
instability of toric Fano manifolds in the toric sense. The reduction of
relative Chow stability on toric manifolds will be investigated using the
Hibert-Mumford criterion in two ways. One is to consider the maximal torus
action and its weight polytope. We obtain a reduction by the strategy of Ono
[Ono13], which fits into the relative GIT stability detected by Sz\'ekelyhidi.
The other way relies on $\mathbb{C}^*$-actions and Chow weights associated to
toric degenerations following Donaldson and Ross-Thomas [D02, RT07]. As
applications of our main theorem, we partially determine the relative
$K$-stability of toric Fano threefolds and present counter-examples which are
relatively $K$-stable in the toric sense but which are asymptotically
relatively Chow unstable. In the end, we explain the erroneous parts of the
published version of this article (corresponding to Sections 1-5), which
provides some inconclusive results for relative $K$-stability in Table 6.

As European leaders convene in Rome on Friday to finalize the new EU constitution, numerous businesses are shifting their focus towards local concerns—particularly how to maintain operations. Lille, a favored tourist spot for British visitors seeking a glimpse of French culture, hosts a strikingly large Victorian Chamber of Commerce situated near the Opera House. However, many visitors ponder whether this building, akin to town halls in other northern English cities, was constructed on the wealth generated by coal, steel, and textile industries. These sectors have experienced prolonged decline, with the final coal mine closing in 1990. Beck-Crespel, a specialized steel firm located approximately 20 miles from Lille, has remained jobless-free since 1945. The company specializes in manufacturing fasteners for power plants and the oil sector, yet few such projects are currently underway in Europe.  

Director Hugues Charbonnier notes that he faces pressure due to competitors in the Far East producing some of his products at lower costs, while his primary markets have shifted to China and India. "Our business is truly global, and even within the expanded EU, we would require only 150 or 200 employees," he states. While globalization poses challenges, France's labor laws mandate a 39-hour workweek despite only 35 hours of actual work. Nevertheless, the steel industry persists, albeit at a diminished scale. Coal has disappeared entirely, and textiles remain in difficulty. New ventures have entered the scene, but they fall short of offsetting the losses.  

This is one of the reasons why locals in the area lack enthusiasm for the EU, according to Frederic Sawicki, a political lecturer at the University of Lille. "The unemployment rate here is 12% in most regions, sometimes reaching 15%. They do not perceive Europe as providing tangible benefits, leading to skepticism, particularly among the working class."

Precise identification of pathological lungs from computed tomography (CT) images is still largely unresolved due to the lack of a reliable, general solution. Existing techniques struggle with the inherent variability in how abnormalities manifest. Local descriptor-driven classification approaches have proven effective in annotating pathologies, yet they often require significant computational resources, limiting their practical application in real-time or near-real-time clinical settings. This paper introduces a new methodology for swiftly and accurately segmenting pathological lungs from CT scans by integrating a region-based segmentation technique with local descriptor classification applied to an optimized sampling grid. The proposed approach operates in two stages: in the first stage, the fuzzy connectedness (FC) image segmentation algorithm is adapted to extract initial lung parenchyma. In the second stage, texture-based local descriptors are employed to identify abnormal imaging patterns using a nearly optimal keypoint analysis, with grid points defined as centroids of supervoxels. Quantitative evaluation demonstrates that our method is efficient, resilient, and enhances existing standards, showing promise for improving the efficiency of routine clinical tasks.

Ernest Leslie Konnyu (born May 17, 1937) is an American businessman and former Republican U.S. Representative from Silicon Valley, California, 12th congressional district, serving one term from 1987 to 1989. He had previously been a California State Assembly Member from the 22nd district, serving from 1980 to 1986. Early life
Ernõ "Ernie" Könnyű was born May 17, 1937, in Tamási, Kingdom of Hungary (present-day Tamási, Hungary) to poet, professor and cartographer Leslie Konnyu and his wife, Elizabeth, a bookkeeper and owner of a home secretarial school, and is the eldest of his two late siblings Gabriela (Helen) and Zoltan (Joseph). In 1949 the 12-year-old Konnyu, together with his family, immigrated to the United States from a post-World War II refugee camp in Ampflwang, Austria. He attended parochial and public schools in Jefferson City and St. Louis, Missouri. He attended University of Maryland, College Park and received his Bachelor of Science degree from Ohio State University in 1965. Konnyu served in the United States Air Force as a captain from 1959 to 1969 and as a major in the Air Force Reserve from 1970 to 1981. In 1959, he married Lillian Muenks of Loose Creek, Missouri.

6 boneless skinless chicken thighs
6 Toulouse sausages (depending on the size of chook the thighs came from) or 6 chipolata sausages (depending on the size of chook the thighs came from)
250 g streaky bacon (6 or 12 rashers depending on how cut) or 250 g pancetta (6 or 12 rashers depending on how cut)
200 g orange duck pate
Preheat oven to 180C (350F). Cover a (rolled out) chicken thigh with a couple of pieces of cling film and clobber until flattened / slightly larger surface area (until the width of the chicken is about the same as the length of the sausage). Take a rasher/slice of bacon/pancetta and lay out on a copping board - if using streaky bacon you may need to run the back of a knife across it to make it wider and longer. Or you may need to use 2 rashers per thigh, depending on the product. Lay a boned thigh on the bacon (outside to the bacon, where the bone was, facing up). Spread 1/6 of the pate into the centre half of the thigh. Place a sausage across the pate and roll up tightly, ensuring that the bacon ends overlap each other over the 'join'. Remove from the oven and leave to stand for 5-10 minutes. Slice each roulade into 1cm thick slices and serve.

Recent advancements in Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs) have demonstrated superior performance in high-level vision tasks like image classification and object detection. This study integrates techniques from DCNNs with probabilistic graphical models to tackle pixel-level classification, also referred to as semantic image segmentation. The research indicates that the final layers of DCNNs produce outputs that lack sufficient spatial localization for precise object segmentation. This limitation stems from the inherent invariance characteristics of DCNNs, which are optimized for high-level tasks. To address this issue, we merge the final DCNN outputs with a fully connected Conditional Random Field (CRF). Our approach achieves accurate segmentation with a qualitative result that surpasses prior methods. Quantitatively, it attains 71.6% Intersection over Union (IOU) accuracy on the PASCAL VOC-2012 dataset. The results are achieved through efficient network redesign and a refined implementation of the 'hole' algorithm from the wavelet field, enabling dense neural network computations at 8 frames per second on a contemporary GPU.

We present a method for segmenting neuron membranes in 2D electron microscopy
imagery. This segmentation task has been a bottleneck to reconstruction efforts
of the brain's synaptic circuits. One common problem is the misclassification
of blurry membrane fragments as cell interior, which leads to merging of two
adjacent neuron sections into one via the blurry membrane region. Human
annotators can easily avoid such errors by implicitly performing gap
completion, taking into account the continuity of membranes.
  Drawing inspiration from these human strategies, we formulate the
segmentation task as an edge labeling problem on a graph with local topological
constraints. We derive an integer linear program (ILP) that enforces membrane
continuity, i.e. the absence of gaps. The cost function of the ILP is the
pixel-wise deviation of the segmentation from a priori membrane probabilities
derived from the data.
  Based on membrane probability maps obtained using random forest classifiers
and convolutional neural networks, our method improves the neuron boundary
segmentation accuracy compared to a variety of standard segmentation
approaches. Our method successfully performs gap completion and leads to fewer
topological errors. The method could potentially also be incorporated into
other image segmentation pipelines with known topological constraints.

State-of-the-art image segmentation algorithms generally consist of at least
two successive and distinct computations: a boundary detection process that
uses local image information to classify image locations as boundaries between
objects, followed by a pixel grouping step such as watershed or connected
components that clusters pixels into segments. Prior work has varied the
complexity and approach employed in these two steps, including the
incorporation of multi-layer neural networks to perform boundary prediction,
and the use of global optimizations during pixel clustering. We propose a
unified and end-to-end trainable machine learning approach, flood-filling
networks, in which a recurrent 3d convolutional network directly produces
individual segments from a raw image. The proposed approach robustly segments
images with an unknown and variable number of objects as well as highly
variable object sizes. We demonstrate the approach on a challenging 3d image
segmentation task, connectomic reconstruction from volume electron microscopy
data, on which flood-filling neural networks substantially improve accuracy
over other state-of-the-art methods. The proposed approach can replace complex
multi-step segmentation pipelines with a single neural network that is learned
end-to-end.

1 cup all-purpose flour  
1 teaspoon baking powder  
1/2 teaspoon kosher salt  
1/4 teaspoon baking soda  
6 ounces plain yogurt  
1/2 cup peeled, finely chopped carrots, or baby-cut carrots  
1/2 cup whole oats  
1/2 cup fresh spinach leaves  
1/4 cup unsweetened cocoa, such as Dutch process  
1/4 cup milk, plus 1/4 cup as needed  
3 tablespoons honey  
1 teaspoon vanilla extract  
1 apple, peeled and finely chopped  
2 eggs  
1/3 cup mini chocolate chips  
Vegetable oil, for greasing the pan  
Fresh fruit, for garnish  
Powdered sugar, for garnish  

Whisk the flour, baking powder, salt and baking soda in a medium bowl. Set aside. Place the yogurt, carrots, oats, spinach, cocoa, 1/4 cup milk, honey, vanilla and apples into a high-quality blender. Blend on high until the mixture is very smooth, resembling melted ice cream, about 1 minute. If the mixture is too thick, add an additional 1/4 cup milk and blend. Add the eggs and pulse to incorporate. Pour the blended mixture into the bowl with the flour mixture and stir gently 6 or 7 times with a wooden spoon. Add the chocolate chips and stir a couple more times. Do not over mix. Heat a pancake griddle or skillet over medium heat. Use a basting brush to grease the pan, brushing on just enough oil to coat the surface. Pour the pancake batter, either using a heaping tablespoon for small pancakes or 1/4 cup measure for large ones. Cook the pancakes on one side until large bubbles appear, about 2 minutes. Flip the pancakes and finish cooking on the other side, about 1 minute. Serve with fresh fruit and powdered sugar.

The USS Indiana (BB-58) was the second of four fast battleships constructed for the U.S. Navy in the 1930s. These vessels were the first American battleships designed after the Washington Treaty system started to fail in the mid-1930s. They benefited from an escalator clause that permitted increasing their main armament to 16 guns, though the navy refused to approve larger battleships, keeping their displacement near the Washington limit of 44,000 tons. The need to protect against the same caliber of guns they carried, along with the displacement restrictions, led to cramped conditions on board. As wartime modifications enhanced their anti-aircraft defenses, the crew size also increased. Indiana joined the navy in April 1942, at a time when the U.S. was already involved in World War II, and was quickly deployed to the Pacific Theater to fight against Japan. Her initial engagement occurred in late 1942, supporting marines during the Guadalcanal Campaign. Over the next three years, she primarily provided naval gunfire support for amphibious operations across the Pacific and defended the fast carrier task force against air attacks. She participated in the Battles of Tarawa in November 1943 and Kwajalein in February 1944. In the latter operation, she collided with the battleship Enterprise and had to withdraw for repairs.

Seedless Cucumbers  
4 cups distilled white vinegar  
1 ½ cans of salt substitute (NuSalt/Morton/NoSalt)  
½ cup of garlic pepper  
½ cup of dill weed  
1 large jar or canister  
Cucumbers  
Wash cucumbers in hot and cold water for about 1 minute and wipe them with a paper towel after. Slice the cucumbers into thick "chip" pieces and set aside.  
Brine  
Combine the salt substitute, garlic pepper, and dill weed in a bowl. Add the vinegar to the jar or canister and then add the dry ingredients, mixing thoroughly. Test the brine's salinity; if needed, add more. Sodium-free salt is safe here. The stronger the brine, the quicker the cucumbers will turn into pickles.  
Mix the cucumbers with the brine, ensuring they are fully covered, and stir well. Cover the jar or container and refrigerate. Let the pickles chill for at least six to eight hours before eating; the longer they marinate, the more intense and flavorful they become.

On a sunny brae, alone I lay
One summer afternoon;
It was the marriage-time of May
With her young lover, June.
From her mother's heart, seemed loath to part
That queen of bridal charms,
But her father smiled on the fairest child
He ever held in his arms.
The trees did wave their plumy crests,
The glad birds caroled clear;
And I, of all the wedding guests,
Was only sullen there!
There was not one, but wished to shun
My aspect void of cheer;
The very grey rocks, looking on,
Asked, "What do you here?"
And I could utter no reply;
In sooth, I did not know
Why I had brought a clouded eye
To greet the general glow.
So, resting on a heathy bank,
I took my heart to me;
And we together sadly sank
Into a reverie.
We thought, "When winter comes again,
Where will these bright things be?
All vanished, like a vision vain,
An unreal mockery!
The birds that now so blithely sing,
Through deserts, frozen dry,
Poor spectres of the perished spring,
In famished troops, will fly.
And why should we be glad at all?
The leaf is hardly green,
Before a token of its fall
Is on the surface seen!"
Now, whether it were really so,
I never could be sure;
But as in fit of peevish woe,
I stretched me on the moor.
A thousand thousand gleaming fires
Seemed kindling in the air;
A thousand thousand silvery lyres
Resounded far and near:
Methought, the very breath I breathed
Was full of sparks divine,
And all my heather-couch was wreathed
By that celestial shine!
And, while the wide earth echoing rung
To their strange minstrelsy,
The little glittering spirits sung,
Or seemed to sing, to me.
"O mortal! mortal! let them die;
Let time and tears destroy,
That we may overflow the sky
With universal joy!
Let grief distract the sufferer's breast,
And night obscure his way;
They hasten him to endless rest,
And everlasting day.
To thee the world is like a tomb,
A desert's naked shore;
To us, in unimagined bloom,
It brightens more and more!
And could we lift the veil, and give
One brief glimpse to thine eye,
Thou wouldst rejoice for those that live,
Because they live to die."
The music ceased; the noonday dream,
Like dream of night, withdrew;
But Fancy, still, will sometimes deem
Her fond creation true.

Protestants in Tuvalu- Tuvalu is one of the most heavily Protestant nations in the world. The Congregational Christian Church of Tuvalu, (Tuvaluan: Te Ekalesia Kelisiano Tuvalu, EKT), is the  de facto state church of Tuvalu, the only established church in the Reformed tradition in the world. Its adherents comprise about 97% of the 12,000 inhabitants of the archipelago, and theologicly it is part of the Reformed tradition. History
Christianity first came to Tuvalu in 1861 when Elekana, a deacon of a Congregational church in Manihiki, Cook Islands became caught in a storm and drifted for eight weeks before landing at Nukulaelae. Elekana began proselytising Christianity. He was trained at Malua Theological College, a London Missionary Society school in Samoa, before beginning his work in establishing the Church of Tuvalu. In 1865, the Rev A. W. Murray of the London Missionary Society – a Protestant congregationalist missionary society – arrived as the first European missionary where he too proselytised among the inhabitants of Tuvalu.

Supervised semantic segmentation normally assumes the test data being in a
similar data domain as the training data. However, in practice, the domain
mismatch between the training and unseen data could lead to a significant
performance drop. Obtaining accurate pixel-wise label for images in different
domains is tedious and labor intensive, especially for histopathology images.
In this paper, we propose a dual adaptive pyramid network (DAPNet) for
histopathological gland segmentation adapting from one stain domain to another.
We tackle the domain adaptation problem on two levels: 1) the image-level
considers the differences of image color and style; 2) the feature-level
addresses the spatial inconsistency between two domains. The two components are
implemented as domain classifiers with adversarial training. We evaluate our
new approach using two gland segmentation datasets with H&E and DAB-H stains
respectively. The extensive experiments and ablation study demonstrate the
effectiveness of our approach on the domain adaptive segmentation task. We show
that the proposed approach performs favorably against other state-of-the-art
methods.

The effectiveness of deep learning in image segmentation is largely dependent on an abundance of densely annotated training data, which is challenging to acquire due to the significant effort and specialized knowledge needed, especially when dealing with 3D medical imaging. While self-supervised learning (SSL) has demonstrated promise in addressing this challenge, existing SSL methods primarily focus on ensuring global consistency at the image level, neglecting the crucial local consistency that is vital for extracting structural details in tasks like segmentation. In this paper, we introduce a PriorGuided Local (PGL) self-supervised model that focuses on learning local consistency within the latent feature space. Specifically, we utilize spatial transformations to generate diverse views of the same image, enabling the determination of the relationship between these views. This information is then employed to align feature maps from the same local region extracted across different views. A local consistency loss is subsequently introduced to reduce discrepancies between aligned feature maps at a voxel level. Consequently, our PGL model captures distinct representations of local regions, allowing it to preserve structural information. This capability supports effective performance in subsequent segmentation tasks. Extensive experiments were conducted on four publicly available computerized tomography (CT) datasets encompassing eleven major human organs and two tumors. The results show that employing a pre-trained PGL model to initialize a downstream network yields notable improvements over random initialization and initialization based on global consistency models. The code and pre-trained weights will be made available at: https://git.io/PGL.

Schloss Heiligenberg is located to the east of Jugenheim, belonging to the Seeheim-Jugenheim region, approximately 12 kilometers southwest of Darmstadt in Germany. The castle stands on the Heiligenberg, offering panoramic views of the Rhineland as far as the Palatinate. Today, it serves as the headquarters of the Amt für Lehrerbildung, although its "Gartensaal" is occasionally used for concerts and art exhibitions.

In the early 19th century, a castle was constructed on the Heiligenberg. Grand Duchess Wilhelmine of Hesse-Darmstadt and her son, Prince Alexander of Hesse-Darmstadt, expanded the structure between 1862 and 1867, designed by Georg Moller. Alexander (1823–1888), the third son of Grand Duke Louis II of Hesse-Darmstadt, resided primarily in Darmstadt or at Schloss Heiligenberg starting in 1852. He often stayed at the castle even when away on military campaigns.

On 28 October 1851, Alexander married countess Julia Hauke, a lady-in-waiting to his sister, Tsarina Maria Alexandrovna of Russia. Alexander and Julia established the Battenberg/Mountbatten lineage. Due to their extensive royal affiliations, the castle hosted the Russian Tsar and his family, along with numerous European monarchs, princes, and diplomats until 1914.

The novel is prefaced by a section entitled "Questions", which consists of four passages numbered in Roman numerals. I Chandra Chagoo is threatened by Abdul Khan, who believes Chagoo has been asking questions in order to gather evidence for the police. II Dr Gauri Subbiah contemplates confronting Chagoo and demanding exactly what he knows about her past. She fears he knows everything. III Dr Ram Mahipal lectures a class of medical students about the importance of asking questions. Privately he contemplates imminent professional ruin for asking the wrong question. IV Professor Phaterpaker also contemplates professional ruin as a result of Ram Mahipal's question, the answer to which Chagoo already knows. The preface ends. The main body of the novel begins with the heading: Answer The Commissioner tells Ghote that a criminal named Abdul Khan has supplied Bombay film stars with drugs from the Mira Behn Institute. Ghote is ordered to find who stole drugs from the institute and arrest them under a false charge to prevent a scandal. Ghote tells the Commissioner that he recently caught an airline stewardess, Nicky D'Costa, smuggling drugs for Abdul Khan. The Commissioner says he will assign another officer to manage Nicky D'Costa as an informant and that it will take a better officer than Ghote to bring Abdul Khan to justice. Ghote questions Asha Rani, a movie star. Her "friend" Mr Ganguly took a sample of a medicine called A.C.E. and nearly died. Khan, who also supplied Mr Ganguly with cocaine, supplied the A.C.E. At the institute, Ghote interviews Professor Phaterpaker. The Professor says he will go to any lengths to protect the institute. The institution's work is largely concerned with making new medicines from the venom of poisonous snakes. Dr Subbiah immediately suspects Chandra Chagoo of having stolen the A.C.E. and leads Ghote to the reptile room. When the door is unlocked they find Chagoo dead with a Russell's viper loose in the room. The next day the Commissioner assigns Ghote to investigate Chagoo's death to prevent the scandal being exposed by another officer. Ghote realises that Chagoo did not have a key to lock the reptile room door and must have been murdered. Ghote interviews Dr Ram Mahipal, who left a reptile-room key in his old office at the institute when he suddenly quit his job. Ghote learns from the building manager that Mahipal returned in order to access his computer files on the night Chagoo died. Dr Subbiah, Professor Phaterpaker, Dr Mahipal and the building manager were all in the building at the time. Ghote suspects that the murder may be an employee at the nearby hospital. He enlists the inspector originally assigned to Chagoo's death to test this theory. On their next meeting Mahipal says he returned to teaching in hopes of instilling integrity in young medical students. Mahipal left the institute because he believed that Phaterpaker faked results, possibly on a regular basis. Phaterpaker takes the news that Chagoo was murdered calmly, remarking that Mahipal was slipshod and implying that he was dismissed for this. Ghote tries to determine exactly why Mahipal left, but Phaterpaker is vague. When Phaterpaker realises he himself is a suspect, he is affronted but admits "cutting corners" and acts like a man with something to hide. Ghote concludes that Phaterpaker is trying to use Mahipal as a scapegoat to protect the institute. Dr Subbiah reacts badly when asked about her relations with Chagoo, however Ghote concludes she is not the killer. Ghote discovers that Dr Mahipal's father works as a cook at the medical school and is a Brahmin, whereas Mahipal claims to be a member of the Dalit caste. Ghote deduces that Mahipal misrepresented himself in order to get a university scholarship reserved for the lower classes. Mahipal confesses this is so. Ghote suggests Chagoo came to learn Mahipal's secret and was murdered because of this. Mahipal denies this and reveals that he left the institute because Phaterpaker was removing lab animals that gave undesirable results. At the police station, Ghote is dismayed when the inspector he is working with points out one of the three scientists must surely hang for the crime and expresses a preference that it be Dr Subbiah. At the institute Ghote accuses Phaterpaker of falsifying test results. Phaterpaker confesses his results are fake. He became aware that Chagoo was stealing drugs from the institute but was forced to agree to a truce because Chagoo knew Phaterpaker was removing lab animals. Ghote considers the reptile room and realises wooden stool must have been used to break the glass, so he decides to have it dusted for fingerprints. At the police station Ghote learns that Nicky D'Costa has murdered, her throat slit after asking too many questions of Abdul Khan. Ghote is angry enough to confront the commissioner, but learns Khan had arranged to be in hospital during the murder. The forensic tests do not find a match between any fingerprints on the stool and Ghote's three suspects. Nor can they prove it was used to break the glass of the viper's cage. Ghote goes home and argues with his wife, then inspiration strikes and he returns to the institute. There he searches the grounds for evidence someone could gain access by night. The security guard catches Ghote and he must call his fellow inspector to rescue him. Afterwards Ghote chances upon Dr Subbiah. Ghote deduces that Phaterpaker persuaded her to "anticipate" the results of her experiments, as Phaterpaker himself was once persuaded. The conversation between Ghote and Subbiah is interrupted when, by chance, they pass the funeral of Nicky D'Costa. Ghote tells Subbiah how Nicky D'Costa was murdered and proceeds to question her about her test results. Subbiah remarks that Abdul Khan was a patient at the teaching hospital recently. Ghote asks whether she anticipated her results before completing the actual experiment. She admits faking her results. Ghote now believes that Subbiah is the murderer. He accuses her and she reacts in amazement, saying that Chagoo was clearly strangled. Ghote realises that he only saw the body laying face down, and the inspector originally assigned to the case never forwarded the medical examiner's report. Ghote realises that Chagoo could not have been strangled by Subbiah or Phaterpaker because neither of them have the necessary strength. Dr Mahipal has a withered arm, eliminating him as a suspect. Returning to the police station, Ghote talks to the forensic expert who examined the stool from the institute reptile room. The expert admits he only compared the fingerprints on the stool to the three suspects Ghote named; Subbiah, Phaterpaker and Mahipal. Without Khan's file in front of him, he could not identify the fingerprints. Khan's file is retrieved and his fingerprints are a perfect match. Ghote realises he can arrest and charge Khan with murder and recalls, with satisfaction, the words used by Commissioner's at the start of the case: "Frankly, Inspector, it will take a better man than you to put paid to Abdul Khan".

Arsenal manager Arsène Wenger has extended his contract to remain at the club until May 2008. He has dispelled concerns about his future by securing a long-term agreement that extends beyond the opening of Arsenal's new stadium in two years. Wenger stated, "Signing a new contract merely confirms my commitment to advancing this club and achieving my goals. I still have much to accomplish, and my aim is to push the club forward. These are thrilling times for Arsenal." 

The 55-year-old Frenchman, according to Arsenal's website, said, "My purpose has always been clear. I cherish this club and am content here." Wenger has won three Premier League titles and the FA Cup three times each during his tenure. Chairman Peter Hill-Wood expressed delight over the contract extension, noting, "We are thrilled that Arsène has agreed to extend his contract. Since his arrival in 1996, he has transformed the club both on and off the field. Alongside the six major honors he has earned, he has played a pivotal role in key developments such as the construction of our new training center and the new stadium."

"The club continues to benefit from Arsène's keen eye for discovering top-tier talent," the statement added. "Currently, we have a strong group of young players emerging and several world-class players excelling in a remarkable style of play." Meanwhile, Arsenal director Danny Fiszman indicated that Wenger may stay beyond 2008, stating, "As we approach the end of his contract, we will assess the situation. I believe we would like him to stay, and I hope he will as well."

The Financial Times reported that Ferrari might be listed on the stock market as part of a restructuring plan for Fiat's automotive operations. The report noted that Fiat was considering a $2 billion (€1.53 billion; £1.05 billion) settlement with General Motors regarding its ownership. Potential steps include listing Ferrari and bringing Maserati and Alfa Romeo closer together. Although Alfa Romeo has seen strong sales, Fiat's car business remains incurring losses. The proposed measures, which the newspaper suggested could be announced soon, could involve separating Ferrari from other operations. Fiat holds a 56% stake in Ferrari, the company best known for its Formula One racing team, which it acquired in 1969. In 2002, it considered floating Ferrari but sold a minority stake to Italian bank Mediobanca for €775 million ($1 billion), valuing Ferrari at €2.3 billion. myself and if I go--

Come! yes,

no good in the world except out of
a woman and certain women alone
for certain. But what if
I arrive like a turtle,
with my house on my back or
a fish ogling from under water?
It will not do. I must be
steaming with love, colored
like a flamingo. For what?

and to smell, pah! like a flamingo
that soils its own feathers behind.
Must I go home filled
with a bad poem?
And they say:
Who can answer these things
till he has tried? Your eyes
are half closed, you are a child,
oh, a sweet one, ready to play
but I will make a man of you and
with love on his shoulder--!
And in the marshes
the crickets run
on the sunny dike's top and
make burrows there, the water
reflects the reeds and the reeds
move on their stalks and rattle drily.

The potential of few-shot semantic segmentation (FSS) in medical imaging is significant. Current FSS methodologies typically necessitate extensive annotated classes for training, but they may not be suitable for medical images due to the absence of such annotations. In response, we introduce several key innovations: (1) A new self-supervised FSS framework tailored for medical images, eliminating the need for annotations during training and generating superpixel-based pseudo-labels for supervision; (2) An adaptive local prototype pooling module integrated with prototypical networks to tackle the prevalent foreground-background imbalance issue in medical image segmentation; and (3) We validate the versatility of our approach across three distinct tasks—abdominal organ segmentation in CT and MRI, and cardiac segmentation in MRI. Our findings indicate that the proposed method surpasses traditional FSS approaches that rely on manual annotations for training.

We examine the finite element approximations of Biot's consolidation model in poroelasticity using MINI and stabilized P1-P1 elements. We evaluate the convergence of the fully discrete system derived from these spatial discretizations combined with an implicit Euler method in time. Additionally, we investigate the occurrence of unphysical oscillations in the pressure solution for scenarios involving low permeability and/or small time steps. Our analysis demonstrates that even in one dimension, a Stokes-stable finite element pair does not ensure a monotonic pressure approximation under these conditions. To address this, we propose a stabilization term that eliminates the oscillations. Numerical experiments confirm the monotonic nature of the stabilized schemes.

Quantitative image analysis frequently relies on precise classification of pixels via a segmentation procedure. Nevertheless, imaging artifacts like the partial volume effect and sensor noise complicate this process. These factors elevate the variability in pixel intensity across each class, leading to overlapping intensities between different classes. Such increased variability renders threshold-based segmentation techniques ineffective due to unclear overlaps in pixel intensity distributions. In systems involving more than two constituents, such as unsaturated moist granular media, class ambiguity becomes even more challenging. In this study, we introduce an image processing framework aimed at enhancing segmentation precision for multiphase systems. Initially, ambiguous transition zones between classes are identified and eliminated, enabling global thresholding of individual-class regions. Subsequently, these transition zones are categorized using a distance metric, and the resulting segmentations are merged into a unified classified image. This method incorporates three strategies for detecting transition pixels, and we validate their effectiveness on diverse synthetic images, demonstrating accurate separation of ambiguous transition pixels from single-class regions. For scenarios with standard levels of image noise, classification errors and area discrepancies between the synthetic images and the segmented outputs range from 0.69–1.48% and 0.01–0.74%, respectively, indicating the high accuracy of this approach. Furthermore, we show that these computationally efficient methods enable accurate segmentation of x-ray microtomography images of moist granular materials.

Ingredients
• 8 each bone-in chicken thighs (about 3 ½ pounds)
• Kosher salt and black pepper
• 2 cups chicken broth
• 2 cups water
• ½ cup white vinegar
• 2 tablespoons olive oil
• 4 medium garlic cloves, peeled and smashed
• 1 large shallot, finely chopped (about ¼ cup)
• Leaves from 3 sprigs fresh thyme, plus 1 sprig
• 1 pound mustard greens, washed, dried, and torn into bite-size pieces
• ¼ cup heavy cream

Instructions
1. Season the chicken with salt and pepper. In a large bowl, combine the broth, water, vinegar, olive oil, garlic, chopped shallot, and thyme leaves; set aside.
2. In a large Dutch oven or heavy pot, layer the chicken thighs, greens, and thyme sprig, alternating and starting and ending with the greens. Pour the broth mixture over the top and press gently on the greens to submerge them.
3. Bring the mixture to a boil over medium-high heat. Reduce the heat to low, cover the pot, and simmer for about 20-25 minutes, or until the chicken is cooked through and the greens are wilted.
4. Transfer the chicken and greens to a platter using a slotted spoon. Cover loosely with foil to keep warm.
5. Increase the heat to medium and bring the liquid to a boil. Cook, stirring occasionally, until reduced by about half. Stir in the heavy cream and return to a boil. Cook, stirring, for about 2 minutes, or until thickened. Season to taste with salt and pepper.
6. Pour the sauce over the chicken and greens. Serve.

Ingredients:

- 4 cloves garlic, minced
- 1 cup apple cider vinegar
- 2 cups chicken broth
- 1 bunch of kale, stems removed and leaves torn into bite-size pieces
- 1 bunch of collard greens, stems removed and leaves torn into bite-size pieces
- 2 tablespoons unsalted butter

Instructions:

1. Season the chicken thighs with salt and pepper on both sides.

2. Heat the olive oil in a large, heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven over medium-high heat.

In this study, we demonstrate the detection of unusually stable valley polarization and valley coherence in bilayer WS₂. The photoluminescence from bilayer WS₂ mirrors the polarization of the excitation source, whether it is circularly or linearly polarized, and maintains this property even at room temperature. The high circular polarization of the emitted light indicates the interplay of spin, layer, and valley degrees of freedom in the bilayer system. Meanwhile, the linearly polarized photoluminescence reflects quantum coherence between the two distinct band extrema in momentum space, which corresponds to valley quantum coherence in atomically thin bilayer WS₂. These findings offer new avenues for manipulating quantum states in two-dimensional semiconductors.

Multiple binomial sums constitute a significant category of multi-indexed sequences, which are closed under partial summation. They encompass most sequences derived from multiple summations of products of binomial coefficients, as well as all sequences whose algebraic generating functions are involved. We examine the representation of the generating functions of binomial sums through integrals of rational functions. The results include two key findings: first, we demonstrate that a univariate sequence is a multiple binomial sum if and only if its generating function is the diagonal of a rational function. Second, we develop algorithms to determine the equality of multiple binomial sums and to calculate their recurrence relations. These methods, combined with geometric simplifications of the integral forms, perform effectively in practical applications. The process circumvents the need for certificate computations and avoids the issue of spurious singularities that arise in discrete creative telescoping, both theoretically and practically.

In this paper, we propose a new challenge and benchmark dataset called VisDA (Visual Domain Adaptation) to evaluate the performance of domain adaptation methods in computer vision tasks. Existing domain adaptation benchmarks focus mainly on text classification and neglect the unique challenges posed by visual data. VisDA addresses this gap by providing a diverse set of image datasets from various domains, including object recognition, scene understanding, and medical imaging.

The VisDA challenge consists of multiple task-specific sub-challenges, each with its own evaluation metric. These sub-challenges are designed to test different aspects of domain adaptation, such as adaptability to new classes, styles, and domains. We also provide a set of baseline models that utilize popular domain adaptation techniques, allowing participants to compare their approaches against established methods.

To further facilitate research in this area, we will host an annual competition where participants can submit their adapted models and compete against others. The winner will be selected based on their performance on a held-out test set.

We believe that VisDA will serve as a valuable resource for researchers working on domain adaptation in computer vision, encouraging them to develop more effective and robust methods that can handle diverse real-world scenarios.

> Medical imaging has been widely used in clinical diagnosis and treatment, which requires accurate segmentation of organs or tissues to provide quantitative information about their morphology and function. However, manual delineations are time consuming and laborious, especially when dealing with large datasets. In this work, we propose a novel framework that combines deep neural networks (DNNs) and active learning (AL). Specifically, our method consists of two main components: a DNN model trained by AL and a saliency map generator. Firstly, we train a DNN model using only a small number of manually labeled samples via AL. Then, we use the trained DNN model as a teacher network to generate pseudo labels for unlabeled data. Finally, we combine these pseudo labels with the original ones to retrain the DNN model. This process can be iterated until convergence. To further improve the performance of the DNN model, we also design a saliency map generator to guide the selection of informative regions during training. Experimental results show that our proposed approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of both accuracy and efficiency.

Time-series remote sensing data provide a diverse set of information that can be applied across various fields, such as tracking land cover changes, monitoring crop conditions, assessing coastal modifications, evaluating flood risks, and analyzing urban growth. This study focuses on addressing the issue of predicting urban expansion using time-series satellite imagery. By building on prior research, we introduce a two-stage method that employs semantic image segmentation to forecast urban expansion. The initial stage involves extracting details about urban areas at varying time intervals and preparing these data for training. The second phase integrates Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) with Long Short-Term Memory (LSTMs) to capture temporal patterns and enable accurate prediction of urban expansion. Experimental validation is performed using multiple satellite images spanning three major cities in Saudi Arabia—Riyadh, Jeddah, and Dammam. Our findings demonstrate that the proposed approach yields enhanced performance, particularly when measured by metrics like Mean Squared Error, Root Mean Squared Error, Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio, Structural Similarity Index, and overall classification accuracy.

As a child, he grapples with complex emotions toward the bourgeois around him. He feels superior due to his keen insights but envies their pure vitality. This tension persists into adulthood, where he becomes a renowned writer in southern Germany. He believes that to be an artist, one must sacrifice the ordinary world. When Tonio visits his northern hometown, he is wrongly accused of being a runaway criminal, deepening his belief that the artist must be an outsider compared to "respectable" society. As Erich Heller, who knew Thomas Mann personally, noted, Tonio Kröger explores the theme of the "artist as an exile from reality" (echoing Goethe's Torquato Tasso and Grillparzer's Sappho). However, Heller himself once identified the central theme of Tonio Kröger as the passion-driven entanglements of a devoted heart, which seeks to express its emotions through art.

The Chancellor has announced a £1.8bn package to help households with the cost of living, in his spring statement.

Rishi Sunak said the measures would help people "get through the next few months" of higher prices.

It includes a cut in the energy price cap, and £500m for households in council tax bands A to D.

The BBC's Laura Kuenssberg said the chancellor was "stepping up to help millions of households".

But shadow chancellor Rachel Reeves said help "should have been sooner" and accused Mr Sunak of "playing catch up".

Here are the key points from the statement:

What's happening to the energy price cap?
The energy price cap, which limits the amount suppliers can charge customers, will be cut in April by £200 per year.

It means around 28 million households will pay less for their gas and electricity.

Earlier this month, supporting measures were announced, including a £150 council tax rebate for most homes in England and a £200 discount on energy bills owed by households who get financial help with their council tax.

Why are people getting money off their council tax?
Mr Sunak said £500m would be available to help those in council tax bands A to D.

He said around 80% of households would receive a £150 council tax rebate. But those in bands A to D - typically the least valuable properties - would receive a minimum £350 payment.

The rebate will be paid directly into bank accounts from April, the chancellor said.

How much is the help worth in total?
The chancellor said the support package would be worth £1.8bn.

On top of the help with council tax, Mr Sunak said the Energy Price Guarantee would be extended, so that all households would pay no more than £2,500 a year for their energy bills.

Without the help, forecasts showed average household energy bills could have been as much as £3,500 from October.

Why did the chancellor make the announcement?
Mr Sunak said the announcement was designed to help people "get through the next few months".

He said: "We have a responsibility to help those who are paying the highest price for global inflation."

What else did he say?
The chancellor said the government would also make a one-off payment of £1bn to help people with business rates and council tax.

Sweet Stay-at-Home, sweet Well-content,
Thou knowest of no strange continent;
Thou hast not felt thy bosom keep
A gentle motion with the deep;
Thou hast not sailed in Indian seas,
Where scent comes forth in every breeze.
Thou hast not seen the rich grape grow
For miles, as far as eyes can go:
Thou hast not seen a summer's night
When maids could sew by a worm's light;
Nor the North Sea in spring send out
Bright hues that like birds flit about
In solid cages of white ice --
Sweet Stay-at-Home, sweet Love-one-place,
Thou hast not seen black fingers pick
White cotton when the bloom is thick,
Nor heard black throats in harmony;
Nor hast thou sat on stones that lie
Flat on the earth, that once did rise
To hide proud kings from common eyes.
Thou hast not seen plains full of bloom
Where green things had such little room
They pleased the eye like fairer flowers --
Sweet Stay-at-Home, all these long hours.
Sweet Well-content, sweet Love-one-place,
Sweet, simple maid, bless thy dear face;
For thou hast made more homely stuff
Nurture thy gentle self enough;
I love thee for a heart that's kind --
Not for the knowledge in thy mind.

> Adversarial patches are small patches that can be attached to physical objects to fool image classifiers. In this paper, we propose a new type of adversarial patch, called an IPatch, that can be used to fool image classifiers remotely. An IPatch is a small patch that can be attached to a physical object to fool image classifiers when the object is viewed from a distance. We show that IPatches can be used to fool image classifiers in a variety of settings, including when the object is viewed from a distance, when the object is viewed through a camera, and when the object is viewed through a camera with a zoom lens. We also show that IPatches can be used to fool image classifiers in a variety of domains, including face recognition, object recognition, and scene recognition.

We introduce a method that allows to automatically segment images into
semantically meaningful regions without human supervision. Derived regions are
consistent across different images and coincide with human-defined semantic
classes on some datasets. In cases where semantic regions might be hard for
human to define and consistently label, our method is still able to find
meaningful and consistent semantic classes. In our work, we use pretrained
StyleGAN2~\cite{karras2020analyzing} generative model: clustering in the
feature space of the generative model allows to discover semantic classes. Once
classes are discovered, a synthetic dataset with generated images and
corresponding segmentation masks can be created. After that a segmentation
model is trained on the synthetic dataset and is able to generalize to real
images. Additionally, by using CLIP~\cite{radford2021learning} we are able to
use prompts defined in a natural language to discover some desired semantic
classes. We test our method on publicly available datasets and show
state-of-the-art results.

Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs) are widely applied in medical image segmentation and 3D navigation for robot-assisted minimally invasive surgeries (MISs). Nevertheless, existing DCNNs typically employ downsampling layers to expand the receptive field and extract abstract semantic information. These downsampling operations reduce the spatial dimensions of feature maps, potentially compromising image segmentation performance. An alternative approach is atrous convolution, which enhances the receptive field without altering the spatial dimensions of feature maps. This paper introduces a novel method for determining the optimal atrous rates to maximize the receptive field while minimizing the number of atrous convolutional layers. Additionally, a new high-resolution DCNN—Atrous Convolutional Neural Network (ACNN)—is proposed, incorporating cascaded atrous II-blocks, residual learning, and instance normalization (IN). Experimental results on MRI and CT image segmentation show that the proposed ACNN achieves superior intersection over union (IoU) metrics compared to U-Net and Deeplabv3+ but requires fewer trainable parameters.

US Open champion Svetlana Kuznetsova has tested positive for a banned drug, according to Belgian authorities.
Belgian sports minister Claude Eerdekens said that the Russian world number five tested positive for the stimulant ephedrine on 19 December. Kuznetsova was playing in an exhibition event in Charleroi at the time. Eerdekens said: "There is a problem. Ephedrine was discovered. She remains innocent until proved guilty. She can ask for it to be tested again." The situation remains unclear as the tournament was not commissioned by the World Anti-Doping Agency (Wada), the International Tennis Federation (ITF) or the Women's Tennis Accosiation (WTA). The test was carried out by regional Belgian authorities and Kuznetsova has not yet been able to have a B sample tested.
Speaking at the Australian Open on Monday, before Eerdekens identified her, Kuznetsova said: "I'm not worried. I'm not using anything to push myself. "I have not been notified of any positive test, and I think it is unfair that it's come out the way it did." Eerdekens said that confirmation of the findings was sent last Friday to the player's address in Spain, as well as to the Belgian prosecutors' office and the Belgian and Russian tennis federations. He conceded Kuznetsova might have taken a medicine which contained the banned substance. "We have simply stated a fact," he said. "It is for the federation concerned to impose the disciplinary measures after a procedure that respects the defence.
"Either the ephedrine was taken to improve her performance or it is because she took some medicine legitimately to cure an infection." However, Kuznetsova's naming was condemned by Russian tennis chief Shamil Tarpishchev. "First of all, this Belgian sports minister has broken every ethical rule in the book by naming a player without any proof of wrongdoing, without any basic evidence," Tarpishchev said. "We all know the basic principle in doping cases. If there is a positive sample, then they should notify the International Tennis Federation (ITF) as well as the national federation within three days," he said. "This is not the case here. As of today we have not received any statement from the doping officials, nor did the ITF. "Today I called the ITF headquarters and they told me they know nothing about it. "If WADA (the World Anti-Doping Agency) was behind the testing, then we would also have known something by now. "Otherwise, all these looks to me as pure fiction and fabrication of the facts."

Ingredients:
- 8 ounces of pasta (fettuccine, penne, or your choice)
- 1 tablespoon olive oil
- 1/2 pound Italian sausage, casings removed
- 1 onion, chopped
- 2 cloves garlic, minced
- 8 ounces mushrooms, sliced
- 1/2 cup black olives, pitted and halved
- 1/2 cup white wine (optional)
- 1 cup tomato sauce
- 1/2 cup heavy cream
- Salt and pepper to taste
- Fresh parsley, chopped (for garnish)

Instructions:
1. Cook the pasta according to package instructions. Drain and set aside.
2. In a large skillet, heat the olive oil over medium heat. Add the Italian sausage and cook until browned, breaking it up into smaller pieces with a wooden spoon.
3. Add the chopped onion to the skillet and cook until translucent. Then, add the minced garlic and cook for an additional minute, until fragrant.
4. Add the sliced mushrooms and cook until they are soft and release their moisture, about 5-7 minutes.
5. If using white wine, pour it into the skillet and let it simmer until it has reduced by half.
6. Stir in the tomato sauce and black olives, and season with salt and pepper to taste. Let the sauce simmer for about 10 minutes to allow the flavors to meld together.
7. Reduce the heat to low and stir in the heavy cream. Let the sauce heat through, but be careful not to let it boil.
8. Add the drained pasta to the skillet and toss it with the sauce until it is well coated.
9. Divide the pasta amongst serving plates and garnish with fresh parsley.
10. Serve hot and enjoy your delicious Pasta Alla Boscaiola!

One whole chicken (approximately 5 1/2 pounds), 8 medium cloves of garlic crushed, 3 medium onions halved, 2 lemons halved, 1 1/2 pounds of assorted fingerling potatoes, 1/4 cup of assorted chopped herbs (such as rosemary, thyme, parsley, or sage), olive oil, kosher salt, and freshly ground black pepper. Preheat oven to 425°F. Rinse chicken thoroughly, pat dry, remove giblets, and discard or save them. Trim excess fat from the chicken's cavity if needed. Place halved onions in the center of a 9x13-inch Pyrex dish, serving as a base for the chicken. Position the chicken on top of the onions. Squeeze halved lemons over the chicken's body and legs, then place the lemons inside the cavity. Add crushed garlic to the cavity as well and secure the chicken legs with kitchen twine. Season the chicken generously with salt and cracked black pepper. Wash the fingerling potatoes, slice the largest ones in half lengthwise, and toss them with olive oil, half of the chopped herbs, and season with salt and pepper. Place the potatoes around the chicken in the roasting dish. Bake until the temperature measured in the thickest part of the breast reaches 150°F and the thighs reach at least 165°F, which takes about an hour. Remove the chicken from the oven and let it rest for 15 minutes. Remove the potatoes, toss them with the remaining chopped herbs, and carve the chicken before serving.

Let me start off by saying that I was introduced to the films of Terrence Malick in 1998 when I watched and was blown away by 'The Thin Red Line.' It is one of the best war movies ever made and while I can rant about it at length, that review belongs on a different page. It was with great anticipation that I waited for 'The New World.' I was lucky enough to get tickets to an advance screening and the theatre was full of people like me. Their take on the film was almost as interesting as the film was.

'The New World' is a film that will draw out one of two very powerful emotions: Love or Hate. I really don't believe there is a middle ground in this case. I think it is quite possibly the most beautifully photographed film I have ever seen. It is astonishing. The score from James Horner is, in my opinion, his greatest work. He's a wonderful composer but he has exceeded himself on every level. This is a movie that can be watched like art (because it is) and listened to as a symphony (it might as well be one). Very few movies leave me stunned and 'The New World' is so luscious that I think it is worth the journey, even if it is only to look at how beautiful it is and listen to how glorious it is. Is that a superficial way of looking at things? Perhaps, but they are the film's two most brilliant qualities.

'The New World' does have problems and I think it falls very much into a 'buyer beware' category. Malick's movie is long -- very long -- and feels every moment of it. I don't mind these things because I found it enchanting; many in the audience with me did not. These are not people who are 'dumb,' or who 'don't get it.' They are people who are used to 99% of the films that you will see. 'The New World' is very self-indulgent at times. No one can reasonably defend the pace of the film. I want to and I can't. This is a movie so full of substance that it is detrimental. It is so rich and textured that it would be hard to say where things could have been improved, but aside from the first forty minutes which deal largely with the question of whether or not the Europeans can survive the first winter or not, the dramatic 'action,' that is, the engine of a script that pushes one scene into the next, is idling at best. 'The New World' has a plodding pace and it took me on a nice quiet stroll that I enjoyed immensely. I can not, in good conscience though recommend to the man on the street that he go to see it. If less than a third of the theatre I was in walked out, I'd be stunned. I lost count because so many people left. Mostly the middle hour and a half of the film is to blame. Scenes drift from one to the next -- they're stunning and textured and personally I enjoyed them -- but they involved a lot of hanging out. Two people hanging out in the woods. I understand that the film has deep meditative and philosophical meanderings about man's relationship with nature and how one impacts the other. I get it. But a lot of the love story is about two people hanging out in the woods. All the time. If one of them had said 'Let us go watch the grass grow for the afternoon,' it would have been the most honest line in the entire film. It is the only thing I will fault Malick for here because it really does kill the film for a lot of people. His intelligence should not be questioned. I wish only he'd tried to focus the script a bit more and been specific rather than general. Can two people from different cultures be together? We get it already. We got it an hour ago. Oh, more grass growing ... must watch ... ha! Forgive my little joke.

The argument to be made though is that this film has not been made for everyone (the studio is no doubt surprised to learn this and will be scrambling to recover their money -- they did a good thing in making it but they're going to lose their shirts). It was made by Terrence Malick for Terrence Malick. I'm glad to have seen it but I spoke with twenty people who were not. There will be constant arguments on the user boards here at the IMDb. The film is going to have rabidly fanatical supporters who think everyone else is just too stupid to get it. And it is going to be criticized by many, many others who died a thousand deaths just trying to sift through the movie.

Two final thoughts: the first is that I hate myself for having to say anything negative about Malick or his film. He's a special film-maker and his films make it worth going to the theatre. 'The New World' is great but flawed and it is dishonest for anyone to pretend otherwise -- such behaviour is deceitful and pretentious.Thought number two is that although the film is equal parts challenging and rewarding (as great movies should be) it is especially important in the case of 'The New World' to see it in the theatre. It is so majestic in scope that I don't believe the greatest home theatre can do it justice. It is truly epic in its cinematography and score. If it doesn't win Oscars for both we will have witnessed a massive artistic injustice. NOTHING this year, NOTHING has come close to being a threat to 'The New World' for either of those two categories. Appreciate them as they were intended to be seen.

Spaghetti with Pan Fried Chicken and Cherry Tomato Puree
 
Serve up a quick and easy pasta dish that's perfect for kids and adults alike with this pan-fried chicken and cherry tomato puree recipe. Both the chicken and the tomato puree can be prepared well in advance, making this a great choice for busy families.

Ingredients 
300g cherry tomatoes, halved
1 garlic clove, chopped
1 tbsp olive oil
1 tsp red wine vinegar
6oz spaghetti
1 small chicken breast, cut into strips
1 tbsp plain flour
1 egg, beaten
30g breadcrumbs
30g grated parmesan
1 tbsp olive oil
freshly ground black pepper

Method
1. To make the tomato puree, place the tomatoes in a small pan with the garlic, olive oil and red wine vinegar. Bring to the boil then reduce the heat and simmer for 5 minutes, until the tomatoes are soft.
2. Season with pepper, then blend until smooth. Pour into a bowl and wipe the pan clean.
3. Bring a pan of water to the boil and cook the spaghetti according to the packet instructions.
4. Meanwhile, prepare the chicken. Place the flour, egg and breadcrumbs in three separate bowls. Dip the chicken strips first in the flour, then the egg (allowing any excess to drip off) and then the breadcrumbs.
5. Heat the oil in the wiped-out pan and fry the chicken strips for 2-3 minutes on each side until golden-brown and completely cooked through.
6. Drain the spaghetti and either stir into the tomato puree or serve with the tomato puree poured over. Serve with the chicken strips and a grating of parmesan.

The Polyglot Petition for Home Protection was the first world-wide proclamation against the manufacturing and international trade in liquor and drugs as well as the prohibition of legalised vice. It served as a first major campaign to raise public awareness of the need for international agreements on controls for opium and its derivatives. Description of the petition
Addressed to all rulers and nations of the world, this petition to adopt prohibition was written by the American Woman's Christian Temperance Union (WCTU) president Frances Willard in 1884. It was carried across the world by at least four World WCTU missionaries who gathered signatures of nearly eight million people in more than fifty countries. The signatures can be categorized in three basic sections: signatures of individual women, written endorsements of men, and attestations of leaders of groups that had endorsed the petition. The signed petitions from the U.S. (over 750,000) were sent to Mrs. Rebecca C. Shuman in Evanston, Illinois who trimmed and mounted them on white muslin, one-half yard in width and bound with red ribbon on one side and blue ribbon on the other. Signed petitions from Great Britain (350,000 signatories) came in already mounted on cloth in time for presentation to the U.S. president in February 1885. The Polyglot Petition is archived in the Woman's Christian Temperance Union Administration Building in Evanston, Illinois, United States of America.

Local communities would be required to vote for their own area police commissioner, according to plans introduced by the Conservative Party. The party leader, Michael Howard, stated that the new position would replace less prominent police authorities. He emphasized that the new role would not take over the duties of a chief constable. The Liberal Democrats expressed concern that such plans might enable extremist groups to influence policing, while Labour criticized the Conservatives' proposals as excessive regarding police matters. 

In response, the head of the Police Federation of England and Wales, representing frontline officers, stressed the importance of maintaining operational autonomy. Jan Berry remarked, "This should be a service, not a political football, and it shouldn't be manipulated each time an election comes around." She warned that these plans could allow individuals with extreme political views to dictate actual policing actions. 

Howard outlined his crime agenda, stating that elected police commissioners would be more accountable than current police authorities composed of local councils and magistrates. He noted that commissioners would possess the same powers as existing authorities. However, he acknowledged that few people know who the members of these authorities are. Howard claimed the current system does not provide the local accountability he seeks and that elected commissioners would be more visible.

Critics raised concerns that the initiative could transfer control of the police to single-issue candidates who may disregard broader community needs. Lord Harris, who heads the Association of Police Authorities, pointed out that the plans suggested chief constables should be directed by a single individual, effectively reversing nearly two centuries of policing organization to prevent the politicization of policing decisions.

In the dim and wet confines of the alley,  
lay a Christmas tree that had never been sold;  
a shopkeeper, gloomy and unmoved,  
stood outside, watching the passing crowd;  
the tree, trampled by the feet of many,  
was buried in mud and silt,  
unfit even for a hearth's embrace...  
Thus I retrieved this rusted tree,  
and in doing so, I heard its tale:  
"Mother was queen of the woodland glade,  
and I thrived beneath her boughs, proud and glad;  
she promised, when she died,  
that I would succeed her, ruling for a century,  
a tower of glory among my peers,  
when I fell in battle, you would rise and take my place."  
So I grew in grace, like a joyous child,  
in the heart of the woods, unbound and free;  
moss and ferns carpeted the ground,  
while tiny creatures scurried through the air;  
a dove perched upon my tallest branch,  
and a squirrel chirped, "How tall! How tall!"  
A timid doe nibbled a tender leaf,  
and a rabbit gnawed beneath my roots...  
I was content in rain and sun,  
thinking of the path that lay before me!  
Then a man with an ax approached,  
and I knew my fate was to fall and die.  
He bundled me with hundreds,  
driving us to a gleaming city of light,  
an avenue lined with Christmas trees,  
where I longed to be one of them,  
tinsel-dressed, glittering with color,  
a spectacle for children to admire;  
shimmering with lights of every shade,  
ruby, emerald, orange, and blue,  
and children dancing, laughing with delight...  
Yet I was so homesick I wished to weep,  
but patient I waited for someone to purchase.  
Some said, "Too big," "Too small,"  
others gave no reply at all.  
Then a young boy cried, "Mom, buy this!"

George Galloway is set to run against Labour's pro-Iraq War MP Oona King in the upcoming general election. Galloway, who received £150,000 in libel damages from the Daily Telegraph, announced he will contest Bethnal Green, London, for Respect. The Glasgow Kelvin MP, expelled from Labour for his opposition to the Iraq War, criticized Ms. King as a "New Labour stooge." Ms. King expressed delight at the opportunity to challenge Galloway.

Galloway's current parliamentary district is set to be redrawn in Scotland. At 50, the MP founded Respect, the Unity Coalition, alongside 1,000 anti-war activists and the Muslim Association of Britain. The party's objectives include ending the Iraqi occupation, repealing anti-union laws, and abolishing privatization. Speaking from a café in Brick Lane, Galloway stated he honored the party's invitation to join forces with "great pride."

He remarked: "In this constituency of Bethnal Green and Bow, there is a New Labour stooge MP. A stooge who will sing any song, deliver any speech, perform any dance, comply with any instruction from Tony Blair—regardless of how her constituents are harmed or how strongly they disagree." Ms. King, who has represented the area since 1997, said: "I am pleased to have the chance to finish him off and believe I will. Many people across the country, including those in Scotland, will be grateful, especially his constituents in Scotland whom he has abandoned."

In June's European Parliament elections, Respect did not secure enough votes for an MEP but came first in Tower Hamlets, much of which falls within the Bethnal Green and Bow parliamentary constituency. A month later, the party secured a council seat in a by-election in St Dunstan's and Stepney Green wards in Tower Hamlets. Galloway indicated that in the coming general election and subsequent local elections, the party would "turn."

Jolanda Ceplak has urged Britain's Kelly Holmes to continue competing at the major championships.
Double Olympic gold medallist Holmes has strongly hinted she will not run in this year's Worlds and is undecided about next month's European Indoors. But World Indoor 800m record holder Ceplak said: "There is never an easy race when she is in the field. There is only excitement at what might happen. "It is good for the sport. She always fetches the best out of everyone." Ceplak has been a great rival of Holmes' during the Briton's career and the pair fell out when Holmes questioned the manner of the Slovenian's runaway 800m victory at the 2002 European Championships. But the controversy has since been forgotten, with Ceplak acting as pacemaker for Holmes' failed attempt on the British Indoor 1500m record at the Norwich Union Grand Prix in Birmingham in 2003.
Ceplak added: "I like running against her - you know the race is always going to be fast. "That is the sort of competition that I like. She is special to me. She was like my idol from the beginning of my career." Meanwhile, Ceplak will be looking to follow up last Saturday's win in Boston with a fast time and victory in Friday's Night of Athletics in Erfurt, Germany. Britain's Jason Gardener had been expected to defend his 60m title in Erfurt but instead he will save himself for a competition in Leipzig on Sunday. Gardener's decision means Scotland's 400m man Ian Mackie will carry British hopes in what looks sure to be a tough preparation for next weekend's Norwich Union European trials in Sheffield.

I have watched this film three times and still find it exceptional, though it isn't suitable for everyone. It's no surprise that even Martin Scorsese spent over two decades trying to secure funding for it.  

I can also see why some people find the film unengaging and lengthy, despite my own lack of boredom or excessive duration. In truth, it is precisely perfect.  

The reason many people don't fully appreciate this film—especially considering Scorsese's extensive body of work—is due to its thematic content. Indeed, in an era of widespread secularism and materialistic thinking, a film like this must inevitably feel outdated.  

At its core, the film explores the authentic spiritual journey of overcoming hidden narcissism and embracing pure, selfless love. It thus presents a true pathway of genuine Christianity.  

What makes this film unique, in my view, is its ability to vividly depict this transformation and connect it to the historical period of Christian missionary youth. The Japanese, although cruel, are far more thoughtful and wise than the Portuguese missionaries who often fail to recognize their cultural arrogance when interacting with them.  

To fully convey these ideas and let the story reach its climax required nearly three hours of outstanding filmmaking.  

For those familiar with the real path of self-transcendence into humble love, this is undoubtedly a masterpiece. For others, it may simply be a tedious experience.  

Fans of this film might also enjoy watching "The Assassin" by Hsiao-hsien Hou, which delves into the Taoist version of the same inner journey.
